question_text: A child presents with a history of foreign body ingestion. The X-ray picture is given in the image. What is the possible site of foreign body impaction?
explanation: The esophagus is the most common site for an acute foreign body or food impaction in the gastrointestinal tract, and 80 to 90% of swallowed objects that reach the stomach will eventually pass without intervention. While a wide variety of objects could be ingested, common accidental esophageal foreign body ingestions include food bolus (mostly meat), fish or chicken bones, dentures, and coins. The most common symptoms are foreign body sensation or difficulty swallowing (dysphagia). Symptoms typically develop in minutes to hours. Foreign bodies in the upper esophagus are more accurately localized by the patient. However, impactions in the mid or lower esophagus may be described as a vague discomfort, ache, or chest pain. Routine x-rays are usually the first step if a radioopaque object is suspected. This will help determine the object, the location, and possible complications. Chest x-ray (posterior-anterior (PA) and lateral views) is usually adequate, but the neck and abdominal x-rays may be needed depending on clinical presentation. Flat objects like coins, bottle caps, or disc batteries are usually oriented in the coronal plane if they are lodged in the esophagus and appear round on the frontal (PA) view.

question_text: A child has swallowed a foreign body. What is the nature of foreign body as per X-Ray
explanation: Disc batteries are smooth and shiny, they are attractive to the children category. Therefore, ingestion of disc batteries is becoming a more frequent encounter. Complications of disc battery ingestion are many, ranging from dysphagia to more severe outcomes like esophageal and tracheoesophageal fistula. Most complications can be minimized by early detection and intervention. Esophagoscopy revealed circumferential burn at the site of the disc battery with moderate to severe inflammatory changes in the mucosa.

question_text: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complain of inability to open the mouth completely. He was a pan masala addict. Examination of the oral cavity revealed the following findings as shown in the figure given below. Which of the following statement is false regarding this condition?
option_a: Weekly sub mucosal intralesional injections of steroids with hyaluronidase is used
option_b: The sub mucosal tissue is replaced by stiff fibrous tissue as it heals.
option_c: White lacy striae called Wickham's striae are seen in oral cavity.
option_d: It is a pre malignant condition
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation and the picture, the diagnosis in this case isoral sub mucous fibrosis.
  • It is a condition characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the sub mucosal tissue (lamina propria and deeper connective tissue) inside the mouth.
  • It is due to chronic exposure ofarecolinepresent in betel nuts.
  • It is a well recognized pre-malignant condition. (Option D)
  • Clinical features:
    • The lesion appears as white fibrotic bands extending from the retromolar trigone to the soft palate, buccal mucosa, tongue and pharynx.
    • It is often associated with trismus, ankyloglossia and restriction of soft palate movements and dysphagia.
    • The patients initially often complain of difficulty in chewing and oral pain/burning sensation in the oral cavity especially on consuming spicy food.
    • There is a progressive inability to open the mouth. The buccal cavity becomesblanched and stiff. (Option B)
  • Treatment if detected in early stages then cessation of betel nuts will be sufficient.
    • Weekly sub mucosal intralesional injections (Inj. Hyalase) can be used. (Option A)
    • Antioxidants may be of help in preventing dysplastic
    • Nutritional supplementation like multivitamins may be tried.
    • Surgical management includes releasing of the fibrous bands and repairing it with buccal fat pad.
  • TheWhite lacy striaecalledWickham's striaeare seen inoral lichenand not in OSMF. (Option C)

Key Takeaway:

Oral Submucous Fibrosis

  • Inflammation & Fibrosis of submucosal tissue due to chronic arecoline exposure
  • Premalignant
  • Initially Managed with Steroid & Hyaluronidase Injection. Later with Surgical Release.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presented with complain of dysphagia to solids since 1 month. She is able to take semi solids and liquids. On blood investigation it was found that her haemoglobin was 6 gm%. Barium swallow was done picture given below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical features and picture, the diagnosis is Patterson brown Kelly syndrome.
  • Patterson brown Kelly syndromeis also known asPlummer Vinson syndrome.It is characterized by triad of post cricoid dysphagia, upper esophageal webs and iron deficiency anaemia.
  • Clinical featuresseen in 40 to 50 year female
    • Dysphagia first develops towards solids than to semi solids and liquids.
    • Choking spells and aspiration occurs.
    • Weakness, fatigue, and koilonychia may be seen.
  • 5 to 10 percentchance of developing post cricoid carcinoma.
  • Diagnosis:Barium swallow shows upper oesophageal webs, biopsy shows epithelial atrophy, blood investigation shows iron deficiency anaemia.
  • TreatmentRigid esophagoscopy and dilatation of the web. Treatment of underlying anemia.

Key Takeaway:

Plummer Vinson syndrome / Patterson brown Kelly syndrome

  • triad of dysphagia, upper esophageal webs and iron deficiency anemia.
  • 5-10 % Patient Post Cricoid Carcinoma
  • Managed with Rigid Endoscopy and Dilatation.

question_text: A 3 year old child while playing with toys suddenly developed swallowing difficulty and is excessively crying. The parents rushed the child to emergency where the X- ray Chest was conducted. The X Ray image is shown in the given picture. What is the best management of this patinet?
explanation:
INDICATIONS Diagnostic

  1. To investigate cause for dysphagia, e.g. cancer oesophagus, cardiac achalasia, strictures, oesophagitis, diverticulae, etc.
  2. To find cause for retrosternal burning, g. reflux oesophagitis or hiatus hernia.
  3. To find cause for haematemesis, g. oesophageal varices.
  4. Secondaries neck with unknown primary (as a part of panendoscopy).

Therapeutic

  1. Removal of a foreign body.
  2. Dilatation in case of oesophageal strictures or cardiac achalasia.
  3. Endoscopic removal of benign lesions, g. fibroma, papilloma, cysts, etc.
  4. Insertion of Souttar's or Mousseau-Barbin tube in palliative treatment of oesophageal carcinoma.
  5. Injection of oesophageal varices.

CONTRAINDICATIONS

  1. Trismus-makes the procedure technically
  2. Disease of cervical spine, e.g. cervical trauma, spondylosis, tuberculous spine, osteophytes and kyphosis. They make rigid oesophagoscopy technically difficult. Flexible fibreoptic oesophagoscopy is performed in these cases.
  3. Receding mandible.
  4. Aneurysm of aorta for fear of rupture and fatal haemorrhage.
  5. Advanced heart, liver or kidney disease may be a relative contraindication.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.501

question_text: 43 year old female presents to ENT OPD with episodes of vertigo without any hearing loss. The physician first does a diagnostic maneovure and later a therapeutic maneovure. Identify the manoeuvre given in image
explanation:
BPPV (BENIGN PAROXYSMAL POSITIONAL VERTIGO)

BPPV is the most common cause of peripheral vertigo. This disease is more common in females.

  • Cause—Otoconia gets displaced and reaches the semicircular canal.

The most commonly involved canal is Posterior SCC

  • Chief complaint- vertigo for few seconds on changing head position. Vertigo is with nausea and vomiting. There is no hearing loss or Tinnitus in this condition.
  • Diagnostic test of BPPV- DIX HALLPIKE’S MANEUVER. This test shows nystagmus (rotational and geotropic) on putting the patient on supine position from sitting position.
  • Treatment of BPPV- EPLEY’S MANEUVER (particle repositioning maneuver)- It is the treatment of choice.



Steps of EPLEYS MANEUVER-

  1. Make the patient sit down.
  2. Turn the head 45° to the affected side.
  3. Make the Patient lie down with head hanging off the table
  4. Rotate the head 90° to the other side.
  5. Rotate the body along with the head 90° on the same side.
  6. Make the patient sit down.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page - 52.

question_text:
A 28-year-old male patient had developed a head injury due to a road accident. He developed a sudden onset of complete facial palsy. His CT scan showed a fracture of the right temporal bone.

Which of the following is the best intervention in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Temporal bone fractures are of two types based on their axis in reference to the long axis of the petrous part of the temporal bone.

They are:

Longitudinal

Transverse

Longitudinal fractures are more common, injury to the tympanic membrane is more common, facial nerve injury is about 20%, vertigo is usually absent, and CSF otorrhoea is common.

Transverse fractures are less common; injury to the tympanic membrane is not present, facial nerve injury is common, vertigo is severe, and CSF otorrhoea is not present.

The investigation of choice for petrous part of temporal bone is HRCT temporal bone.

Management in case of sudden onset and complete palsy, which is seen in most cases, early exploration and decompression of the facial nerve or nerve repair should be carried out immediately.

Delayed onset palsy, which might be because of surrounding oedema, should be treated with systemic steroids and watchful waiting. (Options B, C, D).

question_text: A 35-year-old female patient underwent parotid surgery. Following the surgery, she developed a complaint of sweating over the cheeks on the operated side when she chews food. What is the most likely reason for this complaint?
option_a: Aberrant reinnervation of parasympathetic fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve with sympathetic sweat glands.
option_b: Aberrant reinnervation of parasympathetic fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve with the greater superficial petrosal nerve.
option_c: Abnormal cross-innervation of the facial nerve with the greater auricular nerve.
option_d: Abnormal cross-innervation of the facial nerve with the auriculotemporal nerve.
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical scenario provided, the likely diagnosis is Frey's syndrome.

Frey syndrome, also known as gustatory sweating. When the patient chews food, they develop sweating over the cheek skin over the parotid gland.

Frey syndrome occurs because of injury and aberrant reinnervation of parasympathetic fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve with sympathetic sweat gland fibres.

Treatment involves the injection of botulinum toxin, administered periodically.

question_text: A 7 year old boy was hit by a cricket ball. He has developed diplopia and periorbital swelling. Which wall of the orbit has been fractured?
explanation:

  • Other signs include supratarsal hollowing, hooding of the eye, narrowing of the palpebral fissure width and an infraorbital nerve deficit.
  • A small fracture of the orbital floor can lead to a trap door phenomenon.
  • If the orbital fat or inferior oblique muscle becomes trapped in the fracture configuration, then interference with muscular function results in diplopia on upward gaze

question_text:

explanation:
Explanation:

The patient in this case is suffering from Facial palsy. The test shown in the figure given above is called the Schirmer test.

The test is done to evaluate the site of facial nerve injury.

The first branch of the facial nerve is the Greater petrosal nerve. It arises from the geniculate ganglion and goes to the sphenopalatine ganglion and gives secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands.

Damage to the nerve leads to decreased secretion, resulting in dry eye, which can be assessed using the Schirmer test with Whatman filter paper.

The test results are significant if:

  • 75% unilateral decrease in lacrimation
  • A bilateral decrease in lacrimation (less than 10 mm wetted for both sides at 5 minutes)

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma buccal mucosa with involvement of mandible underwent wide local excision, Hemi mandibulectomy and Type 1 Modified radical neck dissection. Which of of the following structures are preserved in type 1 Modified radical neck dissection?

option_c: Preserves spinal accessory nerve and internal jugular vein
option_d: Preserves spinal accessory and sternocleidomastoid muscle
explanation:
Explanation:

Radical neck dissection (RND): 

  • it involves removal of level 1 to 5 cervical lymph nodes.
  • It also includes removal of all the three structures spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Modified radical neck dissection (MRND):

  • It includes removal of level 1 to 5 cervical lymph nodes but one, two or all three nonlymphatic structures are preserved.
  • It was introduced to reduce the morbidity created in radical neck dissection.
  • They are of 3 types:

Selective neck dissection (SND):

  • It involves preservation of all three: spinal accessory nerve and internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid muscle.
  • Over and above that, it also preserves one or more group of lymph nodes.

Extended Radical Neck dissection (ERND):

  • Removal of one or more additional lymphatic and/or non-lymphatic structures relative to a radical neck dissection.
  • Example: level VII, retropharyngeal lymph nodes, hypoglossal nerve.

Key Takeaway:

MRND Types: Preserve NVM

  1. Preserve XI Nerve
  2. Preserve XI Nerve & IJV
  3. Preserve XI Nerve, IJV & SCM

question_text:
A 10-day-old neonate underwent a neonatal universal hearing screening programme. Transient OAE was performed twice and was absent both times. A follow-up test was performed, as shown in the image below.

option_d: If Wave 1 is delayed but the inter-peak latency of 1 to 5 is normal, then it shows a defect in the cochlea or the middle ear.
explanation:
Explanation:

The test demonstrated in the image is brainstem evoked response audiometry (BERA). It is a non-invasive, objective test often used after the absence of Transient OAE to confirm auditory pathway pathologies.

It consists of 7 waves:

  • Wave 1 represents the distal part of the cochlear nerve.
  • Wave 2 represents the proximal part of the cochlear nerve
  • Wave 3 represents the cochlear nerve
  • Wave 4 represents the superior olivary complex
  • Wave 5 represents the lateral lemniscus (Option B)

question_text: What is the interpretation of the following PTA conducted on a patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The audiogram demonstrates a Mixed Hearing Loss.

This is characterized by elevated Air Conduction (AC) thresholds (indicating a hearing deficit) and elevated Bone Conduction (BC) thresholds (indicating an inner ear or neural component).

Critically, there is a significant Air-Bone Gap (>15 dB), meaning the AC thresholds are significantly worse than the BC thresholds. This gap confirms the presence of a conductive component superimposed on the sensorineural loss.

Explanation of other options:

Sensorineural hearing loss (Option B): It would show elevated AC and BC thresholds that are equal (no air-bone gap).

Conductive hearing loss (Option C): It would show elevated AC thresholds with normal BC thresholds.

Normal (Option D): Both AC and BC thresholds would be within the normal range (≤20 dB).

Key Takeaways:

Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA)

  • Purpose: Assesses hearing thresholds across different sound frequencies.
  • Method: Both air conduction (AC) and bone conduction (BC) are tested using pure tones generated by an audiometer.
  • Recording: Results are plotted on a graph known as an audiogram.
  • Nature of Test: Subjective-depends on patient responses to detect the faintest audible tones.
  • Interpretation:
    • The air-bone gap (A-B gap) reflects the extent of conductive hearing loss.

question_text: Name the audiological investigation in which this type of ear probe is used.

These echoes are called OTOACOUSTIC EMISSION.

OAE is of 3 types Depending on the number of sound stimuli used:

  • O stimulus – it is called spontaneous OAE. (SOAE)
  • 1 stimulus – it is called Transient evoked OAE (TEOAE)
  • 2 stimuli it is called Distortion product OAE (DPOAE).

TEOAE are most commonly used in practice

Glomus is the most common benign tumour of the middle ear. It can be located at the jugular bulb, known as glomus jugulare, or it can be located in the middle ear tympanicum.

It arises from para ganglion cells, non-hormone-secreting cells (non-chromaffin) (Option A).

Management includes pre op embolisation and surgical excision or stereotactic radiosurgery.

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma buccal mucosa underwent wide local excision. The reconstruction of the defect created after surgery was done using a local flap. Picture Is given below. This flap receives blood supply from which of the following vessels?

question_text: What is the name of the sign shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Frontal sinus fracture can lead to CSF leak which presents as rhinorrhea. To confirm the presence of CSF in a bloody nasal discharge after trauma, this test can be done. When the discharge is dropped on absorbent material, the CSF diffuses faster and further than blood, forming a clear outer ring (halo) around a central reddish bloodstain, indicating a potential CSF leak. It is a non specific sign.

Explanation of Other Options:

Beta-2 transferrin (Option A)

This is a biochemical test, not a visual sign. It's the most specific lab test for confirming CSF in nasal or ear discharge, but it is not what's shown visually.

Tear Drop sign (Option B)

The "teardrop sign" on imaging indicates herniation of orbital contents (fat or inferior rectus muscle) into the maxillary sinus following an inferior orbital wall fracture. This herniated tissue, pinched by the fracture, characteristically resembles a teardrop shape.

Handkerchief sign (Option D)

This refers to the clear, watery nature of CSF rhinorrhea versus mucoid nasal secretions. CSF will not stiffen a cloth handkerchief when it dries, unlike mucus. It's a different clinical observation.

Key Takeaway:

The halo sign is a bedside test that indicates the possible presence of CSF in nasal discharge, especially after head trauma. It is suggestive but not confirmatory and should prompt further testing (e.g., beta-2 transferrin assay).

question_text: A50 year old diabetic male patient was admitted with a diagnosis of covid-19, Based on positive RT-PCR. Due to severe lung involvement he was treated with methylprednisolone. question_text: A 50-year-old male patient presented with complain of nasal obstruction and nasal discharge. On examination, a granulation tissue was seen in the nasal cavity and the tip of nose. question_text: Which of the following conditions is associated with Hollman Miller's sign as shown in the CT below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Holman-Miller Sign is a classic finding of Angiofibroma. It refers to anterior bowing/displacement of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (or pterygopalatine fossa widening) due to the locally invasive nature of the angiofibroma arising from the nasopharynx.

Explanation of Other Options:

Maxillary Sinusitis (Option A)

Not associated with the Holman Miller sign. It typically shows mucosal thickening, fluid levels, or opacification within the sinus without bone erosion or displacement of the posterior maxillary wall.

Nasal Polyp (Option C)

Not associated with the Holman Miller sign. It usually appears as soft tissue density filling the nasal cavity/sinuses, often leading to bone remodeling/erosion of the uncinate process (in antrochoanal polyps) but not the characteristic posterior maxillary wall bowing.

Rhinosporidiosis (Option D)

Presents as lobulated, friable, reddish masses with "strawberry-like" appearance (due to sporangia) on endoscopy, and soft tissue masses on CT. It does not cause anterior bowing of the posterior wall of maxillary sinus.

Key Takeaways:

The Holman-Miller sign refers to the anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall and is a highly suggestive CT finding for Juvenile Angiofibroma. This sign indicates the tumor's origin in the nasopharynx and its locally invasive, expansile growth into adjacent spaces.

question_text: Which of the following is the topical use of the medicine shown in the image
explanation:
The drug shown in the image is Mitomycin C, and it is used topically for the treatment of subglottic stenosis. Subglottic stenosis is a condition where the airway just below the vocal cords becomes narrow, leading to breathing difficulties. Mitomycin C is applied topically during endoscopic procedures to help prevent the recurrence of scar tissue formation and reduce the narrowing of the airway in cases of subglottic stenosis. It is also used to prevent synchiae formation after nasal surgeries.

Other options:

B. Inlay type 1 myringoplasty: Mitomycin C is not used topically for myringoplasty procedures. Myringoplasty is a surgical technique to repair a perforated eardrum.

C. Post adenoidectomy to control bleeding: Mitomycin C is not commonly used topically for controlling bleeding post-adenoidectomy. Hemostatic techniques and packing are more commonly used for this purpose.

D. Rhino-cerebral mucormycosis: While Mitomycin C is an antifungal agent, it is not typically used topically for the treatment of rhino-cerebral mucormycosis. Systemic antifungal medications are the primary treatment for this severe fungal infection.

question_text: A 50-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma lower lip. Picture given below. He was undertaken for wide local excision with neck dissection. explanation:
Explanation:

  • Abbe flap is based on the main artery of the orbicularis Oris, the Labial artery. A portion of uninvolved lip is rotated across the mouth and placed into the surgical defect of the involved lip.

question_text: A 45-year-old female patient presented with midline neck swelling since 4 months. USG local part is suggestive of nodule in the left lobe of thyroid gland. Hemi thyroidectomy was done in this patient. Postoperative histopathology report was suggestive of cells with salt and pepper chromatin arranged in sheets, nests or trabeculae in an organoid fashion. Cells were positive of calcitonin, CEA, chromogranin, and synaptophysin. Histopathology picture is given below. What is the type of thyroid neoplasm is seen here?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Medullary carcinomathyroid is a malignant tumour showingC cell differentiation.
  • It constitutes 5 to 10 % of all thyroid malignancy.
  • Histologically it shows cells withsalt and pepperchromatin arranged in sheets, nests or trabeculae in an organoid fashion.
  • Necrotic is infrequent. C cell hyperplasia can be seen in surrounding thyroid tissue adjacent to the invasive tumour.
  • Cells arepositive for calcitonin , chromagranin,CEA, synaptophysin.
  • Amyloid deposits are also seen.

Papillarycarcinoma (Option A): shows cells arranged in monolayer papillae with characteristic nuclear features such asorphan Annie nuclei. It shows metaplasia squamous cytoplasm.

Follicular carcinoma (Option B): showscells arranged in follicles,solid or trabecular fashion. They lack the typical nuclear features.

Anaplastic carcinoma (Option D): have pleomorphic large cells with high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio.

Key Takeaway:

Medullary thyroid Carcinoma:

  • Salt & Pepper Chromatin & Amyloid Deposits
  • Synaptophysin & Chromogranin Positive.

question_text: Which of the anatomical site is marked with arrow in the given image?
explanation: The piriform fossa, also known as the pyriform sinus, is a pear-shaped recess on either side of the laryngeal inlet, and is part of the hypopharynx. It's located posterolaterally to either side of the laryngeal opening, and is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold, and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. This sinus is a common place for food particles to become trapped; if foreign material becomes lodged in the piriform fossa of an infant, it may be retrieved nonsurgically. If the area is injured (e.g., by a fish bone), it can give the sensation of food stuck in the subject's throat.

question_text: What radiological sign is identifiable in the provided X-ray image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given X-ray images (AP and lateral views) show a radiopaque foreign body in the upper oesophagus, with a characteristic double ring appearance. This finding is highly suggestive of an ingested button battery, a medical emergency requiring urgent removal.

  • The double ring sign is due to the two concentric metal components of the button battery:
    • Outer metal casing
    • Inner insulating ring
  • The lateral view helps distinguish between a coin (homogeneous opacity) and a button battery (double ring appearance).

Radiology of foreign bodies in trachea/ oesophagus:

Coin in the oesophagus is identified by a circular-shaped opacity seen on AP view and appears slit-like on lateral view.

Coin in trachea: Slit-like on AP view and Circular opacity on lateral view.

Button battery:

  • It can get dislodged in the oesophagus following accidental ingestion.
  • Peripheral double contour ring (or) Halo sign seen on X-ray distinguishes button battery from a coin in the oesophagus.

Explanation for other options:

Steeple Sign (Option A): is it refers to the subglottic narrowing seen in croup on an AP neck X-ray.

String Sign (Option B): is it refers to the narrowing of the terminal ileum in Crohn's disease, seen in contrast studies.

Thumb Sign (Option C): is it refers to swelling of the epiglottis in epiglottitis, giving the appearance of a "thumb" on lateral neck X-ray.

Reference:

  1. Oesophagal foreign body - coin | Radiology Case | Radiopaedia.org

question_text: Steeple sign on X-ray neck AP view is seen in?
explanation:
The "steeple sign" on an X-ray of the neck (AP view) is indicative of acute laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as croup. Croup is characterized by inflammation of the upper airway, specifically the larynx and trachea, leading to narrowing of the subglottic region and causing the characteristic steeple-like appearance on X-ray.

Other options:

A. Acute epiglottitis: Acute epiglottitis causes inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis, which leads to a "thumbprint sign" on X-ray, not the steeple sign.

C. Laryngomalacia: Laryngomalacia is a congenital condition where the soft tissues of the larynx collapse during inspiration, causing a characteristic "omega-shaped" epiglottis on X-ray, not the steeple sign.

D. Laryngeal web: A laryngeal web is a congenital condition where there is a membrane or web-like structure across the larynx, which may cause respiratory difficulty, but it does not result in the steeple sign on X-ray.

question_text: Considering the findings on the given chest X-ray, which procedure is likely to be the most technically difficult to carry out?
explanation:
Explanation:

The provided chest X-ray suggests fibrotic lung changes with possible tracheal deviation, which can occur due to conditions like pulmonary fibrosis, previous infections, or malignancy. Tracheal deviation makes performing a tracheostomy more difficult because:

  1. Anatomical displacement of the trachea - the deviation can make localization and access to the trachea challenging.
  2. Increased risk of complications - damage to surrounding structures like major blood vessels or the esophagus is more likely in a distorted anatomy.
  3. Difficult airway management - patients with fibrotic lung disease may have decreased lung compliance, requiring careful ventilatory support.

Tracheostomy:

  • Is making an opening in the anterior wall of the trachea and converting it into a stoma on the skin surface.
  • Types:

Explanation for other options:

Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA) insertion (Option B): is incorrect because LMA is a supraglottic airway device that does not require tracheal access.

Ryle's Tube (RT) insertion (Option C): is incorrect because nasogastric tube placement is unrelated to tracheal deviation and is usually not affected.

Indirect Laryngoscopy (Option D): is incorrect because it primarily involves visualization of the vocal cords and is not significantly impacted by lower airway pathology.

question_text: A 70-year-old male who had been chewing tobacco for past 50 years, presents with a 6 months history of fungating soft papillary lesion in the oral cavity picture given below lymph nodes are not palpable. Biopsy from the lesion shows benign appearing papilloma with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. Most likely diagnosis is ?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Verrucous carcinoma is alow-grade SCCthat appears as a cauliflower-like exophytic tumor.
  • There arethree formsof verrucous carcinomas; all of them are recognized in areas of maceration.
  • Verrucous carcinoma of the oral cavity, known asoral floridpapillomatosis,involves large areas of oral mucosa in elderly male tobacco chewers.
  • Verrucous carcinoma of the anogenital region, calledgiant cell condyloma of Buschke Löwenstein, occurs on the glans penis of young uncircumcised males and on the perianal region in both sexes.
  • Plantar verrucous carcinoma, also calledepithelioma cuniculatum, usually involves the skin underlying the first metatarsal head, making numerous deep crypts filled with horny material and pus, and ultimately penetrates the plantar fascia.
  • Managementis surgical excision with an appropriate margin of healthy tissue.

Key Takeaway:

Verrucous Carcinoma : low grade SCC

  • Giant cell condyloma
  • Papilloma with hyperkeratosis
  • Mx with Surgical Excision.

question_text: A 40-year-old female patient known case of papillary carcinoma thyroid was advised radioiodine ablation after total thyroidectomy. All of the following statements about preparation of patient for radioiodine ablation are true except?
option_a: Normal dose of 131 I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is 100 to 140mCi
option_b: Patient is weaned off from iodine containing drugs and iodinated contrast procedures before ablation
option_c: It is mandatory to stop tablet thyroxine prior to imaging or therapy
option_d: Amount of residual thyroid calculation is ideally performed using thyroid uptake probe
explanation:
Explanation:

The following are necessary to be done beforeradioiodine ablation or scan.

  1. Patient is weaned off form iodine containing drugs like cough suppressant and iodine contrast based imaging. (Option B)
  2. Food stuff such as sea foods and iodinated salts should be avoided for 3 to 4 weeks.
  3. It is mandatory tostop tablet thyroxineso that serum thyroid level is elevated to more than 30 micro IU /ml. (Option C)
  4. Amount of residual thyroid is calculated usingthyroid uptake probeat 4, 6 and 24 hours after 20 micro curie 131 I application. (Option D)
  5. Normal dosage of 131I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is in the range of30 to 70 mCi. ( Option A )
  6. Following ablation patient is put on suppressive doses of tablet thyroxine. A post therapy whole body scintigraphy is performed 5 to 7 days after ablation.

Selection of patient for radio iodine ablation:

  1. Patient with I 131 concentrating in distant metastasis.
  2. Patient with multicentric, multifocal, and microscopic differentiated thyroid malignancy.
  3. All patients with follicular, papillary and mixed carcinoma of more than 1.5 cm in size with or without capsular invasion.
  4. Patient with residual thyroid disease in which revision surgery is not possible.

Who should not be ablated:

  1. Patient withlow risk factorsincluding papillary carcinoma with tumor size 1 to 1.5 cm with no capsular invasion or distant metastasis.
  2. Patient withmedullary carcinomabecause they are based on parafollicular C cells which can't concentrate radioiodine. Hence, they are treated with 131 I labelled meta iodo benzyl guanidine (MIBG).

Key takeaway:

Normal dosage of 131I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is in the range of30 to 70 mCi.

question_text: Given below is the X-ray image of a child with a history of ingestion of a coin. What is the most likely site of dislodgement of the foreign body
explanation:
Explanation:

In the given lateral neck X-ray, the coin is seen on its edge, indicating an oesophageal location.

  • In suspected foreign body ingestion, posteroanterior and lateral views of neck and similar views of the chest including abdomen are taken.
  • Xrays reveals most of the radio-opaque foreign bodies.
  • Foreign bodies of the oesophagus lie in the coronal plane in PA view and edge on in the lateral view. It is just the reverse in tracheal foreign bodies because of orientation of vocal cords.
  • Radiolucent foreign bodies may show as an air bubble in cervical oesophagus in X-ray soft tissue lateral view of neck.
  • A disc battery may elude as it may cast a double shadow or stacked coin appearance.
  • Most of the foreign bodies in oesophagus can be removed by oesophagoscopy under general anaesthesia.

Fig: Foreign body food passage.(A) PA view showing a coin.(B) Lateral view of the same.

Explanation of other options:

Larynx (Option A): The typical presentation in a laryngeal foreign body is choking while eating. On x-ray, it may show airway narrowing or obstruction.

Fig: Soft tissue lateral view neck showing a fruit seed in the subglottic region of larynx (arrow). Note: The patient needed tracheostomy (black arrow) to relieve obstruction.

Trachea (Option B): A coin or a flat foreign body in trachea lies edge on in PA view and flat on lateral view. A key sign of a tracheal foreign body can be an audible slap and palpatory thud. A large foreign body may totally obstruct the airway leading to sudden death unless resuscitative measures are taken urgently.

Bronchus (Option D): Bronchial foreign bodies are more common on the right side than the left. In cases of suspected bronchial foreign body, chest X-ray PA view may show segmental or lobar collapse, hyperinflation or even a normal X-ray. A normal x-ray will not rule out the presence of a foreign body.

question_text: A 25-year-old male patient who was in the ICU was intubated for 10 days. Tracheostomy was performed on him, and the image is given below. At what level is the tracheostomy tube inserted?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The procedure shown in the above picture is called
  • It is a procedure in which an opening is made on the anterior wall of the Trachea. It can be planned or an emergency.
  • This procedure is done in the Rose position. After the skin incision, the strap muscles and pre-tracheal fascia are separated.
  • Finally, a vertical incision is made in the midline on the 2nd and 3rdTracheal rings. This is described as mid-tracheostomy. Mid tracheostomy is done in most cases. (Option B)
  • When the incision is made on the 1st Tracheal ringit is called high tracheostomy. High tracheostomy is done for carcinoma of larynx (Option A)
  • If it is made below 4thring, it is called low tracheostomy. Low tracheostomy is done in laryngeal stenosis. (Option C & D)

Key Takeaway:

In Majority Cases Mid tracheostomy is performed which is done at 2nd & 3rd tracheal rings.

question_text: A 40-year-old female came with a complaint of vertigo for 7 days. An examination was performed in which the patient was asked to keep looking at the examiner's finger while her head was moved briskly and abruptly. It was found that her eyes lagged and showed saccades at the end of head movements. What is this suggestive of?
option_a: Injury to SCC and vestibulo-cerebellar tract
option_b: Injury to SCC and vestibulo-spinal tract
option_c: Injury to SCC and vestibulo-ocular tract
option_d: Injury to the organ of Corti and the auditory pathway
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the description given above, the test performed on the patient is called the Head Impulse Test.

Head movements required during the head-impulse test to investigate the horizontal canals (top, a-c) and the vertical canals (bottom, d-f)

The head impulse test examines the vestibulo-ocular reflex. The VOR helps stabilise gaze on the object during different head movements, so that the image remains centred on the fovea of the retina.

The patient is asked to keep looking at an object while his head is moved briskly and abruptly.

  • In a normal patient or in a head-impulse-negative patient, the eyes move in the opposite direction at the same speed as the head movement and will remain fixed on the target.
  • In the absence of VOR or in a Head impulse positive test, the eyes will lag, and there will be jerky catch-up movement called saccades at the end to catch up to the target.

question_text: A 70-year-old elderly male presents with a history of dysphagia since 1 month. Dysphagia is associated halitosis, regurgitation of food, and coughing. Barium swallow was done in this patient, picture is given below. All of the following is true about this condition except?
option_a: It arises from posterior wall of hypopharynx.
option_c: It should be managed by excision
option_d: It arises due to traction from outside the esophagus.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The picture of Barium swallow shown above is suggestive ofZenker's diverticulum.
  • Diverticulum is an outpouching from a tubular structure. It forms when there is neuromuscular incoordination while swallowing.
  • In hypopharynx, the most common site of its formation is theKillian dehiscence,which lies between thethyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus, parts of inferior constrictive muscle.
  • It arises from posterior wall hence it is also calledposterior pouch. (Option A)
  • It is apulsing diverticulumas it occurs due to increase in intraluminal pressure. (Option D)
  • A true diverticulum contains all the layers of wall, but zenker's diverticulum contains only mucosa hence it isa false diverticulum. (Option B)
  • Main management of zenker's diverticulum isexcision of pouch, Endoscopic stapling diverticulotomy. (Option C)
    • Excision of pouch:The pouch is excised and crico pharyngeal myotomy is done to relax the cricoid pharyngeal sphincter.
    • Endoscopic stapling of the diverticulotomy:This is presently preferred mode of therapy. The surgery aims at converting the cricopharyngeal and pouch cavity into one single cavity to avoid collection of food.
    • This is achieved by cutting the cricopharyngeal bar. Historically it was first done byHe used diathermy to achieve this.

Key Takeaway :

Zenker Diverticulum isPulsing False diverticulumcaused due to increased intraluminal pressure in the Posterior wall of hypopharynx. Managed with excision & Endoscopic stapling diverticulotomy.

question_text: A patient with maxillary cancer underwent the surgical procedure as shown in the image below. Identify the type of maxillectomy performed.
explanation:
Explanation:

Since the surgical image in question shows removal of the entire maxilla along with the orbital floor, this matches the description of a total maxillectomy.

  • Total maxillectomy involves the removal of the entire maxilla along with the orbital floor, especially when the tumor invades the bony orbital floor but not the orbital contents.
  • The procedure builds on subtotal maxillectomy, which already removes the entire maxilla, by including resection of the orbital floor for wider tumor clearance.
  • In total maxillectomy, the orbital rim is removed en bloc with the maxilla, and reconstruction of the orbital floor is essential to preserve both cosmesis and function.

Explanation of Other Options:

Medial maxillectomy (Option B) is a more limited resection involving only the medial wall of the maxilla.

Subtotal maxillectomy (Option C) removes the entire maxilla but not the orbital floor.

Infrastructure maxillectomy (Option D) includes the removal of the hard palate, alveolar ridge, and dentition but preserves the orbital floor.

question_text: A 2-year-old was brought to the emergency department with difficulty swallowing for the last few hours. The X-ray is given below. Which is the next best step to manage this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray reveals a radiopaque foreign body within the esophagus, which is a frequent occurrence in children. Esophagoscopy is the investigation of choice as it allows both confirmation of the diagnosis and safe removal of the object.

  • A key diagnostic clue is that on an anteroposterior (AP) X-ray, coins in the esophagusappear with their flat surface visible, whereas in the trachea, the edge is seen in the AP view.

Bronchoscopy (Option A): Not indicated since the foreign body is located in the esophagus, not the airway.

Tracheostomy (Option C): Unnecessary because there is no airway obstruction.

Heimlich maneuver (Option D): Reserved for airway foreign bodies causing choking, not esophageal obstructions.

question_text: Which of the following structures are forming boundaries of MacEwen's Triangle?
option_d: External acoustic meatus, Supramastoid crest & Zygomatic arch
explanation:
Explanation:

McEwen's Triangle (Suprameatal Triangle):

A small depression located posterosuperior to the external acoustic meatus. In adults, the lateral wall of the mastoid antrum corresponds to the suprameatal triangle (MacEwen's triangle) on the outer surface of the skull. This is palpable through the cymba conchae

  • Boundaries:
    • Above: Defined by the supramastoid crest.(Option A)
    • In front: Bounded by the posterosuperior marginof the external acoustic meatus.(Option A)
    • Behind: Marked by a vertical tangentto the posterior margin of the meatus.

  • The superior side of the triangle, the supramastoid crest, is level with the floor of the middle cranial fossa;
  • The anteroinferior side, which forms the posterosuperior margin of the external acoustic meatus, indicates approximately the position of the descending part of the facial nerve canal;
  • And the posterior side, formed by a posterior vertical tangent to the posterior margin of the external acoustic meatus, is anterior to the sigmoid sinus.

Key Takeaway:

McEwen's triangle (suprameatal triangle) is defined by the supramastoid crest above, the posterosuperior margin of the external acoustic meatus in front, and a vertical tangent behind, crucial for understanding the anatomy surrounding the tympanic and mastoid regions.

It is a large, air-containing space in the upper part of the mastoid and communicates with the attic through the aditus. question_text: A 35-year-old male presents with a three-day history of severe headache, fever, and nausea. He also reports pain and swelling behind the left ear, along with blood-tinged ear discharge. On examination, there is tenderness and bluish discolouration over the mastoid process of the left temporal bone. CT imaging reveals an empty delta sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient most likely has lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis, a known complication of otitis media or mastoiditis. The empty delta sign observed on CT imaging is a characteristic indicator of lateral sinus thrombosis.

Lateral sinus thrombosis (Sigmoid sinus thrombosis)

An inflammation of the inner wall of the lateral venous sinus with formation of an intrasinus thrombus, often secondary to otitis media or mastoiditis.

Clinical features

  • Fever: Hectic "picket-fence" type with rigors
  • Headache: Early mild, later severe due to venous obstruction
  • Griesinger's sign:
    • Mastoid tenderness and swelling with bluish discolouration.
    • This is due to blockage of Mastoid emissary veins which are also drained in the sigmoid sinus
  • In lateral sinus thrombosis, compression of the internal jugular vein (IJV) on the affected side does not change CSF pressure due to obstruction of venous outflow.
    • Tobey-Ayer Test: Assesses this phenomenon via lumbar puncture, measuring CSF pressure changes when the IJV is compressed.
    • Crowe-Beck Test: Observed on fundus (retina) examination, where compression of the jugular vein on the healthy side causes retinal vein engorgement, while compression on the thrombosed side shows no change.
  • Papilledema: Depends on venous obstruction
  • Tenderness along jugular vein if thrombosis extends

Investigations:

  • CECT/MRI brain: Empty delta sign (triangular area of central hypodensity with rim enhancement)
  • MR venography: Assess extent and progression
  • X-ray mastoids: Clouding of air cells or bone destruction

Treatment

  • Involves performing a modified radical mastoidectomy (MRM), exposing the lateral sinus and removing the thrombus carefully until fresh, healthy bleeding is seen, confirming that the sinus lumen is cleared.

Explanation of other options:

Meningitis (Option A): Although meningitis can cause headache, fever, and nausea, it does not present with an empty delta sign or the mastoid swelling seen in lateral sinus thrombosis.

Brain Abscess (Option C): A brain abscess typically presents with neurological deficits or altered consciousness and would not show an empty delta sign on CT imaging.

Extradural Abscess (Option D): While an extradural abscess can cause localized pain and swelling, it does not produce an empty delta sign or the characteristic spread of infection seen in lateral sinus thrombosis.

question_text: Which of the following is the most commonly injured nerve after parotid surgery?
explanation:
Explanation :

  • The facial nerve is the most commonly injured in parotid surgery as it traverses perpendicularly through the parotid gland. land.
  • The cervical branch of the facial nerve is usually involved leading to Bell's palsy.
  • Following parotid surgery auriculotemporal nerve and the greater auricular nerve can also be injured, but less frequently than the facial nerve. (Option B, D ruled out)

Iatrogenic injury to facial nerve

  • The most common cause of facial nerve injury is parotid surgery, followed by mastoid surgery.
  • During mastoid surgery, the site most frequently injured is the second genu of the facial nerve, followed by the vertical segment.
  • Management options include surgical exploration with end-to-end anastomosis and facial nerve grafting
  • Commonly used graft sources include:
    • Greater auricular nerve
    • Sural nerve (preferred for long grafts).

Explanation of other options:

Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C): Glossopharyngeal nerve lies deep in the neck and is not related anatomically to the parotid gland. Injury to the nerve causes loss of taste in the posterior one-third of the tongue and loss of the gag reflex.

question_text: The figure is showing the structure of chochlear canal. Identify the marked cavity.
explanation:
Explanation:

There are three longitudinal channels within the cochlea.

  • Scala vestibuli (1): Located above the vestibular membrane (Reisnners membrane), continuous with the vestibule at the base of the cochlea.
  • Scala media (2): Also known as the cochlear duct, located between the basilar and vestibular membranes, contains endolymph.
  • Scala tympani (3): Located below the basilar membrane, opens into the middle ear via the round window.

Key Takeaways:

  • The cochlear canal comprises three distinct parts: scala vestibuli, scala media, and scala tympani, essential for auditory function.
  • Understanding these structures aids in grasping the mechanics of sound transmission and hearing processes.

question_text: Ductus Reuniens connects which two structures of inner ear?
explanation:
Cochlear Duct: Also called membranous cochlea or the scala media. It is a blind coiled tube.

It appears triangular on cross-section and its three walls are formed by:

  1. the basilar membrane, which supports the organ of Corti;
  2. the Reissner's membrane, which separates it from the scala vestibule; and
  3. the stria vascularis, which contains vascular epithelium and is concerned with secretion of endolymph.

Cochlear duct is connected to the saccule by ductus reuniens.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9th edition, Pg.no.12

question_text: What is Cupula in inner ear?
option_a: Sensory end organ of Utricle and saccule
option_b: Sensory end organ of semicircular canals
explanation:
Cupula is the gelatinous layer around Crista (the sensory end organ of Semicircular canals). Cristae are concerned with angular acceleration.

Macula is the sensory end organ of utricle and saccule. It has otoconia or otoliths which are calcium carbonate crystals in the gelatinous layer of macula. They are concerned with the function of linear balance.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page - 20

question_text:
Mark the correct statement/ statements regarding inner and outer hair cells:
I. Inner hair cells are in single row and transit auditory impulses
II. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate function of inner hair cells
III. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of tectorial membrane
IV. Inner hair cells are in single row and transmit auditory impulses
V. Outer and inner hair cells present in ratio of 3:1
option_a: I, II and V are correct
option_b: I, II and III are correct
option_d: II, IV and V are correct
explanation: The tectorial membrane is connected to stereocilia of outer hair cells and participate in mechano transduction.

question_text:
Mark the correct statement(s) regarding Inner and Outer hair cells:
Inner hair cells are in a single row and transmit auditory impulses.II. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate the function of inner hair cells.III. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of the tectorial membrane. IV. Outer and inner hair cells are present in the ratio of 3:1.
option_a: I, II and IV are correct
option_b: I, II and III are correct
explanation:
Explanation:

  1. Inner hair cells (IHCs): IHCs are single row cells responsible for transmitting auditory impulses to the brain via afferent fibers.
  2. Outer hair cells (OHCs): OHCs are arranged in 3-4 rows and modulate the function of inner hair cells via efferent pathways, amplifying cochlear sensitivity.
  3. Outer hair cells and tectorial membrane movement: OHCs do not primarily move the tectorial membrane. Their role is mainly cochlear amplification; tectorial membrane motion is a passive mechanical response. (Statement 3 is incorrect)
  4. Ratio of Outer: Inner hair cells: OHCs (~12,000) outnumber IHCs (~3,500), approximately a 3:1 ratio.

question_text: Which of the following structures is responsible for balance and hearing?
explanation:
Explanation:

The vestibule is a part of the inner ear which is responsible for both hearing and balance.

  • Vestibule contains the utricle and saccule, each with a sensory epithelium called the macula.
  • The utricle detects horizontal linear acceleration, while the saccule detects vertical linear acceleration.
  • These structures help the brain maintain static balance and posture.

Explanation of other options:

Semicircular canal (Option A): The semicircular canals are responsible for maintaining balance; have no role in hearing.

Cochlea (Option B), Organ of Corti (Option D): The cochlea is the main organ of hearing, containing the sense organ called Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane.

question_text: As per the travelling wave theory of hearing given by Von Bekesy, sound energy creates a wave-like movement in which structure of the inner ear?
explanation:
Travelling wave theory of hearing has been given by Von Bekesy which states that - A sound wave depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude on a particular place in the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment.

Therefore, higher frequencies are sensed in the basal turn and low frequencies are sensed in the apex of cochlea.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number- 20.

question_text: A patient with presbycusis has been found to have high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry. Which of the following parts of the inner ear is affected in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

High-frequency sounds are perceived at the basal turn of the cochlea and if damaged, can cause the high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in presbycusis.

  • A sound wave, depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude on at particular place on the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment (travelling wave theory of von Bekesy).
  • Higher frequencies are represented in the basal turn of the cochlea and the progressively lower ones towards the apex. (Option A ruled out)

Presbycusis

  • Presbycusis is the sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological ageing process in the ear.
  • Manifests usually at the age of 65 years.

Explanation of other options:

Utricle (Option C), Saccule (Option D): The utricle and saccule are vestibular (otolithic) organs containing the macula. The macula acula acts as a sensory organ which detects linear balance: utricle for horizontal and saccule for vertical movements.

question_text: A patient of Presbycusis has been found to have high frequency sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry. Which of the following parts of the inner ear is affected in this patient?
explanation:
• Presbycusis is sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological aging process in the ear calling presbycusis.
  • It usually manifests at the age of 65 years but may do so early if there is hereditary predisposition, chronic noise exposure or generalized vascular disease.
  • Four pathological types of presbycusis have been identified. One of them is:
  • Sensory type. This is characterized by degeneration of the organ of Corti, starting at the basal coil and progressing gradually to the apex. Higher frequencies are affected but speech discrimination remains good.

KEY TAKE AWAY

question_text: A 5 year old boy while having dinner suddenly becomes aphonic and is brought to the casualty with the complaint of respiratory difficulty. What should be the appropriate management?
explanation:
Heimlich manoeuvre

Heimlich manoeuvre is sudden thrust directed upward and backwards below the epigastrium. It squeezes the residual air from lungs, which dislodges the foreign body. This manoeuvre should not be done if there is partial obstruction.

Cricothyroidotmy or emergency tracheostomy is done if Heimlich maneuver fails.

question_text: The Hallpike maneuver is used to assess which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Hallpike maneuver, also known as the Dix-Hallpike test, is primarily used to assess vestibular function.

Hallpike maneuver

  • The Hallpike manoeuver is the diagnostic test for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).
  • Diagnosis is made by provoking vertigo and nystagmus related to inner ear dysfunction.
  • During the test, the patient's head is rapidly positioned in a specific manner to assess the function of the posterior semicircular canal, which plays a key role in balance.
  • A positive test is indicated by a sudden burst of vertigo accompanied by nystagmus, confirming BPPV.
  • This maneuver is specifically designed for evaluating vestibular disorders and is not used to assess hearing or corneal reflexes.

Explanation of other options:

Audiometry (Option B), Cochlear function (Option C): Audiometry and cochlear function evaluates hearing, not balance or vestibular function.

Corneal test (Option D): The corneal reflex assesses sensory and motor pathways for blinking, which is unrelated to vestibular or auditory function

question_text: A 30 year old male is having Attic cholesteatoma of left ear with lateral sinus thrombophlebitis. Which of the following will be the operation of choice?
explanation:
The main treatment of Cholesteatoma is surgery → MRM.

Treatment :

Surgery is called MRM (Modified Radical Mastoidectomy) also called as TYMPANOMASTOID EXPLORATION.

Main aim of MRM is to make ear safe.

After making adequate clearance of cholesteatoma, we remove the posterior wall of EAC to open the mastoid cavity into EAC.

Hence, MRM is a classical example of canal wall down surgery (CWD).

Canal wall means posterior wall of EAC and down means removed.

Most common site of residual cholesteatoma after mastoid surgery is SINUS TYMPANI.

MEATOPLASTY :

This surgical step is aimed at widening the EAC. It is done by removing the part of Conchal cartilage.

Uses

  • Adequate ventilation of mastoid cavities.
  • Proper inspection & cleaning of mastoid cavities.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Cholesteatoma and Chronic Otitis Media, Page number: 87

question_text:
A 40-year-old male patient presents with foul-smelling ear discharge. Discharge was scanty in nature; the patient also experienced vertigo intermittently. HRCT of the temporal bone was done, which is suggestive of cholesteatoma in epitympanum and mesotympanum with erosion of the incus. On endoscopy, the tympanic membrane appeared as shown in the picture below.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_a: Topical antibiotics and decongestant for 4 weeks
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shown above suggests an attic retraction pocket with cholesteatoma flakes, suggestive of Cholesteatomatous CSOM (AKA Unsafe CSOM or Atticoantral disease).

Cholesteatoma is the presence of keratinising stratified squamous epithelium in any part of the temporal bone where it is usually not present. E.g. middle ear, mastoid, petrous Apex.

In its basal layer, cholesteatoma expresses enzymes such as collagenase and acid phosphatase, which cause bony erosion, helping the middle ear infection spread to surrounding areas and leading to various complications.

Patient presents here with scant, painless and foul-smelling discharge because of otitis and bone erosion by cholesteatoma and infection with anaerobic organisms.

The main management of such CSOM is mastoid exploration with removal of disease from the mastoid, followed by removal of disease from the middle ear.

The discharge is mainly due to bone erosion; hence, medical management with local and systemic antibiotics has little effect on the discharge's drying (Option A).

Myringoplasty alone is not sufficient in eradicating the disease from the middle ear and mastoid cavity (Option C).

Radical mastoidectomy is indicated in extensive cholesteatoma following unsafe csom with dead ear (Option D).

question_text: A patient having foul smelling ear discharge and cholesteatoma in the middle ear presents with facial nerve palsy, treatment of choice is:
explanation:
The main treatment of Cholesteatoma is surgery → MRM.

Treatment :

Surgery is called MRM (Modified Radical Mastoidectomy) also called as TYMPANOMASTOID EXPLORATION.

Main aim of MRM is to make ear safe.

After making adequate clearance of cholesteatoma, we remove the posterior wall of EAC to open the mastoid cavity into EAC.

Hence, MRM is a classical example of canal wall down surgery (CWD).

Canal wall means posterior wall of EAC and down means removed.

Most common site of residual cholesteatoma after mastoid surgery is SINUS TYMPANI.

This surgical step is aimed at widening the EAC. It is done by removing the part of Conchal cartilage.

question_text: The most common hidden site for residual cholesteatoma after the mastoid surgery in Atticoantral CSOM is
explanation:
One of the ways the surgical treatment of CSOM is done is Canal wall-up procedures. Here disease is removed by combined approach through the meatus and mastoid but retaining the posterior bony meatal wall intact, thereby avoiding an open mastoid cavity. It gives dry ears and permits easy reconstruction of the hearing mechanism. However, there is a danger of leaving some cholesteatoma behind. The incidence of residual or recurrent cholesteatoma in these cases is very high and therefore long-term follow-up is essential. Some surgeon’s even advise routine re-exploration in all cases after 6 months or so. Canal wall up procedures are advised only in selected cases. In a combined approach or intact canal wall mastoidectomy, disease is removed both permeatally, and through cortical mastoidectomy and posterior tympanotomy approach, in which a window is created between the mastoid and middle ear, through the facial recess, to reach sinus tympani

question_text:
A 7 year old male presents to emergency with a two day history of worsening ear pain and drainage. explanation:
Mastoid surface is found to be smooth, red and shiny. This is called the Ironing of the mastoid surface. It is the first sign of Mastoiditis.

MASTOIDITIS :

It is an infection of the mastoid air cells. It is a complication of ASOM and CSOM.

Chief complaint-

  1. Pain behind the pinna,
  2. Profuse ear discharge

On examination-

  • Mastoid surface is found to be smooth, red and shiny. This is called the Ironing of the mastoid surface. It is the first sign of Mastoiditis.

  • Mastoid Tenderness is positive.
  • RESERVOIR SIGN on cleaning, the pus fills immediately again, this is because pus is continously flowing from mastoid to middle ear this is called PULSATILE OTORRHOEA.
  • Light House sign is seen due to this pulsatile otorrhoea.

Investigation :

X ray mastoid right and left lateral oblique view. It is called Schuller's view. This is the most used x-ray view for mastoids in ENT.

This X-ray shows two findings.

  1. Clouding of air cells.
  2. Coalescence of air cells.

question_text: A 22-year-old male patient with a known case of CSOM attico-antral type develops Gradenigo syndrome. Which of the following symptoms will not be a part of Gradenigo syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gradenigo syndrome results from the spread of a middle ear infection into the petrous part of the temporal bone, leading to petrousitis.

It is the triad of:

  • Persistent Ear Discharge (Due to involvement of the petrous apex)
  • Diplopia (Due to VI nerve palsy)
  • Retrobulbar Pain (Due to irritation of the Trigeminal ganglion)

The air cells of the petrous part of the temporal bone communicate with the mastoid bone. Thus, infection in the mastoid region can transmit to the petrous bone, leading to persistent ear discharge.

The 6th cranial nerve runs in the Dorello's canal at the petrous Apex, and the 5th nerve lies in the Meckel's canal.

So, there is palsy of the VI nerve leading to diplopia. Involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve leads to retrobulbar pain.

The Facial nerve is not involved in petrositis; therefore, its palsy is not part of Gradenigo syndrome.

question_text: A 28-year-old male with a history of chronic ear discharge and hearing loss undergoes an otoscopic evaluation. The image below shows a large central perforation of the tympanic membrane with visible middle ear structures. What is the most appropriate surgical intervention for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has features of Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) – Tubotympanic type, evidenced by:

  • Chronic ear discharge
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Large central perforation of the tympanic membrane without cholesteatoma

The most appropriate surgical treatment is Tympanoplasty.

Tympanoplasty:

  • Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure aimed at repairing a perforated eardrum (tympanic membrane) and, in some cases, reconstructing the ossicles (the small bones in the middle ear) to restore hearing function. This surgery is commonly recommended when a perforation does not heal on its own, often due to chronic ear infections or trauma.
  • Anaesthesia: Typically performed under general anaesthesia
  • Surgical Approach: The surgeon may access the eardrum through the ear canal or make an incision behind or in front of the ear, depending on the location and size of the perforation.
  • Graft Material: A graft, often taken from the patient's tissue (such as fascia or cartilage), is used to patch the eardrum.
  • Additional Procedures: If the ossicles are damaged, procedures like ossiculoplasty (reconstruction of the ossicles) or mastoidectomy (removal of infected mastoid bone) may be performed concurrently.

The Wullstein classification categorizes the procedure based on the extent of the defect and the method of reconstruction.

Explanation of Other Options:

Atticotomy (Option A): Performed for attic cholesteatoma or retraction pockets in the pars flaccida. Not indicated in simple central perforation.

Modified radical mastoidectomy (Option B): Indicated in atticoantral disease (cholesteatoma type of CSOM) or unsafe ear. Not required in safe central perforation.

Myringoplasty (Option C): It only repairs the tympanic membrane without addressing ossicular continuity, making it inadequate in this case, where middle ear structures are exposed.

question_text: A patient with CSOM presented to the OPD with seizures, headache and complaints of nausea and vomiting. CT image of patient is given. Identify the clinical condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

CT shows a low-density lesion with a thin, smooth, and uniformly "ring-enhancing" peripheral rim in the temporal region. These findings combined with history of CSOM point towards Temporal Abscess.

Complications of Acute and Chronic Otitis Media:

  1. Extracranial:
    • Acute and chronic mastoiditis
    • Tympanic membrane perforation
    • Facial nerve palsy
    • Cholesteatoma (Chronic)
    • Subperiosteal abscess
    • Suppurative labyrinthitis
  2. Intracranial:
    • Meningitis
    • Brain abscess
    • Lateral/sigmoid sinus thrombosis
    • Otitic hydrocephalus (Pseudotumor cerebri)

Explanation of Other Options:

Extradural Abscess (Option B)

While extradural abscesses can also occur in CSOM, they typically present with less severe symptoms such as localized pain, tenderness, or a discharging sinus rather than seizures or marked raised intracranial pressure. CT would not show a focal abscess.Meningitis (Option C)

Meningitis presents with fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. Seizures can occur, but the CT scan would not show a focal abscess; instead, you might see meningeal enhancement or sometimes a normal scan. Also, meningitis is a diffuse condition, not localized like a temporal abscess.

Petrositis (Option D)

Petrositis, or inflammation of the petrous apex, presents with Gradenigo's syndrome- a triad of lateral rectus palsy (diplopia), ear discharge, and retro-orbital pain. It doesn't cause seizures or intracranial signs like a temporal abscess.

Key Takeaway:

A temporal lobe abscess is a serious intracranial complication of CSOM, often presenting with headache, seizures, and signs of raised intracranial pressure, and is typically confirmed on CT imaging as a ring-enhancing lesion in the temporal lobe.

question_text:
Which of the following is present in complicated Otitis media?
1. Bezold Abscess
2. Battle Sign
3. Delta Sign
4. Griesinger Sign
explanation:
A) Bezold Abscess: It can occur following acute coalescent mastoiditis when pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck. The abscess may

(i) lie deep to sternocleidomastoid, pushing the muscle outwards,

(ii) follow the posterior belly of digastric and present as a swelling between the tip of mastoid and angle of jaw,

(iii) be present in upper part of posterior triangle,

(iv) reach the parapharyngeal space

Bezold Abscess.

B) Battle's Sign: It can be related to otitis media. Battle's sign refers to bruising or discoloration behind the ear, specifically in the mastoid region. It is associated with basilar skull fractures, which can occur as a complication of severe otitis media or mastoiditis

C) Delta Sign: "Delta Sign" is commonly used in radiology to describe a characteristic radiographic finding in certain medical conditions, particularly in the context of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).

In the context of CVST, the "Delta Sign" refers to a triangular or delta-shaped filling defect within the dural venous sinuses, most commonly seen in the superior sagittal sinus. This sign is observed on contrast-enhanced imaging, such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and indicates the presence of a blood clot or thrombus within the sinus.

D) Griesinger's Sign: This is due to thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein. Oedema appears over the posterior part of the mastoid.

question_text: Identify the abscess.
explanation:
Explanation:

The abscess described is a zygomatic root abscess, a rare extracranial complication of acute otitis media. It occurs when a mastoid infection erodes the root of the zygomatic process, leading to swelling in the temporo-parietal region.

  • It is an extracranial complication of acute otitis media, though very rare.
  • First described by Friedrich Bezold, who reported the erosion of the zygomatic root due to mastoid abscess.
  • Clinically presents as swelling in the temporo-parietal or zygomatic region, often causing facial asymmetry.
  • The abscess forms secondary to mastoid infection that erodes the zygomatic process.
  • Radiographic imaging of the mastoid is helpful for diagnosis, especially to detect associated cholesteatoma.
  • Treatment: Typically involves modified radical mastoidectomy with drainage of the abscess to prevent further complications.
  • Importance: Early recognition is crucial, as misdiagnosis or delay in treatment can lead to serious morbidity.

Explanation of Other Options:

Citelli abscess (Option A): Occurs in the occipital region from mastoid infection.

Bezold abscess (Option B): Forms in the sternocleidomastoid region due to erosion of the mastoid tip.

Luc abscess (Option C): A subperiosteal temporal abscess without intraosseous involvement.

question_text: What is ideal choice of treatment for a patient with diphtheria and a right vocal fold palsy?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient with diphtheria and right vocal fold palsy, thyroplasty type 1 is the most appropriate treatment.

  • Thyroplasty type 1 is a surgical procedure used to improve vocal fold closure in cases of vocal fold paralysis.
  • This procedure involves the insertion of an implant to push the paralysed vocal fold towards the midline, improving voice quality and airway protection.
  • It is especially helpful in cases of vocal fold paralysis caused by infections like diphtheria, which can result in nerve damage affecting vocal fold movement.

Explanation of other options:

Wait and watch (Option A): Waiting and watching may be appropriate in some cases of vocal fold paralysis that resolve spontaneously over time. However, given that the patient has vocal fold palsy with potential functional impairment (speech and airway protection), active intervention such as thyroplasty is typically preferred to improve outcomes.

Gelfoam injection (Option B): Gelfoam injection is sometimes used in laryngeal procedures for temporary volume augmentation, but it is not the definitive treatment for vocal fold paralysis. It may not provide long-term results compared to thyroplasty.

Fat injection (Option D): Fat injection, similar to Gelfoam, is another method for increasing vocal fold bulk and improving closure, but it is less commonly used for permanent correction compared to thyroplasty. Fat injections can lead to resorption over time, reducing their long-term efficacy.

question_text: Ideal treatment for Reinke's Oedema
explanation:
Reinke's oedema is due to oedema of the subepithelial space of the vocal cord (Reinke's space).

TREATMENT-

  • Decortication of the vocal cord (removal of strip of epithelium is done on one side and 3 - 4weeks on the other).
  • Voice rest, speech therapy, cessation of smoking

question_text: What is the preferred treatment for a primipara who is experiencing hearing impairment that has worsened during her pregnancy? The Rinne's test yields negative results in both ears, while the Weber's test shows lateralization to the right side. The otoscopy reveals normal tympanic membranes, and audiometry indicates a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz.
explanation:
Explanation:
The clinical presentation is classic for otosclerosis, a condition where abnormal bone growth fixes the stapes footplate, causing conductive hearing loss. Key diagnostic clues include:

  • Negative Rinne test (bone conduction > air conduction) indicating conductive loss.
  • Weber test lateralizing to the worse-hearing (right) ear.
  • Carhart's notch (bone conduction dip at 2000 Hz) on audiometry.
  • Worsening during pregnancy due to hormonal influences.
    Stapedotomy is the preferred surgical treatment. It involves creating a small fenestration in the fixed stapes footplate and inserting a prosthesis, effectively bypassing the fixation and restoring sound transmission to the inner ear.

Explanation of other options:
Sodium fluoride (Option A) : This is a medical therapy used to potentially slow the progression of otosclerotic activity by promoting bone mineralization, but it is not a definitive treatment to restore hearing.
Tympanoplasty (Option B): This procedure repairs the tympanic membrane or ossicles in cases of chronic otitis media or trauma. It is not indicated for otosclerosis, where the tympanic membrane is normal.
Stapedectomy (Option C): While also a treatment for otosclerosis, the more modern stapedotomy technique is generally preferred as it is less invasive, has a lower risk of complications (e.g., sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo), and offers faster recovery.

Key Takeaways:

  • The classic triad for otosclerosis is :
    • conductive hearing loss
    • normal TM
    • Carhart's notch on audiometry.
  • Stapedotomy is the gold standard surgical treatment for otosclerosis.

question_text: A young lady presents to OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. On examination, Rinne's test and fistula test were found positive. However, she initially refused treatment and again presented with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. Further examination, revealed a negative fistula test. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient with otitis media, has developed labyrinthine fistula as a complication, which caused sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), tinnitus, and vertigo. This will result in a:
    • Positive Rinne's test
    • Positive fistula test: Due to perilymph leak or fistula
  • Since treatment was refused, the condition progressed, resulting in complete labyrinthine destruction or the dead ear. This caused a negative fistula sign.
  • However, the ear now has profound unilateral SNHL, where Rinne's test remains positive (a true positive result).

Rinne's Test:

  • The Rinne test compares bone conduction (BC) to air conduction (AC) of sound. In conductive hearing loss, BC > AC (i.e., the sound is heard better through bone conduction).
  • In sensorineural hearing loss, AC > BC (i.e., the sound is heard better through air conduction).

question_text: A 38-year-old male presents with suspected diagnosis of suppurative labyrinthitis. A positive Rinne test and a positive fistula sign were recorded on initial examination. What would be the expected finding on repeating the Rinne test?
explanation:
The patient was earlier having labyrinthine fistula. Because of no treatment, he developed dead labyrinth. A negative fistula sign in this case indicates a dead labyrinth which implies severe sensorineural hearing loss. In such cases a false negative Rinne's test is most likely.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with complaints of slowly progressive difficulty hearing in the right ear and pulsatile tinnitus. On examination, a reddish mass was seen behind the tympanic membrane, and an audible bruit was heard over the mastoid on auscultation. The Rinne's test was found negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The likely diagnosis in this scenario is a glomus tumor, a vascular middle ear lesion often causing conductive hearing loss reflected by a negative Rinne's test.

Glomus tumors

  • Also known as glomus jugulare tumors are skull based jugular foramen tumour.
  • These are vascular lesions that occur in the middle ear, often behind the tympanic membrane.
  • Tumours originate from the dome of the jugular bulb and can extend into the middle ear and surrounding structures.
  • More common in females.
  • The most common blood supply to this tumour is the ascending pharyngeal artery.

Clinical features and findings

  • Pulsatile tinnitus
  • Hearing loss
  • IX, X, XI CN involvement
  • Rising sun sign
    • The red vascular tumour behind the tympanic membrane gives the characteristic rising sun sign.
  • Bleeds on touching
  • Brown sign
    • Tumor blanches on siegelisation.
  • Aquino sign
    • Pulsatile mass in the ear, these Pulsations will disappear on pressing carotid arteries

Investigations

  • Biopsy is contraindicated.
  • CT scan
    • Shows Phelps sign: Erosion of bony septum between the carotid canal and Jugular foramen
  • MRI
    • Done to rule out intracranial extension.
    • MR Angiography helps to find out the main source of blood supply for the tumour.
  • Pre-operative embolisation will reduce blood loss during surgery.
  • Urinary VMA levels (24 hours)
  • Pune tone audiometry shows CHL
  • Histopathology
    • Show the Zell Ballen pattern, where epithelioid chief cells and sustentacular supporting cells form clusters (Zell Ballen) encircled by extensive vascular sinusoids.

Treatment

  • Treatment Of choice is surgery.
  • Alternative: Gamma knife therapy

If a similar tumor found to be arising from glomus cells lying around promontory (bulge on the medial of the middle ear). Then this tumor is called glomus tympanicum

Explanation of other options:

CSOM (Option A): CSOM is a chronic ear infection, often associated with purulent drainage and ear discomfort. While it can cause hearing loss, the presence of a reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane and pulsatile tinnitus would not be typical for CSOM, which typically presents with a history of recurrent ear infections and persistent drainage.

ASOM (Option B): ASOM is an acute ear infection, typically presenting with severe pain, fever, and sometimes a perforated tympanic membrane. It does not commonly cause pulsatile tinnitus or the specific signs seen in this case, such as the reddish mass and bruit.

Mastoiditis (Option C): Mastoiditis is an infection of the mastoid air cells, often resulting from a prolonged middle ear infection. It presents with fever, pain behind the ear, and swelling over the mastoid. The pulsatile tinnitus and reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane are more consistent with a vascular tumor like a glomus tumor, rather than mastoiditis.
