question_text: All of the following statements about the Eustachian tube function test are true except?
option_a: Sonotubometry: the sound is measured by a microphone in the EAC while the patient keeps swallowing.
option_b: Frenzel manoeuvre: on closed nose negative pressure is generated in middle ear which can be observed on pneumatic otoscopy
option_c: Valsalva test: Eustachian tube and middle ear is inflated by a forced expiration with mouth closed and nose pinched.
option_d: High negative middle ear pressure >90dapa in impedance audiometry is suggestive of Eustachian tube dysfunction.
explanation:
Explanation:

Closed nose negative pressure is generated in the middle ear, which can be observed on pneumatic otoscopy, in the Toynbee test, and not in the Frenzel manoeuvre.

This development of negative pressure in the middle ear is termed as positive Toynbee's test and signifies eustachian tube patency.

The Frenzel manoeuvre is a technique divers use to equalise ear pressure, using the tongue and throat muscles to move air into the Eustachian tubes.

question_text: In the given image, which anatomical structure is indicated by the yellow arrow?
explanation:
Explanation:

The structure marked in the image is the Fossa of Rosenmüller.

  • The Fossa of Rosenmüller is a small indentation in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx located behind the posterior opening of the nasal cavity. In an image, it may appear as a small, rounded depression in the nasopharynx tissue on either side.

Explanation for other options:

Tubal Ligation (Option B): The Tubal Tonsil is a lymphoid tissue near the Eustachian tube's opening. It is typically found in the superior aspect of the nasopharynx and may appear as a small, rounded tissue mass in an image.

Opening of the Eustachian tube (Option C): The opening of the Eustachian tube is located in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, near the posterior border of the nasal cavity. It may appear as a small, slit-like opening in an image.

Adenoids (Option D): A rectangular mass of lymphatic tissue called the adenoids is present in the nasopharynx. The adenoids on the nasopharynx's roof and back wall are midline structures. They are a component of the Waldeyer ring, which also consists of the adenoids, palatine tonsils, and lingual tonsils. Beginning in the seventh month of pregnancy, they typically develop until they reach adulthood.

question_text: Which of the following interventions should not be done in an 8-year-old boy with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss?
explanation:
Explanation:

Adenoidectomy with grommet (ventilation tube) insertion is a treatment for conductive hearing loss caused by Eustachian Tube Dysfunction (ETD) and middle ear effusion.

It is contraindicated and ineffective for sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), which originates in the cochlea or auditory nerve.

Explanation of other options:

Preferential sitting (Option A): A simple, effective non-amplification strategy to improve the signal-to-noise ratio for any child with hearing loss.

Hearing aid (Option C): The primary and first-line amplification device for managing bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

Cochlear implant (Option D): A standard and effective intervention for severe-to-profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss when hearing aids provide insufficient benefit.

question_text: A 6 year old child presents to the hospital with history of mouth breathing, mal-occlusion of teeth and conductive hearing loss due to glue ear. Which of the following will be best management plan for this patient?
option_d: Adenoidectomy with Myringotomy with grommet insertion
explanation:
History of mouth breathing, mal-occlusion of teeth in a 6 year old child are features of adenoid facies arising from adenoid hypertrophy.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes bilateral eustachian tube blockage leading to formation of glue ear(serous otitis media). This causes conductive hearing loss.

This child would need adenoidectomy(for adenoid hypertrophy) along with Myringotomy with Grommet insertion(to treat glue ear).

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no. 288, 77

question_text: Which of the following best describes Trotter's Triad?
option_a: Palatal Palsy, Temporo-parietal pain, Conductive Hearing Loss
option_b: Palatal Palsy, Temporo-parietal pain, Sensorineural Hearing Loss
option_c: Palatal Palsy, Retro-orbital pain, Conductive Hearing Loss
explanation: Nasopharyngeal cancer can cause conductive deafness (eustachian tube blockage), ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia (involvement of CN V) and palatal paralysis (CN X)-collectively called Trotter's triad.

question_text: Cerebrospinal rhinorrhea is usually due to a fracture of:
explanation:
CSF from anterior cranial fossa reaches the nose via

  • Cribriform plate
  • Roof of ethmoid air cells
  • Frontal sinus.

CSF from middle cranial fossa follows injuries to sphenoid sinus.

In fractures of temporal bone, CSF reaches the middle ear and then escapes through the eustachian tube into the nose (CSF otorhinorrhoea)

Overall most common site of CSF rhinorrhea is cribriform plate (Ethmoid bone).

Most common cause now a days is iatrogenic (E.g. FESS)

Second common cause is traumatic CSF leak – site of leak – Fovea Ethmoidalis (Frontal bone)

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th edition, page 192

question_text: A patient has sustained a fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. Which clinical symptom is most likely to occur?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The most common cause of CSF rhinorrhea is the fracture of the cribriform plate.
  • A cribriform plate fracture can tear the overlying dura mater, causing the cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the nasal cavity, resulting in CSF rhinorrhea.
  • This occurs because the cribriform plate forms the roof of the nasal cavity and separates it from the anterior cranial fossa.

Causes of CSF rhinorrhea

  • Iatrogenic: Most common nowadays
    • Injury to the cribriform plate during functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS).
  • Trauma / Head Injury (second most common):
    • Especially Le Fort II & III fractures and nasal-ethmoid fractures.
  • Other Causes:
    • Brain tumors causing increased intracranial pressure.
    • Spontaneous CSF leaks in individuals with chronically raised intracranial pressure.

Sites of CSF leak

  • CSF from anterior cranial fossa reaches the nose via
    • Cribriform plate
    • Roof of ethmoid
    • Frontal sinus.
  • CSF from middle cranial fossa follows injuries to sphenoid sinus.
  • In fractures of temporal bone, CSF reaches the middle ear and then escapes through the eustachian tube into the nose (CSF otorhinorrhea).
  • Most common site of CSF leak is Crista galli
  • The most common site of traumatic CSF leak is Fovea ethmoidalis.

Explanation of other options:

Hearing loss (Option A): Hearing loss can results from fracture of the temporal bone or injury to the inner ear following trauma; not seen with cribriform plate injury.

Visual loss (Option B), Diplopia (Option D): Visual disturbance following trauma is associated with injury to the optic nerve, occipital lobe or orbital fracture.

question_text: What is the appropriate approach to treat a child who is attending school and has a repeated occurrence of infections in the upper respiratory tract, difficulty in breathing through the nose, and hearing problems, along with the observation of a palate that is significantly raised in shape?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion is the preferred approach for a child presenting with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, nasal breathing difficulty, hearing problems, and a high-arched palate.
  • These symptoms suggest adenoid hypertrophy causing upper airway obstruction and Eustachian tube dysfunction, leading to otitis media with effusion (OME).
  • Adenoidectomy relieves nasal obstruction and reduces recurrent infections.
  • Grommet insertion helps in draining middle ear fluid, improving hearing.

Explanation of other options:

Tonsillectomy (Option A): Tonsillectomy alone is not indicated as the child primarily has symptoms related to adenoid hypertrophy and Eustachian tube dysfunction, not recurrent tonsillitis.

Adenoidectomy (Option B): While adenoidectomy addresses the nasal obstruction and infections, it does not directly manage the hearing problems caused by OME. Grommet insertion is essential for addressing middle ear fluid.

Myringotomy with grommet insertion (Option D): While this resolves middle ear fluid, it does not address the underlying issue of adenoid hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction and recurrent infections

question_text: Which of the following is associated with CSF otorrhea?
option_b: Traumatic rupture of the tympanic membrane
option_d: Fracture of the roof of the nose
explanation:
Explanation:

CSF otorrhea refers to the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the skull through the ear.

Battle's sign is a clinical finding associated with CSF leakage into the mastoid air cells following a temporal bone fracture.

It presents as bruising over the mastoid process, typically occurring after head trauma.

CSF Rhinorrhea

  • Refers to the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into the nasal cavity.
  • It may present as clear watery discharge or as fluid mixed with blood, especially after acute head injury.

Common Sites of CSF Rhinorrhea

  • Anterior cranial fossa
  • Middle cranial fossa
  • Temporal bone fracture
  • Cribriform plate (most common site)
  • Roof of ethmoid air cells
  • Frontal sinus
  • Sphenoid sinus (often post-traumatic)

In some cases, CSF first enters the middle ear and then escapes through the eustachian tube into the nose- termed CSF otorhinorrhea.Etiology

  • Trauma (most common):Accidental injury or iatrogenic following procedures such as sinus surgery, nasal polypectomy, or skull base surgery.
  • Inflammatory causes:Mucocele, fungal infections, osteomyelitis, chronic sinusitis with polyposis.
  • Neoplasms:Benign or malignant skull base tumors.
  • Congenital defects:Meningocele, meningoencephalocele, nasal glioma with skull base defects.
  • Idiopathic:Spontaneous leaks without an identifiable cause.

Investigations

  • Handkerchief (Halo) test: Simple bedside test -CSF separates out as a clear ring around a blood spot.
  • Beta-2 transferrin assay: Gold standard; highly specific for CSF.
  • High-resolution CT (HRCT): Detects bony defects in the skull base.
  • CT cisternography: Uses contrast to precisely localize active leaks.
  • MRI cisternography: Non-invasive, helpful in detecting meningocele or encephalocele.
  • Fluorescein test: Intrathecal fluorescein dye, useful for intraoperative localization.

Traumatic rupture of the tympanic membrane, Penetrating injury to the eye, and Fracture of the roof of the nose (Options B, C, and D): are not typically associated with CSF otorrhea.

question_text: Trotter's Triad include all except:
explanation:
Trotter’s triad is a feature of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presenting with

  • Temporoparietal neuralgia - (due to Vth nerve involvement)
  • Palatal palsy - (due to Xth nerve involvement)
  • Unilateral conductive hearing loss - (due to serous otitis media due to Eustachian tube blockage).

All the cranial nerves can be involved in Nasopharyngeal cancer except 1st, 7th and 8th nerves.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 297

question_text: Which of the following signs is not associated with otitis media with effusion?
option_b: AD curve on tympanometry with conductive hearing loss
option_c: Adenoid hypertrophy is a cause of SOM
explanation:
Explanation:

An AD (Deep/Hypercompliant) curve on tympanometry is seen in conditions like ossicular discontinuity or a hypermobile tympanic membrane.

Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) is characterized by a Type B (Flat) tympanogram due to the presence of fluid in the middle ear, which impedes the mobility of the tympanic membrane. OME is very commonly bilateral, especially in children. (Option B ruled out)

Adenoid hypertrophy causing Eustachian Tube Obstruction is a leading cause of OME. (Option C ruled out). A large proportion of OME cases resolve spontaneously, which is why a "watchful waiting" period of 3 months is often recommended. (Option D ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

  • OME → Type B (Flat) Tympanogram.
  • Normal/High Compliance → Type AD Tympanogram.

question_text: A 45-year-old patient presents with autophony, bilateral limb weakness, and a normal tympanic membrane that moves with respiration. What is the most likely underlying cause of these symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of autophony (an abnormally loud perception of one's own voice), bilateral limb weakness, and a tympanic membrane that moves with respiration points toward Patulous Eustachian Tube (PET).

  • This condition is often linked to marked weight loss, which causes atrophy of the surrounding peritubal fat that normally maintains closure of the Eustachian tube.

Explanation of Other Options:

Meningioma (Option A): Meningiomas are slow-growing tumors arising from the meninges and can produce neurological symptoms depending on their location. Although they may present with headaches, seizures, or focal deficits, they are unlikely to cause the triad of autophony, bilateral limb weakness, and a tympanic membrane moving with respiration.

Multiple Sclerosis (MS) (Option B): MS is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system that presents with varied symptoms such as limb weakness, vision impairment, coordination problems, and sensory changes. However, it does not typically produce autophony or abnormal tympanic membrane movement.

Wegener's Granulomatosis (Option D): Also called Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), this rare autoimmune disease mainly involves the respiratory tract and kidneys. While it can lead to sinus, lung, and renal symptoms, it does not usually account for the combination of features described in this case.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4725712/#:~:text

question_text:
A 35-year-old male patient presented with a complaint of 6 months of ear discharge, discharge was non-foul-smelling and associated with hearing loss. An endoscopy picture is given below.

The patient was undertaken for tympanoplasty. During surgery, the malleus handle was found to be present, but the incus and stapes superstructures were absent. What grade of defect will this patient have according to Austin's classification?
explanation:
The picture shown above is suggestive of the Tubotympanic Type of CSOM. It is a long-standing type of CSOM confined to the lower part of the middle ear and eustachian tube.

According to Austin's classification, ossicular erosions are graded into four types depending upon the presence or absence of the malleus handle (M) and the stapes suprastructure (S).

In the given scenario, the malleus is present, but the superstructures are absent, corresponding to Austin Group B.

question_text: A pregnant woman presents with 50 dB hearing loss. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this hearing loss?
option_a: Ossicular fixation with an intact tympanic membrane
option_b: Ossicular fixation with a damaged tympanic membrane
explanation:
Explanation:

A hearing loss of ~50 dB in adults is commonly due to otosclerosis, which is characterized by fixation of the stapes with intact tympanic membrane.

Otosclerosis

  • Otosclerosis is a primary disease of bony labyrinth leading to fixation of the foot plate of stapes.
  • In otosclerosis, the dense endochondral bone of otic capsule is replaced by spongy bone (woven bone) which is later replaced by more of mature bone.
  • More common in females.
  • Most common site of origin: Fissula ante fenestrem.
  • Symptoms often worsens during pregnancy due to hormonal influences on bone metabolism

Symptoms:

  • Painless, progressive hearing loss
  • Paracuisis willisii: Patients hear better in noisy area
  • Tinnitus

Evaluation and diagnosis

Otoscopic finding

  • Normal tympanic membrane and eustachian tube.
  • Sometimes flamingo pink appearance behind the tympanic membrane may be seen in early stages: Schwartze sign.

Tuning fork test

  • Rinne test: Negative (BC > AC) initially at 256 Hz, then 512 Hz, and later at 1024 Hz when stapes fixation is complete.
  • Weber test: Lateralizes to the ear with greater conductive loss

Pure tone audiometry

  • Shows conductive hearing loss, with greater loss of air conduction at lower frequencies.
  • Carhart's notch: A characteristic dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz.
  • Tympanometry shows Type As curve and absent stapedial reflex

Explanation of other options:

Ossicular fixation with a damaged tympanic membrane (Option B): This would suggest chronic otitis media with likely tympanosclerosis, and not typically seen in pregnancy. It is usually associated with visible scarring or perforation.

Erosion with tympanic membrane injury (Option C): Seen in chronic suppurative otitis media complicated with cholesteatoma. This causes conductive loss but also presents with discharge and visible perforation, not a normal membrane.

Erosion without tympanic membrane injury (Option D): Erosion without tympanic membrane injury may occur in cholesteatoma, but is typically associated with retraction pockets or infection.

question_text: Which of the following muscle is used for opening of Eustachian Tube
explanation:
• The medial fibers of the tensor veli palatini are attached to the lateral lamina of the tube and when they contract help to open the tubal lumen.
  • These fibers have also been called dilator tubae muscle which is used for opening of Eustachian tubes.

Other options:

B: Tensor tympani retracts the tympanic membrane by medial movement at the level of the neck of the malleus and helps in reducing the phonotrauma.

C: Levator velin palatini elevates the palate while swallowing

D: Stylohyoid muscle is not associated with the opening of Eustachian tube

option_b: Measurement of CO2 in exhaled air (Etco2)

question_text: Which of the following structures contain Ostmann fat pad?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The nasopharyngeal end of the eustachian tube contains the Ostmann pad of fat.
  • It is a mass of fatty tissues related laterally to the membranous part of the cartilaginous tube.
  • It helps to keep the tube closed and thus protects it from the reflux of nasopharyngeal secretions.

question_text: The wall of the pharynx consists of Muscle layer. A gap exists between the superior constrictor and the base of skull. What is the name of this gap and which structure passes through this gap?
option_b: Sinus of Morgagni- Tensor veli palatine
option_d: Space of Gillette - retropharyngeal lymph nodes.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The muscular layer of pharynx is made up ofinner longitudinal and outer circular muscle layers.
  • The outer circular muscle layer contains three muscles namely superior, middle and inferior constrictor muscles.
  • The upper border of the superiorconstrictor is not directly attached to the base of skull, a gap exists between the two and this gap is filled only by pharyngobasilar fascia. This gap is known as sinus of Morgagni.
  • The following structures passes through this gap (mnemonic: TAALA)
    1. Tensor veli palatini.
    2. Ascending pharyngeal artery
    3. Ascending pharyngeal artery's pharyngeal branch
    4. Levator veli palatini
    5. Auditory tube (Eustachian tube)

Key Takeaway:

The following structures pass through sinus of Morgagni (mnemonic: TAALA)

  1. Tensor veli palatini.
  2. Ascending pharyngeal artery
  3. Ascending pharyngeal artery's pharyngeal branch
  4. Levator veli palatini
  5. Auditory tube (Eustachian tube)

question_text: Endoscopic image is given. Identify the marked structure with a yellow circle?
explanation:
• Each lateral wall presents the pharyngeal opening of eustachian tube situated 1.25 cm behind the posterior end of inferior turbinate.
  • It is bounded above and behind by an elevation called torus tubarius raised by the cartilage of the tube.
  • Above and behind the tubal elevation is a recess called fossa of Rosenmüller (as shown by arrows in the image), which is the commonest site for origin of carcinoma.

explanation:

question_text: A patient of thyroidectomy was being extubated the anaesthesiologist realized that when he removes the tube the patients being to have recurrent cyanotic spells which of the following could be the cause
explanation:
Bilateral Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN) Palsy- In such cases only muscle which is working is cricothyroid which is supplied by external branch of superior laryngeal artery whose function is adduction.It can lead to vocal cord paralysis and bilateral vocal cord immobility. In such cases, when the endotracheal tube is removed, the vocal cords cannot abduct resulting in recurrent cyanotic spells.

Other options and brief explanations:

B. B/L SLN Palsy (Bilateral Superior Laryngeal Nerve Palsy): Bilateral Superior Laryngeal Nerve Palsy does not cause vocal cord paralysis, and it would not result in the described recurrent cyanotic spells.

C. Edema: While post-thyroidectomy edema can cause airway compromise, it would not lead to recurrent cyanotic spells upon extubation.

D. Hemorrhage: Hemorrhage can be a complication after thyroidectomy but would not directly cause recurrent cyanotic spells upon extubation.

question_text: What is the most commonly used test for newborn hearing screening?
explanation:
Explanation:

OAE is the best and most commonly used test for newborn hearing screening.

Otoacoustic emissions (OAE)

  • OAEs are low-intensity sounds generated by the outer hair cells of a healthy cochlea.
  • These are recorded using a very sensitive microphone placed in the external ear canal and the signals are analyzed by a computer to assess cochlear function.

Applications

  • OAEs are used as a screening test of hearing in neonates
  • To test hearing in uncooperative or mentally challenged individuals after sedation.
  • They help to distinguish cochlear from retrocochlear hearing loss.
    • OAEs are absent in cochlear lesions, e.g. ototoxic sensorineural hearing loss.
    • Detects ototoxic effects earlier than pure tone audiometry.

Explanation of other options:

Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (Option B): Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) is used to confirm hearing loss in infants and only in neonates who have failed OAE.

Pure Tone Audiometry (Option C): Pure tone audiometry (PTA) s a subjective test of hearing in air conduction and bone conduction. It helps to find the degree of handicap for medicolegal purposes.

Tympanometry (Option D): Tympanometry is the best test for assessment of the eustachian tube.

question_text:
What are the objective tests used to assess hearing ability?
i. BERA
ii. OAE
iii. PTA
iv. Tympanometry
explanation:
Explanation:

All the above mentioned tests: BERA, OAE, PTA and tympanometry are objective methods used to assess hearing ability:

BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry)

  • An electrophysiological test that measures the brainstem's response to sound stimuli.
  • It is useful for assessing auditory pathways and diagnosing hearing impairment, especially in infants and individuals unable to cooperate with traditional hearing tests.

OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions)

  • OAE measure sound waves produced by the inner ear (cochlea) in response to auditory stimuli.
  • The presence of these emissions suggests normal cochlear function, particularly the outer hair cells of the cochlea.
  • It is widely used in newborn hearing screening and assessing cochlear health.

PTA (Pure Tone Audiometry)

  • PTA is a standard test for assessing hearing sensitivity by presenting pure tones at different frequencies and intensities.
  • The results provide a threshold of hearing and help in diagnosing the type and degree of hearing loss.

Tympanometry

  • Tympanometry measures the movement of the tympanic membrane in response to changes in air pressure, providing information about the middle ear's health, such as fluid, eustachian tube dysfunction, or tympanic membrane perforation.

question_text:
Which of the following Hearing tests are objective tests of hearing:
A. tympanometry
B. Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry Ladder
C. OtoAcoustic Emissions
D. Pure Tone Audiometry
explanation:
Correct answer is option C: Tympanometry, Otoacoustic Emissions, and Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) are objective tests of hearing.

  1. Tympanometry: Tympanometry is an objective test that measures the movement of the eardrum (tympanic membrane) in response to changes in air pressure. It helps evaluate the middle ear function and detects conditions such as fluid accumulation or eustachian tube dysfunction.Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA): BERA, also known as Auditory
  2. Brainstem Response (ABR), is an objective test that measures the electrical activity of the auditory nerve and brainstem in response to sound stimuli. It is commonly used to assess hearing in infants and individuals who are unable to participate in conventional behavioral hearing tests.
  3. Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE): OAEs are sounds generated by the inner ear in response to external auditory stimuli. They can be measured using a sensitive microphone placed in the ear canal. OAEs are used to assess the function of the cochlea and are particularly helpful in screening for hearing loss in newborns.
  4. Pure Tone Audiometry: Pure Tone Audiometry is a subjective test that relies on the patient's response to pure tone sounds of different frequencies and intensities. The patient indicates when they hear the tones, and the results are plotted on an audiogram. It is not an objective test.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Examination reveals conductive hearing loss with a negative Rinne test, along with a reddish mass visible behind the tympanic membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Definition

Paragangliomas are tumors that originate from paraganglionic tissue, and glomus tumors represent a specific type of paraganglioma.

Nature

  • Benign(most common benign tumor of the middle ear).
  • Originates from paraganglionic cells or glomus bodies.

Epidemiology

  • Most frequently seen in middle-aged adults (40-50 years).
  • More common in females.

Types

  • Glomus tympanicum:Arises from the promontory of the middle ear (tympanic plexus).
  • Glomus jugulare:Originates from the dome of the jugular bulb (sympathetic plexus around the jugular vein).

Tumor Spread

  • Inferiorly:Into the jugular foramen.
  • Anteriorly:Toward the nasopharynx, leading to Eustachian tube obstruction.
  • Posteriorly:Into the mastoid.
  • Superiorly:Toward the posterior and middle cranial fossae → cranial nerve palsies (IX-XII).
  • Laterally:Into the tympanic membrane, presenting as a bleeding polyp in the external auditory canal.
  • Medially:Into the labyrinth and petrous pyramid → dizziness and facial paralysis.

Clinical Features

  • Gradually progressive conductive hearing loss.
  • Pulsatile tinnitus(synchronous with pulse, may stop temporarily with carotid pressure).
  • Bleeding from the ear(severe if a polyp is present).
  • Dizziness/vertigoand facial paralysisin advanced cases.
  • Systemic symptoms(headache, sweating, palpitations, hypertension, anxiety) due to catecholamine secretion.

Histopathology

  • No capsule (locally invasive).
  • Classic 'Zell Ballen' pattern: clusters of epithelioid chief cells and supporting sustentacular cells, surrounded by vascular sinusoids.
  • Preoperative biopsy is avoideddue to the risk of severe bleeding from vascular sinusoids and possible injury to adjacent vascular structures (high jugular bulb or aberrant ICA).

Otoscopic Findings

  • Glomus tympanicum:Red reflex behind an intact tympanic membrane with bulging.
  • Glomus jugulare:'Rising sun' appearance from tumor at the floor of the middle ear.

Diagnosis

  • CECT (Investigation of Choice):Shows erosion of the carotico-jugular spine (Phelp's sign).
  • MRI:Reveals microhemorrhages with characteristic 'salt and pepper' appearance (white and gray dots).
  • Angiography:Identifies feeding vessels supplying the tumor.

Explanation of Other Options:

Acute otitis media (Option A): Less likely, as it usually presents with ear pain, fever, and middle ear fluid or pus.

Chronic otitis media (Option B): May cause conductive hearing loss but typically does not present with a reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane.

Serous otitis media (Option D): Can lead to conductive hearing loss, but it is not usually associated with pulsatile tinnitus or a reddish mass.

question_text: A patient presents with a foul-smelling discharge from the nose, anosmia, and nasal obstruction. On examination, the following findings were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows crusting with a wide, roomy nasal cavity. In the background of symptoms such as foul-smelling discharge, nasal obstruction, and anosmia, the findings are suggestive of atrophic rhinitis.

Atrophic rhinitis

  • Also known as ozaena, it is the chronic inflammation of nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones.
  • More common in females.
  • Etiology:
    • Autoimmune process. The body reacts by a destructive process to the antigens released from the nasal mucosa.
    • Estrogen deficiency: Disease usually starts at puberty, involves females more than males, the crusting and foetor associated with disease tends to cease after menopause;
    • Nutritional deficiency. Disease may be due to deficiency of vitamin A, D or iron or some other dietary factors.
    • Infection by Klebsiella ozeanae

Clinical presentation

  • Foul smelling discharge: Due to infected nasal crusts.
  • Mericful anosmia: Despite the foul smell patient is unaware of it due to marked anosmia with degenrative changes.
  • Nasal obstruction despite roomy nasal cavities due to large crusts.
  • Epistaxis: May occur when crusts are removed.
  • Hearing impairment: Due to obstruction to eustachian tube and middle ear effusion.
  • Paranasal sinuses are usually small and underdeveloped with thick walls.

Examination findings:

  • Greenish or greyish black dry crusts covering the turbinates and septum.
  • Roomy, wide nasal cavities with atrophied turbinates.
  • Pale nasal mucosa.
  • Septal perfortaion and dermatitis of nasal vestibule.
  • Sometimes saddle nose deformity.

Treatment

  • The treatment of choice for atrophic rhinitis is alkaline nasal douching or washing to remove the crusts.
  • Anti-Ozena Nasal Drops: After nasal washing, special antiozeana nasal drops can be applied. These drops may contain vitamin D, estradiol, and chloramphenicol.
  • Surgical Treatment: If frequent nasal washing is not desired, surgical treatment may be considered.
    • Modified yound operation: permanent partial closure of both nostrils by placing stitches to narrow the nasal orifices

Lautenslager operation: medialization of the lateral wall of the nose.

Explanation of other options:

Rhinitis sicca (Option B): Typically seen in people working in high temperature, like bakers and blacksmiths. Condition is confined to the anterior third of nose particularly of the nasal septum

Rhinitis medicamentosa (Option C): Rhinitis medicamentosa is associated with the excessive use of topical decongestants like alpha adrenergic agonists - xylometazoline.

Allergic rhinitis (Option D): Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated immunologic response of the nasal mucosa to the airborne allergens. It presents with nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, sneezing and itching. However, there is no associated foul-smelling discharge or nasal crusting.

question_text: A female homemaker presents with nasal congestion, reduced sense of smell, and a greenish, crusty nasal discharge. On examination, her nasal passages are wide, and the turbinates appear atrophied. Which surgical procedure would be appropriate for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms of nasal dryness, crusting, foul-smelling discharge, congestion, and reduced sense of smell are indicative of atrophic rhinitis. Young’s operation is the surgical procedure used to treat this condition.

Atrophic rhinitis

  • Also known as ozaena, it is the chronic inflammation of nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones.
  • More common in females.

Clinical presentation

  • Foul smelling discharge: Due to infected nasal crusts.
  • Merciful anosmia: Despite the foul smell patient is unaware of it due to marked anosmia with degenerative changes.
  • Nasal obstruction despite roomy nasal cavities due to large crusts.
  • Epistaxis: May occur when crusts are removed.
  • Hearing impairment: Due to obstruction to eustachian tube and middle ear effusion.
  • Paranasal sinuses are usually small and underdeveloped with thick walls.

Examination findings:

  • Greenish or greyish black dry crusts covering the turbinate and septum.
  • Roomy, wide nasal cavities with atrophied turbinates
  • Pale nasal mucosa.
  • Septal perforation and dermatitis of nasal vestibule.
  • Sometimes saddle nose deformity.

Treatment

  • The treatment of choice for atrophic rhinitis is alkaline nasal douching or washing to remove the crusts.
  • Anti-Ozena Nasal Drops: After nasal washing, special antiozeana nasal drops can be applied. These drops may contain vitamin D, estradiol, and chloramphenicol.
  • Surgical Treatment:
    • If frequent nasal washing is not desired, surgical treatment may be considered.
    • Young's operation is performed in such patients.
    • It involves removing atrophic mucosa and restoring nasal passage function to reduce dryness, crusting, and improve breathing.

Explanation of other options:

Submucous resection (Option A), Septoplasty (Option C): Submucous resection (SMR) and septoplasty are surgical procedures aimed at correcting nasal septal deviation.

Vidian neurectomy (Option D): Vidian neurectomy is a surgical procedure that involves cutting or removing the Vidian nerve (nerve of the pterygoid canal) to reduce excessive nasal secretions. Interrupting parasympathetic innervation to the nasal mucosa decreases profuse nasal discharge. This procedure is mainly indicated in chronic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, or allergic rhinitis with persistent watery nasal discharge.

question_text: A 5-year-old child is brought by his mother with hearing loss, mouth breathing, and poor performance in school. Which of the following is the expected type of hearing loss in this child?
explanation:
Explanation:

The child's symptoms of hearing loss, mouth breathing, and poor school performance suggest complications from adenoid hypertrophy, which is common in pediatric patients around this age.

  • Adenoid enlargement can obstruct the Eustachian tube, leading to otitis media with effusion. This causes a conductive hearing loss (CHL) because sound transmission through the middle ear is impaired.
  • Studies show that the degree of hearing loss correlates with the size of adenoids, with larger adenoids (third- and fourth-degree) causing more significant CHL.
  • Early recognition and management, including medical therapy or adenoidectomy, can prevent further complications.

Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) and Adenoidectomy

  • Traditional View: Adenoidectomy helps OME by relieving anatomical obstruction of the Eustachian tube.
  • Limitation of Size Alone: Adenoid size is not significantly different in children with or without OME, so obstruction alone does not fully explain benefits of adenoidectomy.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Recurrent acute or chronic inflammation of adenoids.
    • Increased bacterial load, especially Haemophilus influenzae.
    • Leads to:
      • Squamous cell metaplasia
      • Extension of reticular epithelium
      • Fibrosis of interfollicular connective tissue
      • Reduced mucociliary clearance
    • Biofilm Formation:
      • Inflammatory changes increase bacterial adherence.
      • Biofilm: structured bacterial community enclosed in a self-produced matrix, adherent to surfaces.
      • Biofilm contributes to middle ear effusion and persistence of OME.
    • Clinical Evidence:
      • MRC TARGET study supports adjuvant adenoidectomy in children over 3 years undergoing ventilation tube (grommet) insertion.
    • Conclusion: Adenoidectomy benefits in OME are due to both relief of obstruction and removal of chronically inflamed tissue with bacterial biofilm.

Explanation of Other Options:

SNHL (Sensorineural Hearing Loss) (Option A): Typically results from inner ear or auditory nerve problems, such as congenital defects, infections (like meningitis), or ototoxic drugs. The child's history suggests middle ear involvement due to adenoid hypertrophy and Eustachian tube obstruction, not inner ear pathology.

Mixed Hearing Loss (Option C): This involves both conductive and sensorineural components. There is no evidence of inner ear involvement in this case.

Normal (Option D): The child is presenting with hearing loss, mouth breathing, and school difficulties, indicating a problem.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10544040/

question_text: A 52 year old male has presented to the ENT OPD with right sided cervical lymphadenopathy and right sided hearing loss. The diagnosis is?
explanation:

Other options:-

B) juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, typically present in young age group with recurrent epic tax.

C) adenoid hypertrophy also occurs in young children, which presents with hypo nasal voice and difficulty breathing with adenoid faces

D) tuberculous lymphadenitis present with typical symptoms of tuberculosis.

question_text: A 60-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and right ear pain. On examination, the right ear reveals conductive hearing loss with a dull tympanic membrane. Moreover, decreased mobility of the soft palate was also noted. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This presentation is highly suspicious for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC). The classic findings include:

  • Painless cervical lymphadenopathy (often the presenting symptom).
  • Unilateral conductive hearing loss and ear pain due to Eustachian tube dysfunction from the tumor obstructing the torus tubarius, leading to middle ear effusion (dull TM).
  • Soft palate dysfunction (decreased mobility) due to tumor invasion or involvement of the vagus nerve (CN X).
    NPC has a strong association with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).
  • Clinical Features of Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
    • Local Nasal Symptoms:
    • Nasal obstruction
    • Blood-stained nasal discharge (epistaxis)
    • Denasal speech (rhinolalia clausa)
    • Otologic Symptoms (from Eustachian tube blockage):
    • Conductive hearing loss
    • Unilateral serous otitis media (a key indicator in adults)
    • Tinnitus
    • Earache
    • Dizziness
    • Ophthalmoneurologic Symptoms (from cranial nerve involvement):
    • Most common: Cranial nerve VI palsy (causing diplopia and squint)
    • Ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI)
    • Facial pain/numbness and reduced corneal reflex (CN V)
    • Jugular foramen syndrome (hoarseness, dysphagia - CN IX, X, XI)
    • Horner syndrome
    • Blindness (CN II)
    • Headache
    • Cervical Metastases:
    • A common presenting sign.
    • Nodes located between the angle of the jaw and mastoid, or in the posterior triangle.
    • Constitutional Symptoms & Distant Metastases:
    • Weight loss
    • Distant metastases to bone, lungs, and liver.

Explanation of other options:
Adenoid cystic cancer (Option B): Typically arises in salivary glands (e.g., palate) and is characterized by perineural invasion. It does not classically present with Eustachian tube symptoms or as a primary nasopharyngeal mass with neck nodes.
Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option C): A benign, highly vascular tumour that presents in adolescent males with epistaxis and nasal obstruction, not in 60-year-olds.
Quinsy (Peritonsillar abscess) (Option D): Presents with severe unilateral throat pain, fever, trismus, and a hot-potato voice. It does not cause painless lymphadenopathy or hearing loss.

question_text: Arrange the structures in peripheral to central order constituting the auditory pathway
option_a: Cochlear nucleus - spiral ganglion - superior olivary nucleus - lateral lemniscus
option_b: Spiral ganglion Cochlear nucleus - superior olivary nucleus - lateral lemniscus
option_c: Spiral ganglion superior olivary nucleus cochlear nucleus - lateral lemniscus
option_d: Spiral ganglion Cochlear nucleus lateral lemniscus superior olivary nucleus
explanation:
Pathway of hearing:

  • The first neurons of the pathway are located in the spiral ganglion. They are bipolar. Their peripheral processes innervate the spiral organ of Corti, while central processes form the cochlear nerve. This nerve terminates in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei.
  • The second neurons lie in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei. Most of the axons arising in these nuclei cross to the opposite side (in the trapezoid body) and terminate in the superior olivary nucleus. (Many fibres end in the nucleus of trapezoid body or of the lateral lemniscus.) Some fibres are uncrossed
  • The third neurons lie in the superior olivary nucleus. Their axons form the lateral lemniscus and reach the inferior colliculus.
  • The fourth neurons lie in the inferior colliculus. Their axons pass through the inferior brachium to reach the medial geniculate body. (Some fibres of lateral lemniscus reach the medial geniculate body without relay in the inferior colliculus.)
  • The fifth neurons lie in the medial geniculate body. Their axons form the auditory radiation, which passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule to reach the auditory area in the temporal lobe.

Reference: Textbook of B. D. Chaurasia, Volume-4, 9th Edition, Page No - 82 to 84

question_text:
A patient presents to the OPD with complaints of bilateral hearing loss with worsened right ear hearing loss. On examination, the doctor diagnoses otosclerosis and recommends stapedectomy as the final resort to the problem.

option_b: Rinne's test - positive: Weber's test - lateralized to right ear
option_c: Rinne's test - negative: Weber's test - lateralized to left ear
option_d: Rinne's test - negative: Weber's test - lateralized to right ear
explanation:
Hearing loss is a presenting symptom in otosclerosis, usually starts in early twenties, often bilateral conductive type.

In conductive type of hearing loss, Rinne's test shows negative result for frequencies (BC>AC) and Weber's test is lateralized to affected (worse) ear.

Tuning fork test will show negative Rinne (BC>AC) first for 256 and then 512 Hz and after complete stapes fixation, for 1026 Hz. Weber will be lateralized to ear with greater conductive hearing loss. Absolute bone conduction may be normal.

question_text: A 50 year old male presented with vertigo, episodic tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss. The audiogram is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the given image?
explanation:
The history in the question gives clues to the diagnosis of Meniere's disease. The audiogram given is a rising curve typical of Meniere's disease.

Meniere’s disease

  • Ménière's disease, also called endolymphatic hydrops, is a disorder of the inner ear where the endolymphatic system is distended with endolymph.
  • The main pathology in Ménière's disease is distension of the endolymphatic system due to increased volume of endolymph. This can result either from increased production of endolymph or its faulty absorption or both.
  • Cardinal symptoms of Ménière’s disease are
    • (i) episodic vertigo,
    • (ii) fluctuating hearing loss,
    • (iii) tinnitus and
    • (iv) sense of fullness or pressure in the involved ear.
  • Tuning Fork Tests indicate sensorineural hearing loss.
    • Rinne test is positive,
    • absolute bone conduction is reduced in the affected ear and
    • Weber is lateralized to the better ear.
  • PTA shows sensorineural hearing loss. In early stages, lower frequencies are affected and the curve is of rising type. When higher frequencies are involved curve becomes flat or a falling type
  • Speech audiometry tests are helpful
  • Electrocochleography shows changes diagnostic of Ménière's disease.
    • Normally, ratio of summating potential (SP) to action potential (AP) is 30%.
    • In Ménière'sdisease, SP/AP ratio is greater than 30%.
  • Caloric and Glycerol tests are also useful

question_text: A 25-year-old female came with complaints of decrease in hearing(CHL) and pulsatile tinnitus. On examination, the tympanic membrane appeared red and bulging. What would be the diagnosis?
explanation:
The combination of decreased hearing, pulsatile tinnitus,and a red,bulging tympanic membrane suggests the presence of a glomus tumor.

Glomus tumors are highly vascular tumors that commonly arise in the middle ear.

They can cause symptoms such as hearing loss, pulsatile tinnitus, and changes in the appearance of the tympanic membrane.

Other options are incorrect:

Option B: Serous otitis media: Serous otitis media is characterized by fluid accumulation in the middle ear without infection or inflammation. It typically does not present with a red, bulging tympanic membrane.

Option C: Acute otitis media: Acute otitis media is an infection of the middle ear characterized by fluid accumulation and inflammation. However, it is less likely to present with pulsatile tinnitus and a red, bulging tympanic membrane.

Option D: Chronic otitis media: Chronic otitis media is a persistent inflammation and infection of the middle ear. While it can cause hearing loss, it is less likely to present with pulsatile tinnitus and a red, bulging tympanic membrane.

question_text: A patient presented to the ENT OPD with the complaint of vertigo with no hearing loss. The doctor performed a diagnostic manoeuvre and then performed a therapeutic manoeuver. Which is the diagnostic manoeuver?
explanation:
The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is a diagnostic maneuver that is used to induce nystagmus, which is a jerking of the eyes. Nystagmus can be caused by a number of conditions, including BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo). The maneuver is performed by having the patient lie down quickly with their head turned to one side and extended below the horizontal plane. If the patient has BPPV, they will experience nystagmus that is directed towards the side that their head is turned.

The other options are:

  • Epleys manoeuvre- This is a therapeutic maneuver that is used to treat BPPV. It is similar to the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, but the patient is rotated through a series of positions in order to reposition the otoliths that are causing the nystagmus.
  • Hemlich manoeuvre- This is a diagnostic maneuver that is used to assess the function of the vestibular system. It involves having the patient sit upright and rotate their head quickly to one side and then the other. If the patient has a vestibular problem, they will experience nystagmus that is directed towards the side that their head is turned.
  • Muller's manoeuvre- This is a therapeutic maneuver that is used to treat Ménière's disease. It involves having the patient lie down with their head tilted down and then rotated quickly to one side and then the other. This maneuver is thought to help to drain the excess fluid that is causing the symptoms of Ménière's disease.

question_text: A patient experiences vertigo and vomiting specifically when turning in bed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A patient experiencing vomiting and rotational vertigo, particularly when turning the head in bed, most likely has Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

Clinical features:

  • BPPV is characterized by brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head movements.
  • It is not associated with hearing loss or other neurological deficits.
  • The condition arises from a disorder of the posterior semicircular canal, caused by free-floating calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) that have become dislodged from the utricle.
  • The vertigo is provoked by positional changes, especially tilting or turning the head toward the affected side.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by a positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which reproduces vertigo and nystagmus in the affected canal

Pathophysiology:

  • Otoconia migrates into the posterior semicircular canal, interfering with normal endolymph flow and stimulating abnormal vestibular signals, leading to transient vertigo during specific movements.

Steps of the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre:

  • The manoeuvre starts with the patient in a sitting position.
  • Their head is turned 45 degrees towards the ear to be tested.
  • The examiner quickly brings the patient to a supine position with their head 30 degrees below the horizontal.
  • The 45-degree head rotation is maintained during the procedure.
  • Now the examiner observes the patient's eye for nystagmus.

Explanations for other Options:

Vestibular neuritis (Option B): Characterized by a sudden onset of intense vertigo that can persist for several days to weeks, without any cochlear involvement such as hearing loss or tinnitus.

Ménière's disease (Option C): Presents with sudden episodes of vertigo lasting minutes to hours, accompanied by fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and a feeling of fullness or pressure in the affected ear.

Labyrinthitis (Option D): Causes unilateral vestibular dysfunction with abrupt, continuous vertigo, often associated with nausea, vomiting, and sensorineural hearing loss.

question_text:
Arrange in order from a cochlear nerve in the hearing pathway
A. Cochlear nucleus
B. Superior olivary nucleus
C. Medial geniculate
D. Inferior colliculus
explanation:
The correct sequence of auditory pathway from the cochlear nerve in the hearing pathway is as follows:

  • A. Cochlear nerve: The auditory nerve (cochlear nerve) carries auditory information from the cochlea (the sensory organ of hearing) to the brainstem.
  • B. Cochlear nucleus: The cochlear nerve fibers synapse at the cochlear nucleus, which is located in the brainstem.
  • D. Superior olivary nucleus: After the cochlear nucleus, the auditory information ascends to the superior olivary nucleus, another structure in the brainstem.
  • C. Medial geniculate: From the superior olivary nucleus, the auditory pathway continues to the medial geniculate body, which is part of the thalamus.
  • From the medial geniculate body, auditory information is further relayed to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe of the brain for further processing and interpretation of sound.

The correct order is ABCD: Cochlear nerve → Cochlear nucleus → Superior olivary nucleus → Medial geniculate.

question_text: A steel factory worker is suffering from noise induced hearing loss. Which of the following is most likely to be affected?

question_text: 65 year old person with hearing loss with normal speech discrimination is suffering from?
explanation: Ans. is 'B' i.e., Presbycusis Information in this question are :- (i) Old age (65 years), (ii) Hearing loss, and (iii) Preserved speech discrimnation. Diagnosis is Presbycusis. Presbycusis Presbycusis refers to sensorineural hearing loss in elderly individuals Characteristically, presbycusis involves bilateral high frequency hearing loss associated with difficulty in speech discrimination and central auditory processing information. Four pathological types of presbycusis have been identified :- Sensory presbycusis There is epithelial atrophy with loss of sensory hair cells and supporting cells in the organ of corti. This process starts in the basal turn of cochlea and slowly progress towards the apex. Higher frequencies are affected but speech discrimination is preserved. Neural presbycusis :- There is atrophy of nerve cells in the cochlea and central neural pathways. Atrophy occurs throughout the cochlea, with the basilar region only slightly more predisposed than the remainder of the cochlea. Therefore, no precipitous drop in threshold on audiometry is observed. Speech discrimination is poor. Metabolic (strial) presbycusis ;;- There is atrophy of stria vascularis. Atrophy results in hearing loss represented by flat audiogram, but speech discrimination is preserved. Mechanical (cochlear conductive) presbycusis :- There is thickening and secondary stiffening of the basilar membrane of the cochlea. The thickening is more severe in the basal turn of cochlea where the basilar membrane is narrow. This correlates with a gradually sloping high frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Speech discrimination is average.

question_text: Hearing loss on right side is 60 dB, 60dB and 90 dB on 500, 1000 and 2000Hz respectively. Hearing loss on left side is 30dB, 40dB and 50 dB on 500, 1000 and 2000Hz respectively. How much is the percentage of handicap?

  3. Multiply this by 1.5 to get a percentage.

TOTAL % OF HANDICAP = [(better ear% x 5) + Worse ear%] / 6

In the given case,

Applying the above formula → Total hearing impairement = [(22.5 × 5) + 67.5] / 6 = 30%

question_text: A patient presents to ENT OPD with complaints of hearing loss. Rinne's test was negative on the right side and positive on the left side. The Weber test is lateralized to the left. Bone conduction is reduced in the right ear and similar in the left ear. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has Right SNHL because,

  • Weber lateralized to the left means Left CHL or Right SNHL (Option A & D ruled out)
  • Bone conduction is reduced on right means Right SNHL (Option A, B & D ruled out)
  • Negative Rinne usually means CHL, but it can be false negative in severe SNHL as seen in this case.

The tuning fork test is a quick and simple way to assess hearing and can help differentiate between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. It primarily involves two tests: the Rinne test and the Weber test, both typically using a 512 Hz tuning fork.

Key Takeaway:

In sensorineural hearing loss, Weber lateralizes to the normal ear, and bone conduction is reduced in the affected ear. Rinne can give false negatives in severe SNHL. A right SNHL explains all findings here.

question_text: A 36-year-old male patient presents with a history of ear discharge for 2 weeks. On examination, a mild perforation is observed in the antero-inferior segment of the tympanic membrane. What is the expected result from Rinne's test?
explanation:
Explanation:

A perforation in the tympanic membrane typically results in conductive hearing loss (Rinne's negative), as the perforation disrupts the normal conduction of sound through the middle ear.

  • When performing Rinne's test, which compares air conduction (AC) to bone conduction (BC), Rinne's negative would be expected in cases of conductive hearing loss, meaning that bone conduction (BC) is heard louder than air conduction (AC).
  • In the presence of a tympanic membrane perforation, air conduction is compromised due to the disrupted integrity of the eardrum, while bone conduction remains relatively intact.
  • Therefore, the result would likely be Rinne's negative, where the patient hears the tuning fork louder when placed on the mastoid (bone conduction) compared to in front of the ear canal (air conduction).

Explanation for other options:

Rinne's positive (Option A): Incorrect because Rinne's positive is seen in sensorineural hearing loss or when conductive hearing is intact, which is not expected in the case of a tympanic membrane perforation.

Rinne's equivocal (Option C): Incorrect because an equivocal result is rare in this situation. The perforation typically causes a clear conductive hearing loss, making the result more definitive (negative).

Cannot be determined (Option D): Incorrect because, based on the presence of a tympanic membrane perforation, we can reasonably predict Rinne's negative.

question_text:
A 30-year-old male patient presented with decreased hearing in the left ear. His audiogram is given below.

What would have been the tuning fork test findings in his left ear?
option_a: Left ear Rinne positive, Weber lateralized to the right.
option_b: Left ear Rinne negative, Weber lateralized to the right.
option_c: Left ear Rinne positive, Weber lateralized to the Left.
option_d: Left ear Rinne negative, Weber lateralized to the Left.
explanation:
Explanation:

The red line in the given audiogram depicts the right ear. Findings in the right ear appear normal.

The blue line in the audiogram depicts the left ear. The blue line shows increased air and bone conduction threshold.

There is no air-bone gap. This shows sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear.

The Rinne test is positive in a normal ear and in sensorineural hearing loss. Here in this case, Rinne will be positive in both ears.

The Weber test is lateralized towards the normal ear in sensorineural hearing loss. Thus, in this case, the Weber is lateralized towards the right ear. Hence, option A is the correct answer.

question_text: A female patient undergoing evaluation for hearing loss demonstrates a negative Rinne test at 256 Hz and 512 Hz, but a positive result at 1024 Hz. Based on these findings, what is the most likely range of the air-bone gap in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the described scenario, the Rinne test is negative at 256 Hz and 512 Hz (indicating that bone conduction is better than air conduction at these frequencies) but positive at 1024 Hz (indicating that air conduction is better than bone conduction at this frequency).

  • This pattern suggests a sensorineural hearing loss at 256 Hz and 512 Hz frequencies, and a conductive hearing loss at 1024 Hz frequency. 
  • The anticipated gap between air conduction and bone conduction in this case would be in the range of 30-45 dB, indicating a moderate to moderately severe sensorineural hearing loss at 256 Hz and 512 Hz frequencies, and a mild conductive hearing loss at 1024 Hz frequency.

question_text: A Patient is not able to hear properly from the left ear given an audiogram. What will be finding of Rinne and weber test and which ear is asked?

option_c: Left rinne's positive, weber lateralized to left ear
option_d: Left rinne negative, weber lateralized to left ear
explanation:
In this case, the patient is experiencing hearing loss in the left ear. The Rinne and Weber tests are used to assess the patient's hearing and lateralization of sound perception.

  • Right Rinne's positive: When the tuning fork is placed on the mastoid bone (bone conduction) and then moved to the front of the ear (air conduction), the patient can hear the sound better through air conduction (front of the ear) than bone conduction (mastoid bone) in the right ear.
  • Weber lateralized to the right ear: When the tuning fork is placed on the center of the forehead, the patient perceives the sound as being louder or localized to the right ear.
  • This is a case of left side Sensorineural hearing loss. Thus Left Rinne's test positive and weber lateralized to the right ear is the correct option.

question_text: Which is the diagnostic investigation of choice in assessing hearing loss in children?
explanation:
BERA (brainstem evoked response audiometry) is to elicit brainstem responses to auditory stimulation by clicks or tone bursts. It is a noninvasive technique to find the integrity of central auditory pathways through the VIIIth nerve, pons and midbrain. In this method, electrical potentials are generated in response to several click stimuli or tone bursts and picked up from the vertex by surface electrodes. It measures hearing sensitivity in the range of 1000-4000 Hz. ABR is used:

  1. As a screening procedure for infants.
  2. To determine the threshold of hearing in infants; also in children and adults who do not cooperate and in malingerers.
  3. To diagnose retrocochlear pathology particularly acoustic neuroma.
  4. To diagnose brainstem pathology, e.g. multiple sclerosis or pontine tumours.
  5. To monitor CN VIII intraoperatively in surgery of acoustic neuromas to preserve the function of cochlear nerve.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9th edition, Pg.no.31,32

question_text: A 48-year-old man with a history of trauma to the right ear presents with pain and hearing loss. Examination showed blood clots filling the ear canal. What is the next step in management?
option_c: Keep the ear dry and give analgesics
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient is most likely to have sustained traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, resulting in blood clots in the ear canal.
  • In cases of traumatic tympanic membrane perforation with blood clots, the safest initial step is to keep the ear dry and provide analgesics.
  • Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane usually heals automatically.
  • Its important to keep the ear dry to prevent infections, thus use of ear drops and syringing is best avoided. (Option B, D ruled out).
  • Aspirating the clot, which seals the bleeding, may potentially cause further complications and is usually unnecessary, as the clot typically resolves spontaneously. (Option A ruled out)
  • Overall, conservative management allows for natural healing of the tympanic membrane and pain relief.

question_text: A patient presents to OPD with a complaint of hearing loss and can understand only shouted or amplified speech. What will be the degree of impairment according to WHO classification of ability to understand speech?

A 78-year-old female complaints of vertigo, intermittent weakness of right lower limb since 2 days, severe headache. On physical examination plethoric face and conjunctive injection, over all dusky cyanotic complexion, pulse 60 BPM, regular, BP 250/110 mm Hg. CBC shows RBC count: 7 to 8 million/mm3, Hematocrit - 60 to 70% and also increase in WBCs and platelets. Which of the following statement is true?
option_a: In this disease the viscosity of blood is drastically decreased
option_b: Given clinical case is of chronic myeloid leukemia
option_c: In this case, there is infective lesion in bone marrow
option_d: Given clinical case is of polycythemia Vera
explanation:
• Polycythemia Vera (PCV) is a myeloproliferative disorder characterized by increased RBCs, WBCs, and platelets. Erythropoietin levels are reduced in PCV. Erythromelalgia is also seen in PCV.
  • Key findings in PCV include:
    • High RBC count and hematocrit (60-70%).
    • Plethoric appearance (red, flushed face) and dusky cyanosis due to increased blood viscosity.
    • BP 250/110 mm Hg and slowed circulation.
  • Increased blood viscosity leads to complications like headaches, vertigo, and thrombotic events.

Why Not Other Options

  • A (Increased blood viscosity, not decreased): Blood viscosity is drastically increased in PCV, causing circulatory issues, not decreased.
  • B (Chronic myeloid leukemia): CML primarily affects WBCs and presents with different clinical features, lacking the characteristic high RBCs and hematocrit seen in PCV.
  • C (Infective lesion in bone marrow): PCV is not caused by infection but by a genetic mutation (JAK2 mutation) in hematopoietic stem cells.

Key Takeaways:

  • Correct Diagnosis: Polycythemia Vera (PCV).
  • Main Issue: Increased RBC production, elevated blood viscosity, and associated symptoms like plethoric face and hypertension.
  • Other myeloproliferative disorders: Essential thrombocytosis, CML, Myelofibrosis.

question_text:
A 20-year-old female patient presented with a complaint of heaviness in her left ear and decreased hearing for 3 months. An endoscopic picture of the affected ear is shown below.

Impedance audiometry was performed, suggesting a type B curve. Which of the following statements is true for this condition?
option_a: Sensorineural deafness occurs as a complication in 80% of patients.
option_b: Tympanostomy tubes are usually required for treatment
option_c: Intracranial spread of infection complicates the clinical course.
option_d: Gram -negative organisms are grown routinely in culture aspirate.
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the endoscopic findings and the type B curve on impedance audiometry, the diagnosis in this case is serous otitis media.

Its management primarily includes antihistamines and decongestants. But if the condition does not resolve even after 3 months, then Myringotomy is performed, followed by placement of a grommet tube or tympanostomy tube to maintain ventilation.

The collected fluid in the middle ear impairs the function of impedance matching of the middle ear and usually does not affect the inner ear. Thus, it leads to conductive deafness. Hence, option A is also not true.

Since it's a sterile fluid collection, the risk of bone erosion and the development of an intracranial abscess is negligible, and on aspiration of this fluid, no organisms are usually isolated; thus, options C and D are not true.

question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with reduced hearing for the past 2-3 months. The otoscopy finding is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

The otoscopic finding of a dull, opaque, and retracted tympanic membrane with visible fluid behind it points towards serous otitis media (SOM). It is also called otitis media with effusion and is one of the most common causes of hearing loss in children.

Serous Otitis Media (SOM)

  • Symptoms
    • Conductive hearing loss: usually mild to moderate (20-40 dB), gradual, and sometimes fluctuating.
    • Speech delay or impaired speech development.
    • Mild ear discomfort or ear fullness.
    • Children may not complain directly; parents often notice inattentiveness or reduced responsiveness.
  • Signs
    • Tympanic membrane: retracted, dull, opaque, may appear yellowish or bluish.
    • Absence of normal light reflex.
    • Fluid or air bubbles may be seen behind the eardrum.
    • Decreased or absent mobility of tympanic membrane (on pneumatic otoscopy).
  • Diagnostic tests
    • Rinne test: negative (bone conduction > air conduction).
    • Weber test: lateralizes to the affected ear.
    • Schwabach test: prolonged bone conduction in the patient compared to examiner.
    • Absolute bone conduction: normal (bone conduction preserved).
    • Impedance audiometry (tympanometry): shows flat or dome-shaped curve.
    • Audiometry: conductive hearing loss of 20-40 dB; sometimes mixed if sensorineural component develops.
    • Imaging: X-ray or CT may reveal mastoid air cell opacification.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Myringitis bullosa (Option A): This presents with painful, blood-stained blisters on the tympanic membrane, usually associated with viral infection or Mycoplasma. It is not seen as a chronic effusion with retracted drum.

Acute otitis media (Option C): Presents with fever, ear pain, irritability, and a red, bulging tympanic membrane. Chronic effusion without bulging is not typical.

Pneumo tympanum (Option D): Seen when there is air in the middle ear due to trauma, barotrauma, or blast injury. Tympanic membrane usually looks hypermobile or abnormally inflated, not retracted with fluid levels.

Key TakeawayIn a child with persistent hearing loss, retracted opaque tympanic membrane, and fluid behind the drum, the diagnosis is serous otitis media.

question_text: You see a child with delayed speech development as part of a health visit at a local school. The otoscopic appearance of the ear is shown below. Hearing loss of 20 dB is detected in audiometric tests. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:
Serous Otitis Media (SOM) or Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) is characterized by:

  • Fluid in the middle ear without signs of acute infection (otoscopy: dull, retracted TM, possible air-fluid levels or bubbles).
  • Conductive hearing loss (typically mild, 20-40 dB).
  • Delayed speech development is a common consequence in children due to the persistent mild hearing impairment.
    This is a classic presentation of OME.
  • Otoscopic Findings:
    • Tympanic membrane may appear dull, translucent, or retracted.
    • No purulent discharge (distinguishes it from acute/chronic suppurative OM).

Pathogenesis:

  1. Eustachian Tube Dysfunction: Failure to aerate/drain the middle ear.
  2. Increased Secretory Activity: Of the middle ear mucosa.

Aetiology:

  • Mechanical Obstruction:
    • Adenoid hyperplasia.
    • Chronic rhinitis/sinusitis.
    • Chronic tonsillitis (enlarged tonsils).
    • Nasopharyngeal tumours (unilateral SOM in adults warrants investigation).
    • Palatal defects (e.g., cleft palate).
  • Inflammatory/Allergic:
    • Allergies (seasonal/perennial).
    • Unresolved otitis media.
    • Viral infections (adenoviruses/rhinoviruses).
  • Other:
    • Down's syndrome.
    • Inadequate antibiotic therapy (leading to persistent low-grade infection).

Treatment

First-Line (Initial Management):

  • Observation & Monitoring: Recommended for the first 3 months if no significant hearing loss or developmental concerns exist. Most cases resolve spontaneously.

Medical Management (Limited/Selective Use):

  • Autoinflation: (e.g., Otovent®) to promote Eustachian tube opening.
  • Treat Contributing Factors: Nasal corticosteroids for associated allergic rhinitis.

Surgical Intervention (If Persistent):

  • Indications: Effusion >3 months with persistent hearing loss (>25-40 dB), speech delay, learning problems, or structural damage.
  • Tympanostomy Tubes: Placement of pressure-equalizing (PE) tubes is the primary and most effective surgical treatment.
  • Adenoidectomy: Considered, especially in cases of nasal obstruction or recurrent OME, typically in children ≥4 years old.

Explanation of other options:
Acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM) (Option A): Presents with acute symptoms like ear pain, fever, and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane. It is an acute infection, not a cause of chronic speech delay.
Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) (Option C): Involves a chronic perforation of the tympanic membrane with persistent purulent discharge. The TM is not intact.
Glomus tumor (Option D): A vascular middle ear tumor that presents with pulsatile tinnitus and a reddish mass behind the TM, not fluid or speech delay.

Key Takeaways:

  • OME is a common cause of conductive hearing loss and subsequent speech delay in children.
  • Otoscopic findings are crucial for diagnosis (dull TM, loss of light reflex, fluid).

question_text: In a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with no improvement after using hearing aids, what should be the ideal next line of management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • For a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) who has not experienced improvement with hearing aids, a cochlear implant is the next appropriate step.
  • A cochlear implant bypasses the damaged parts of the cochlea and directly stimulates the auditory nerve, enabling hearing in individuals with severe-to-profound SNHL who derive limited or no benefit from conventional hearing aids.

Cochlear implantation is recommended in individuals with

  • Severe-to-profound SNHL as confirmed by audiological assessments.
  • Hearing aids provide insufficient benefit.
  • Speech and language development is at risk due to hearing impairment especially in children.

Indications:

  • B/L severe (70-90 dB) to profound (>90 dB) SNHL
  • Prelingual deafness: A child who is born deaf and has not yet developed speech.
  • Post lingual deafness: Child/adult who has become deaf but has already developed speech.

Contraindications:

  • Cochlear aplasia
  • 8th nerve abnormality (like aplasia or retro cochlear pathology, conduction via the auditory nerve is dysfunctional)
  • Central auditory lesions
  • Michel aplasia: Complete absence of the bony and membranous labyrinth, including the petrous apex, while the external and middle ears remain unaffected.

Prerequisites:

  • Age in prelingual deafness: Minimum age as early as possible, maximum age 7 years
  • There is no age limit for post-lingual deafness
  • Failed trial of hearing aid
  • Intact acoustic nerve and central hearing tract

Explanation of other options:

Bone-anchored hearing aid (Option A): This is suitable for patients with conductive or mixed hearing loss, or those with anatomical issues preventing the use of regular hearing aids (e.g., chronic otitis media, atresia). It is not appropriate for severe-to-profound SNHL.

Tympanoplasty (Option B): Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure to repair the tympanic membrane or middle ear structures and is used in conductive hearing loss, not in sensorineural hearing loss.

Normal hearing aid (Option C): The child has already tried hearing aids without improvement. Recommending a different hearing aid would not be beneficial in cases of severe-to-profound SNHL.

Reference:

  1. Cochlear Implants - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: A 43 year old mechanical engineer has presented to outpatient clinic with the complaint of right sided hearing loss and Tinnitus. These symptoms have been troubling him for last one year. The hearing loss is progressive in nature. Ear examination of the patient is normal. Pure tone audiometry has shown right sided sensorineural hearing loss. MRI Brain shows space occupying lesion at right cerebellopontine angle. Which of the following is the most likely & earliest clinical finding which can be detected on nervous system examination in this patient?
explanation:
• Vth nerve. This is the earliest nerve to be involved. There is reduced corneal sensitivity, numbness or paraesthesia of face. Involvement of this nerve indicates that the tumour is roughly 2.5 cm in diameter and occupies the cerebellopontine angle.
  • VIIth nerve. Sensory fibres are affected early. There is hypoaesthesia of posterior meatal wall (Hitzelberger's sign), loss of taste (as tested by electrogustometry) and reduced lacrimation on Schirmer test. Motor fibres are more resistant and are affected late. Delayed blink reflex may be an early manifestation.
  • IXth and Xth nerves. There is dysphagia and hoarseness due to palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal paralysis.
  • Other cranial nerves. XIth and XIIth, IIIrd, IVth and VIth are affected when tumour is very large.

question_text: Which of the following structures are in close proximity to the affected structure in a 70-year-old male patient presenting with decreased hearing in higher frequencies, where the basilar membrane has been affected?
explanation:
Explanation

In presbycusis, high-frequency hearing loss occurs first because the basilar membrane at the base of the cochlea (nearest to the oval window) is responsible for detecting high-frequency sounds. With aging, degeneration of hair cells in this region leads to progressive hearing loss.

  • The oval window lies close to the basal turn of the cochlea and directly transmits vibrations from the stapes into the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
  • These vibrations initiate movement of the basilar membrane, with the base tuned to high-frequency sounds.
  • Hence, in elderly patients with high-frequency hearing loss, pathology involves the portion of the basilar membrane nearest to the oval window.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Modiolus (Option A): The modiolus is the central bony core of the cochlea, housing the spiral ganglion cells and providing support for the cochlear nerve. While important structurally, it is not directly adjacent to the basal basilar membrane where high-frequency sound detection occurs.

Stria vascularis (Option B): Located along the lateral wall of the cochlear duct, this structure produces endolymph and maintains the ionic composition necessary for hair cell function. It is not in direct proximity to the basal turn of the basilar membrane affected in high-frequency hearing loss.

Helicotrema (Option D): Found at the apex of the cochlea, it connects the scala vestibuli and scala tympani. The apical basilar membrane is sensitive to low-frequency sounds, not high frequencies, and is far from the oval window.

Key Takeaway

In age-related high-frequency hearing loss, the basilar membrane near the oval window is most affected, as this region is specialized for high-frequency sound detection.

question_text: All of the following are features of retrocochlear hearing loss, except?
option_b: Only wave 1 is present in BERA; the rest are absent or affected.
explanation:
Explanation:

Retrocochlear hearing loss shows tone decay, often markedly so, because the affected nerve cannot maintain continuous firing.

Recruitment is seen in cochlear lesions. In retrocochlear pathology, recruitment is typically absent (Option A).

Retrocochlear lesions (especially at the level of the VIII nerve) show normal wave I (generated by the cochlea/auditory nerve periphery) but delayed or absent waves II to V (Option B).

The SISI (Short Increment Sensitivity Index) is low in retrocochlear lesions because small intensity increments are poorly perceived. High SISI is a feature of cochlear lesions (Option C).

A 31-year-old female patient presented with complaints of Bilateral impairment of hearing for the past 3 years. On examination, the Bilateral tympanic membranes were normal and intact.
