question_text: A 30 year old female patient presents with hearing loss. The pure tone audiometry shows the audiogram given below. What is tge most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
The image in the question shows a PTA with dip at 2000 Hz in bone conduction i.e. Carhart's notch.

  • PTA in Otosclerosis shows loss of air conduction, more for lower frequencies.
  • Bone conduction is normal. In some cases, there is a dip in bone conduction curve. It is different at different frequencies but maximum at 2000 Hz and is called Carhart's notch (5 dB at 500 Hz, 10 dB at 1000 Hz, 15 dB at 2000 Hz and 5 dB at 4000 Hz)
  • Carhart's notch disappears after successful stapedectomy.
  • Meniers ds cause rising type of curve
  • Noise induced hearing loss shows boiler notch.

question_text: Which of the following tests is the initial test for neonatal screening of hearing of a healthy newborn?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard initial screening test for hearing in a healthy newborn is Evoked Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE), specifically Transient Evoked Otoacoustic Emissions (TEOAE).

Principle of OAE:

Otoacoustic emissions are sounds generated by the Outer Hair Cells (OHC) of the cochlea in response to an acoustic stimulus. These "echoes" are recorded by a probe placed in the ear canal.

  • If echoes are recorded (PASS), it indicates the cochlear mechanism is functioning normally.
  • It is objective, non-invasive, rapid, and cost-effective, making it ideal for mass screening of healthy infants.

Universal Newborn Hearing Screening Protocol:

  • Healthy Newborns (Well-Baby Nursery): OAE is the first-line screening tool.
  • High-Risk Newborns (NICU, Meningitis, Severe Jaundice, Family History): Automated Auditory Brainstem Response (AABR/BERA) is the screening test of choice. This is because high-risk infants have a higher incidence of auditory neuropathy (neural conduction defects) where the cochlea may function normally (OAE Pass), but the nerve does not (Hearing Loss).

Types of OAE:

  1. Spontaneous OAE (SOAE): Occurs without stimulus.
  2. Evoked OAE: Occurs in response to sound.
    • Transient Evoked OAE (TEOAE): Elicited by a click (1 stimulus). This is the type most commonly used for screening.
    • Distortion Product OAE (DPOAE): Elicited by two simultaneous pure tones.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Automated auditory brainstem response (Option A): While highly accurate and testing the entire auditory pathway up to the brainstem, it is more time-consuming and expensive than OAE. It is reserved for high-risk infants (NICU) or as a confirmatory test for babies who fail the OAE screen.
  • Spontaneous Oto acoustic emissions (Option B): These occur without external sound stimulation but are present in only about 50-70% of people with normal hearing. Therefore, the absence of SOAE does not imply hearing loss, making it useless for screening.
  • Pure tone audiometry (Option D): This is a subjective test requiring the patient to respond to sound (raise a hand or press a button). It cannot be performed on newborns.

Key Takeaway:

  • Healthy Newborn Screening: Evoked OAE (TEOAE).
  • High-Risk/NICU Screening: BERA/AABR.
  • OAE tests Outer Hair Cell function.

question_text: Which of the following statements correctly describes BERA?
option_a: It can be used for screening for hearing loss
option_c: It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss
explanation:
Explanation:

  • BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) measures the electrical activity of the auditory pathways in response to clicks or tone bursts.
  • It is non-invasive, using surface electrodes on the scalp, and does not require surgery or insertion of instruments. (Option B ruled out).

Key Features

  • Objective test: Does not rely on patient feedback. (Option D ruled out)
  • Evaluates auditory pathway up to the brainstem.
  • Shows 7 waves (I-VII); Wave V, generated by the lateral lemniscus, is the most important.

Uses

  • Assessment of sensorineural hearing loss, especially in infants, young children, or uncooperative patients.
  • Differentiating cochlear vs retrocochlear hearing loss.
  • Evaluation of malingerers (for medico-legal cases).
  • Considered the gold standard investigation for hearing loss. (Option A ruled out)

Limitations

  • Frequency non-specific.
  • Does not assess the auditory cortex.

question_text: Cause of decreased bone conduction on audiogram?
explanation:
• Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from lesions of the cochlea, VIIIthnerve or central auditory pathways.
  • It may be present at birth (congenital) or start later in life (acquired). The characteristics of sensorineural hearing loss are:
  1. A positive Rinne test, i.e. AC > BC.
  2. Weber lateralized to better ear.
  3. Bone conduction reduced on Schwabach and absolute bone conduction tests.
  4. More often involving high frequencies.
  5. No gap between air and bone conduction curve on audiometry
  6. Loss may exceed 60 dB.
  7. Speech discrimination is poor.
  8. There is difficulty in hearing in the presence of noise.

Other options:

Other three options A, C and D give conductive hearing loss on audiogram.

question_text: An industrial worker presents with hearing loss. On examination, Rinne's test was negative on the left side and positive on the right side. Weber's test lateralized to the left side. Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) was done with the results as shown below. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is a left conductive hearing loss, which is consistently supported by all the provided findings.

  1. Rinne's Test: A negative result on the left (Bone Conduction > Air Conduction) is the classic sign of a conductive hearing loss in that ear. The positive result on the right is normal.
  2. Weber's Test: The sound lateralizing to the left ear indicates a conductive hearing loss on that same side.
  3. Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA):
    • Right Ear: The audiogram shows hearing thresholds within the normal range (0-20 dB).
    • Left Ear: The audiogram shows normal bone conduction thresholds (upper line, squares) but significantly elevated air conduction thresholds (lower line, crosses). I.e., AC is poor, BC is normal. The difference between these two lines is the air-bone gap, which is the hallmark of a conductive hearing loss.
    • In SNHL, both AC & BC are poor

Explanation of Other Options:

Right conductive hearing loss (Option A): Incorrect, since Rinne's test was positive on the right and no air-bone gap on the right PTA.

Right sensorineural hearing loss (Option C): Incorrect, would cause Weber lateralization to the left, but Rinne would also be positive on the left, not negative.

Left sensorineural hearing loss (Option D): A left SNHL would present with a positive Rinne's test (as both AC and BC would be reduced), Weber's lateralizing to the right (better) ear, and an audiogram showing both air and bone conduction thresholds depressed together, with no significant air-bone gap.

Key Takeaway:

question_text: Most common hearing test done in neonates for screening:
explanation:
Explanation:

Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the primary, first-line screening test for neonatal hearing. It is quick, non-invasive, objective, and does not require a behavioral response from the baby. It tests the integrity of the outer hair cells of the cochlea.

Pathway:

  • Normal functioning outer hair cells → generate sound vibrations → detected in external ear canal.
  • Absence of OAE suggests outer hair cell damage, as seen in cochlear or middle ear pathologies.

Types:

  1. Spontaneous OAE:
    • Occur without external stimulation.
    • May be absent in up to 50% of normal individuals.
  2. Evoked OAE:
    • Require an external auditory stimulus.
    • Transient Evoked OAE (TEOAE): Elicited by click sounds containing multiple frequencies.
    • Distortion Product OAE (DPOAE): Produced when two pure tones of different frequencies are presented simultaneously, generating distortion products.

Clinical Applications:

  • Newborn hearing screening.
  • Assessment in uncooperative or cognitively impaired patients.
  • Differentiates cochlear from retrocochlear hearing loss.
  • Early detection of noise-induced hearing loss.

Explanation of other options:

Clap & smile (Option A): A subjective behavioral observation, not a reliable screening test.

BERA/ABR (Option B): Used as a diagnostic test or for screening in high-risk neonates (e.g., NICU graduates). It is more complex and time-consuming than OAE.

PTA (Option D): Requires a conscious behavioral response, which is impossible for a neonate.

Key Takeaways:

  • Neonatal Screening: OAE (first line) → BERA/ABR (for confirmation/follow-up).

question_text:
The parents bring in a 6-month-old child with the complaint of not responding to any auditory stimulation. A hearing assessment of the child was done using a test. The test picture is shown below.

Which of the following is true about this test?
option_a: It can differentiate between cochlear and retrocochlear hearing loss
option_b: It cannot differentiate the site of sensorineural hearing loss
option_c: It can differentiate barbiturate poisoning from other causes of coma.
option_d: It is used as a screening test for hearing assessment in infants.
explanation:
Explanation:

The test shown in this picture is called Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA).

BERA is an objective test. It detects spontaneous electrical activity in the entire auditory pathway (Option B).

In a normal person, a 5 to 7 wave graph is formed, out of which wave 5 is the most important one.

Uses:

It is the best audiometric test for confirming hearing loss in infants. OAE is the best screening test; thus, OAE is used for screening, and BERA is used for confirmation (Option D).

It is the best test for differentiating cochlear from retrocochlear hearing loss.

It is the best test for detecting nonorganic hearing loss (malingering) (Option C).

It is the best test for acoustic neuroma and central auditory disorders.

Cochlear cause: Delayed Wave 1

Retrocochlear cause: Normal Wave 1, but other waves absent / reduced.

option_c: Absent acoustic brainstem evoked auditory responses
option_d: Absent contralateral suppression of otoacoustic emissions
explanation:
Otoacoustic Emissions are useful to diagnose retrocochlear pathology, especially auditory neuropathy. Auditory neuropathy is a neurologic disorder of CN VIII. Audiometric tests, e.g. SNHL for pure tones, impaired speech discrimination score, absent or abnormal auditory brainstem response, show a retrocochlear type of lesion but OAEs are normal.

question_text:
If OAE is absent in a patient, which other screening test can be done?
A. BERA
B. Tympanometry
C. Audiometry
D. Speech Audiometry
explanation:
OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions) is a test that measures sound emissions produced by the cochlea in response to acoustic stimuli. If OAE is absent, it may indicate a problem in the cochlea's function. To further assess the patient's hearing, the following tests can be done:

B. Tympanometry: Tympanometry is a test that measures the compliance of the middle ear and the mobility of the eardrum (tympanic membrane). It helps detect conditions such as middle ear effusion (fluid), tympanic membrane perforation, or other disorders affecting the middle ear.

D. Speech Audiometry: Speech audiometry evaluates the patient's ability to hear and understand speech at different volumes. It is used to determine the patient's hearing threshold for speech and assess their ability to discriminate speech sounds.

A. BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry): It is suitable for assessing cochlear function or detecting OAE since it measures auditory brainstem responses, mainly focusing on the function of the auditory nerve and brainstem pathways.

C. Audiometry: It is not a suitable alternative for OAE because audiometry assesses hearing sensitivity at different frequencies but does not directly measure the cochlear emissions detected by OAE.

question_text: A 64-year-old female presents with difficulty in comprehension. On examination: fluency intact, poor comprehension, poor repetition. Pure tone audiometry and ABR are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent speech but impaired comprehension and repetition.
  • Speech may have normal rate and grammar but lacks meaningful content.
  • Most common cause: Ischemic stroke affecting the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere.
  • Normal audiometry and ABR indicate that the auditory apparatus and brainstem pathways are intact; the deficit is cortical (processing and comprehension).

Explanation of Other Options:

Malingering (Option A): Deliberate feigning or exaggeration of deficits; not supported by clinical pattern.

Auditory cortex lesion (Option B): Lesions may cause deficits in sound perception but typically involve ABR changes and additional auditory deficits.

Broca's aphasia (Option C): Non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension, impaired speech production, and grammatical errors; does not match this patient's presentation.

question_text: All of the following are smell perception tests except?
explanation:
The Arnold stick test is a test for olfaction that involves the use of a cotton swab dipped in a chemical called amyl acetate. The swab is then waved in front of the patient's nose, and the patient is asked to identify the smell. This test is not a reliable measure of smell perception because the smell of amyl acetate is very strong and can be easily detected even by people with impaired smell.

All of the options except Arnold stick test are used to measure smell perception. Arnold stick test is not a reliable measure of smell perception because the smell of amyl acetate is very strong and can be easily detected even by people with impaired smell.

A. Smell diskettes

Smell diskettes are small, disposable disks that contain a variety of different odors. The patient is asked to smell the diskettes and identify the odors. This test is a measure of the patient's ability to smell.

B. UP-SIT

UP-SIT stands for Upper Airway Resistance Sensitivity Index Test. This test is used to assess the resistance of the upper airway to airflow. The test is performed by measuring the pressure drop across the upper airway when the patient breathes in and out.

C. CC-SIT

CC-SIT stands for Conductance Change Sensitivity Index Test. This test is also used to assess the resistance of the upper airway to airflow. The test is performed by measuring the change in conductance of the upper airway when the patient breathes in and out.

question_text: Which of the following tests cannot be used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance?
explanation:
Nasal mucociliary clearance refers to the process by which mucus and debris are cleared from the nasal passages through the action of cilia on the nasal epithelium. Several tests can be used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance, but electron microscopy is not one of them.

These are valid methods to assess nasal mucociliary clearance:

A. Saccharine Test: This is a simple test in which a small amount of saccharine is placed in the nostril, and the time it takes for the patient to perceive a sweet taste in the mouth is measured. The movement of saccharine through the nasal passages indicates mucociliary clearance.

C. Charcoal powder method: In this test, charcoal particles are insufflated into the nasal cavity, and the time it takes for the patient to expectorate the particles is measured. The clearance of charcoal particles indicates mucociliary clearance.

D. Scintigraphy: Radioactive particles are used in this test to assess the movement of mucus through the nasal passages and the clearance of radioactive particles indicates mucociliary clearance.

Electron microscopy is not a method used for assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Instead, it is a microscopic technique used to study the ultrastructure of cilia and mucociliary function in certain research settings.

question_text: The framework of the external nose:
option_b: Upper ½ is bony, and lower 1/2 is cartilaginous
option_c: The upper 2/3rd is bony and the lower 1/3rd is cartilaginous
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The external nose is formed by both bone and cartilage.
  • The upper one-third of the structure is bony, while the lower two-thirds are cartilaginous.

External nose anatomy:

  • Shaped like a pyramid, with its root directed upward and the base downward.
  • The framework is osteocartilaginous and covered by skin and small muscles.
  • Bony part → nasal bones, frontal bone, and the ascending process of the maxilla.
  • Cartilaginous part → includes upper lateral cartilage, lower lateral (alar) cartilages, sesamoid cartilages, and septal cartilage.
    • Upper lateral cartilages: extend downward from the nasal bones and join the septal cartilage; their lower edge forms the nasal valve (limen nasi).
    • Lower lateral (alar) cartilages: U-shaped with a lateral crus forming the ala and a medial crus forming the columella; they overlap the lower border of the upper lateral cartilages.
    • Lesser alar (sesamoid) cartilages: small accessory cartilages situated above the alar cartilage.
    • Septal cartilage (quadrangular cartilage): supports the cartilaginous dorsum; damage or resection may cause a supratip depression.

Explanation of other options:

  • Option B & C: Misrepresent the relative proportions of bony and cartilaginous parts.
  • Option D: Incorrect since the framework is well-defined as 1/3 bony and 2/3 cartilaginous.

question_text: A 5-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with bleeding from the nose. Examination reveals trauma to Little's area. Which of the following arteries does not contribute to the vascular plexus in this region?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Little's area, or Kiesselbach's plexus, is formed by an anastomosis of several arteries supplying the anterior nasal septum.
  • The posterior ethmoidal artery does not take part in this plexus.

Kiesselbach's Plexus Arterial Contributions:

  • Anterior ethmoidal artery (septal branch)
  • Sphenopalatine artery (septal branch) (Option A)
  • Greater palatine artery (septal branch) (Option B)
  • Superior labial artery (branch of facial artery) (Option C)

These vessels form a dense vascular network, making Little's area the most common site of anterior epistaxis in children.

Posterior Ethmoidal Artery:

  • Supplies the superior and posterior part of the nasal cavity.
  • Does not participate in the anterior septal arterial plexus.

question_text: A 75-year-old male who is a known case of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with epistaxis, which does not respond to conservative measures and nasal packing. Which of the following arteries should be prioritised for ligation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The sphenopalatine artery is the main blood supply to the posterior nasal cavity. Posterior epistaxis (especially in elderly hypertensive patients) commonly involves this artery. It is often called the "artery of epistaxis."

When packing fails, endoscopic ligation or embolisation of the sphenopalatine artery is the preferred next step.

The following arteries are ligated for control of epistaxis.

  • Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation(TESPAL) is done first.
  • If uncontrolled, ligation of the maxillary arteryis done.
  • Then, ligation of the external carotid arteryabove the origin of the superior thyroid artery should be done.
  • If still uncontrolled, ligation of the ethmoidal arteries is done.

Explanation of other options:

Posterior ethmoidal artery  (Option A): supplies the Roof of the nasal cavity, ethmoid sinuses, and has a rare role in epistaxis

Anterior ethmoidal artery(Option B): more involved in anterior/superior epistaxis.

Greater palatine artery (Option D): supplies the inferior nasal septum and palate and has a Minor, accessory role in epistaxis

question_text: A child is suffering from goitre and sensorineural hearing loss. He is diagnosed to be the case of Pendred syndrome. This syndrome occurs due to defect in which of the following transporter?
explanation:
• Pendred syndrome is caused by a defect in the iodide-chloride antiporter, also known as Pendrin. Occurs due to mutation in SLC26A4 gene mutation on chromosome 7.
  • This defect leads to:
    • Goitre: due to impaired iodide transport into the thyroid gland, resulting in insufficient iodide for thyroid hormone synthesis.
    • Sensorineural hearing loss: associated with defects in the inner ear due to the malfunction of Pendrin, which is involved in ion transport in the cochlea.

Triad of pendred syndrome: congenital sensorineural hearing loss,goitre,impaired ioidide organification.

Why Not Others

  • A (Sodium Iodide Symporter): This transporter is essential for iodide uptake in the thyroid but is not the defect in Pendred syndrome.
  • C (Sodium potassium pump): This pump maintains membrane potential and is not directly related to iodide transport or Pendred syndrome.
  • D (Sodium chloride hydride cotransporter): This transporter is not involved in Pendred syndrome.

Key Takeaways

  • Correct answer: Option B, the iodide-chloride antiporter (Pendrin) is defective in Pendred syndrome, causing goitre and sensorineural hearing loss.
  • The syndrome highlights the critical role of Pendrin in both thyroid function and auditory health.

question_text: Name the anterior most ethmoidal cell marked in the figure

It is an important landmark in functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) and plays a role in creating access to the frontal recess.

A. Concha bullosa: It refers to the pneumatization or presence of an air-filled cavity within one of the nasal turbinates (conchae). Concha bullosa can be found in the middle or inferior turbinates and is a common anatomical variation.

B. Bulla ethmoidalis: Bulla ethmoidalis refers to a rounded, bubble-like prominence or a pneumatized cavity in the middle meatus region of the nasal cavity. It is formed due to the pneumatization of ethmoid air cells.

D. Onodi cells: Onodi cells are the part of posterior ethmoid air cells. They line in close proximity to the sphenoid sinus, carotid artery and optic nerve.

question_text: Which structure does the anterior ethmoidal sinus drain into?
explanation:
Explanation:

The anterior ethmoidal sinus drains into the middle meatus.

Lateral nasal wall

  • The lateral wall of the nose has three scroll-like bony projections covered by mucous membrane called the inferior, middle, and superior conchae.
  • They extend medially across the nasal cavity, separating it into four air channels: the inferior, middle, and superior meatus and a sphenoethmoidal recess.
  • The nasolacrimal duct and most of the paranasal sinuses open onto the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.
  • The frontal sinus opens into the middle meatus infront of the hiatus semilunaris.
  • The maxillary sinus also opens into the middle meatus, posteriorly within the hiatus semilunaris.
  • The ethmoid sinuses are divided into anterior, middle, and posterior groups, each opening into a different meatus.
    • Anterior ethmoid air sinuses open into the middle meatus within the hiatus semilunaris.
    • Middle ethmoid air sinuses also open into the middle meatus on the ethmoid bulla, a rounded elevation.
    • Posterior ethmoid air sinuses open into the superior meatus.
  • The sphenoid sinus opens above the superior turbinate into the sphenoethmoidal recess.
  • The nasolacrimal duct, carrying tears from the eye, opens into the inferior meatus. Its opening is guarded by a valve called Hasner's valve.
  • The opening of the Eustachian tube (pharyngotympanic tube), connecting the nasopharynx to the middle ear cavity, is located in the nasopharynx just behind the inferior turbinate at the level of the inferior meatus.

explanation:
Explanation:

Frontal sinuses typically become visible on X-ray around 4 years of age. Although their development begins earlier, they are too small to be clearly seen on radiographs until this age and continue to grow throughout childhood.

question_text: Which structure cannot be approached through transnasal endoscopic surgery?
explanation:
Think about the anatomy of the eye - lacrimal glands lie in lateral part of orbit. So cannot be approached via transnasal route.

Endoscopic surgery can be used to access the orbit, optic nerve, lacrimal sac and pituitary gland in addition to the nose and paranasal sinuses.

question_text: Which of the following is not true about physiology of nose?
option_a: The inspiratory and expiratory air currents pass through middle part of nasal cavity
option_b: Sinuses are mainly ventilated during inspiratory phase of respiration
option_c: Nasal cilia beat 10-20 times per second and mucociliary clearance time is 10 -20 minutes.
option_d: Nasal cycle of rhythmic congestion and decongestion varies every 2.5 to 4 hours
explanation:
The sinuses are ventilated mainly during expiratory phase of respiration.

During expiration, friction offered at limen nasi converts part of the air currents into eddies under cover of inferior and middle turbinates and this ventilates the sinuses through the ostia.

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no 162

question_text: Which of the following is not true about physiology of nose
option_a: The inspiratory and expiratory air currents pass through middle part of nasal cavity
option_b: Sinuses are mainly ventilated during expiratory phase of respiration
option_c: Nasal cilia beat 10-20 times per second and the mucociliary clearance time is 10 -20 minutes
option_d: The rhythmic congestion and decongestion  is seen in vasomotor rhinitis
explanation:
Nasal cycle of rhythmic congestion and decongestion is seen in all normal individuals. The duration of this cycle varies every 2.5 to 4 hours.

This occurs because of the autonomic nerve supply of the nose. Nasal mucosa has rich blood supply. Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction and shrinkage of mucosa, while parasympathetic stimulation causes vasodilation and engorgement.

Autonomic system is unstable in cases of vasomotor rhinitis. So the rhythmic congestion and decongestion is disturbed.

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no 162, 198

question_text: All statements are true about Ringertz tumour of Nose except
option_a: Arises  from upper part of nasal septum
explanation:
Ringertz tumor arises from lateral wall of nose.

Inverted Papilloma (Transitional Cell Papilloma or Ringertz Tumour or Schneiderian Papilloma)

  • It is a tumour of the non-olfactory mucosa of nose (Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses.
  • Most common site of origin is lateral wall of nose in the middle meatus
  • It is a benign but locally invasive tumour and can show malignant conversion.
  • Human papilloma virus is thought to be responsible for its aetiology.
  • Clinically, men are affected more than women in the age group of 40–70.

question_text: All of the following investigations are helpful in the diagnostic assessment of a patient of CSF Rhinorrhea except
explanation:
X ray of paranasal sinuses has no role in the diagnosis of CSF rhinorrhea.

Beta-2 transferrin is the best confirmatory test.

CT cisternogram - requires intrathecal injection of iohexol and a CT scan to localize the site of leak in cases when beta-2 transferrin cannot be done.

Nasal endoscopy can be done to identify the site of leak and for its repair.

OTHER TESTS FOR LOCALIZATION OF SITE OF CSF LEAK-

  • High-resolution CT scan - important to see the bony defects.
  • MRI - requires that CSF leak is active at the time of scan.
  • Intrathecal fluorescein study- Dye appears bright yellow but when seen with a blue filter it appears fluorescent green.

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8th edition, page 192

question_text: Occipitomental view with open mouth view to check for nose and paranasal sinus?
explanation:
The Occipitomental view with an open mouth view is commonly known as the "Pierre view." This imaging technique is used to visualize the nose and paranasal sinuses and is particularly useful in assessing the maxillary sinuses and the nasal bones.


Other options:

B.Waters view: The Waters view is a radiographic view used to visualize the maxillary sinuses and their relationship to the orbital floor. It does not require the open mouth position.

C.Caldwell view: The Caldwell view is an X-ray projection used to evaluate the frontal sinuses and their relationship to the orbits. It is taken with the patient's head tilted backward but does not involve an open mouth view.


D.Townes view: The Townes view, also known as the "jug-handle" view, is used for imaging the skull base, including the sella turcica. It is not used to check the nose and paranasal sinuses. It helps to visualize foramen magnum, petrous temporal bone

question_text: Identify the structure marked with black arrow on nasal endoscopy
explanation:
Three and occasionally four turbinates or conchae mark the lateral wall of nose. They are scroll-like bony projections covered by mucous membrane. The spaces below the turbinate is called meatus.

MIDDLE TURBINATE

  • It is an ethmoturbinal—a part of ethmoid bone.
  • It is attached to the lateral wall by a bony lamella called ground or basal lamella – the attachment is not straight but in an S-shaped
  • The ostia of various sinuses draining anterior to basal lamella form anterior group of paranasal sinuses while those which open posterior and superior to it form the posterior group.

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no 156,157

question_text: During a nasal endoscopy, a surgeon observes the opening of the nasolacrimal duct. Into which of the following structures does the nasolacrimal duct drain?
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct answer is the Inferior meatus. The lateral wall of the nasal cavity contains three shelf-like projections called turbinates (or conchae): superior, middle, and inferior. The space beneath each turbinate is called a meatus. These meatuses are clinically important as they are the drainage sites for the paranasal sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct.

The nasolacrimal duct, which drains tears from the eye into the nose, opens into the inferior meatus.

Drainage into Nasal Meatuses:

Explanation of Other Options:

Superior meatus (Option A): This is the drainage site for the posterior ethmoidal air cells.

Middle meatus (Option B): This is the common and complex drainage pathway for the frontal, maxillary, and anterior/middle ethmoidal sinuses.

Sphenoethmoidal recess (Option D): This small area, located above the superior turbinate, is the drainage site for the sphenoid sinus.

question_text: A diabetic patient presented to OPD with blood stained nasal discharge and progressive blackish nasal discoloration. Which of the following is the choice of therapy?
explanation:
• The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mucormycosis.
  • Mucormycosis is acute invasive fungal infection involving nose and paranasal sinuses, where fungal hyphae invade blood vessels causing ischaemic necrosis.
  • Commonly involves lateral nasal walls and turbinates and quickly spreads to orbit, palate, face and cranium.
  • Treatment is surgical debridement and Amphotericin-B.

question_text: A 60-year-old post-COVID male patient came with complaints of one-sided facial swelling, headache, and nasal sinus congestion. He is diabetic and it is uncontrolled. On examination black lesions on the nasal bridge and upper inside of the mouth were observed. Which investigation would you do to confirm the diagnosis of this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's presentation-unilateral facial swelling, sinus congestion, black eschar in the nasal and oral cavity, and uncontrolled diabetes post-COVID-is highly suggestive of mucormycosis.
  • The gold standard for confirming mucormycosis is biopsy with histopathologic examination, which demonstrates broad, aseptate fungal hyphae with tissue invasion.
  • Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount and fungal culture may also support the diagnosis, but tissue biopsy is definitive.

Mucormycosis:

  • Aggressive fungal infection affecting the nose and paranasal sinuses, which rapidly spreads to orbit, brain, and meninges.
  • The fungus invades arteries, leading to thrombosis, necrosis, and tissue destruction.
  • Clinical features: Black necrotic debris in nasal cavity, involvement of septum, turbinates, or palate; "black turbinate sign" on contrast-enhanced MRI.
  • Risk factors:
    • Uncontrolled diabetes (especially ketoacidosis)
    • Prolonged corticosteroid therapy (common in post-COVID patients)
    • Immunosuppression (chemotherapy, neutropenia, HIV, organ transplantation, chronic kidney disease)
  • Diagnosis:
    • Endoscopy: Initially pale mucosa, later black crusting and necrosis.
    • Biopsy: Gold standard; shows angioinvasive broad aseptate hyphae.
    • Imaging:
      • CT: Detects sinus involvement and bony destruction.
      • CECT: Better defines sinus opacification, mucosal thickening, and extent of bone erosion.
      • MRI: Evaluates soft tissue spread, orbital and intracranial extension.
    • Treatment:
      • Antifungals: Amphotericin B (0.6-1 mg/kg/day IV) or Liposomal Amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day); Posaconazole as step-down oral therapy.
      • Surgery: Endoscopic debridement; in severe cases, maxillectomy or orbital exenteration.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

X-ray (Option A): Conventional X-rays are inadequate for diagnosing mucormycosis. They fail to detect early fungal invasion or soft tissue extension. CT and MRI are superior imaging tools.

Serum ferritin (Option C): Elevated ferritin and iron overload predispose patients to mucormycosis, but ferritin testing is not diagnostic. It cannot confirm or exclude the infection.

HbA1c (Option D): Reflects long-term blood sugar control. Poor control is a risk factor for mucormycosis, but HbA1c has no role in confirming fungal infection.

Key Takeaway: -In a post-COVID diabetic patient with black necrotic nasal or palatal lesions, biopsy with histopathology is the gold standard for diagnosing mucormycosis. Imaging supports staging, but tissue confirmation is mandatory to establish the diagnosis and guide urgent antifungal and surgical management.

question_text: Obstruction of which sinus drainage is seen in the image provided?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image appears to show a nasal endoscopy view of inflamed and polypoidal mucosa obstructing the middle meatus, which is the drainage site of the maxillary sinus.

The maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus via the ostiomeatal complex (OMC), which includes the hiatus semilunaris and infundibulum. Any obstruction in this pathway leads to maxillary sinusitis, commonly seen with nasal polyps.

The maxillary sinus:

The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore, is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, occupying the body of the maxilla.

  • Shape - Pyramidal
  • Size - 15mL
  • Base - toward the lateral wall of the nose
  • Apex - extends into the zygomatic process of the maxillary bone

Relations:

  • Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla.
  • Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa.
  • Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity.
  • Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit
  • Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro antral fistula.
  • Arterial supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, specifically the infraorbital artery, greater palatine artery, and the posterior superior alveolar artery.
  • Venous drainage: Pterygoid venous plexus and the facial vein.
  • Lymphatic drainage: Submandibular lymph nodes.
  • Nerve supply: Infraorbital nerve, greater palatine nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve, which are branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2).

Ethmoid Sinus (Option B): is incorrect because the ethmoid sinuses primarily drain into the middle and superior meatus, and their obstruction is associated with frontal or sphenoethmoidal recess involvement.

Sphenoid Sinus (Option C): is incorrect because it drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess, located superiorly, which is not prominently obstructed in this image.

Frontal Sinus (Option D): is incorrect because it drains into the middle meatus via the frontal recess, and its obstruction is more commonly associated with frontal headaches and pain above the eyes.

question_text: Which fungal infection is frequently observed in the maxillary sinus?
explanation:
Explanation:
Aspergillosis is the most common fungal infection of the paranasal sinuses, with the maxillary sinus being the most frequently involved site.

It can present in various forms: fungal ball (non-invasive), chronic invasive, or allergic fungal sinusitis.

Explanation of other options:
Blastomycosis (Option A): A systemic fungal infection endemic to certain regions (e.g., North America); primarily involves the lungs and skin; sinus involvement is rare.
Candidiasis (Option C): Typically causes mucocutaneous infections (oral thrush, vaginitis); isolated sinus involvement is very uncommon.

Histoplasmosis (Option D): Another systemic fungal infection endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys; primarily involves the lungs; sinus involvement is not characteristic.

Key Takeaways:

  • Aspergillus species are the predominant fungi causing sinus infections.
  • The maxillary sinus is the most common location for fungal sinusitis.

question_text: Identify the sinus marked in the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The labelled sinus in the given Xray - Water's view is the maxillary sinus.

  • The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore, is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, occupying the body of the maxilla.
  • It is pyramid-shaped and lies lateral to the nasal cavity, with its base forming the lateral wall of the nose and its apex extending towards the zygomatic process of maxillary bone.
  • On radiographic or anatomical images, it appears as a large, air-filled cavity inferior to the orbit and lateral to the nasal cavity.
  • Drains into the middle meatus of the nasal cavity through the semilunar hiatus.
  • Commonly involved in sinusitis due to the high location of its drainage opening.

Maxillary sinus: Relations

  • Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla.
  • Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa.
  • Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity.
  • Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit
  • Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro antral fistula.

Explanation of other options:

Frontal sinus (Option A): Located above the orbit in the frontal bone; appears superior to the nasal cavity and orbits in images.

Pyriform sinus (Option B): This is a structure in the hypopharynx, not a paranasal sinus. It is unrelated to the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses.

Ethmoid sinus (Option C): Consists of multiple small air cells located between the eyes, medial to the orbit, and posterior to the nasal cavity. These appear as smaller clusters on imaging.

Reference:

  1. Anatomy, Head and Neck, Nose Paranasal Sinuses - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: Identify the X-ray view shown in the given image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray shown is the Waters' view, also known as the occipitomental view.

Xray Views of Paranasal sinuses:

Water's view

  • Water's view is the radiographic projection that provides the best visualization of the maxillary sinus.
  • In this view, the chin touches the X-ray plate.
  • Opening the mouth in Water's view helps visualize the sphenoid sinus from the base of the sphenoid area because the teeth, which are opaque, are moved out of the way.
  • Water's view shows all sinuses except the posterior ethmoid most clearly.

Pierre's view

  • Water's view with open mouth is also referred to as Pierre's view.
  • Best view to visualise sphenoid sinus.

Caldwell's view

  • Caldwell's view (occipito-frontal view) is the best view for the frontal and ethmoid sinuses.
  • In this view, the forehead touches the X-ray plate.
  • The ethmoid air cells are nicely visible in this view.

Lateral View

  • Allows visualization of all sinuses (frontal, maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoidal).
  • Helps to understand the pneumatization pattern of the sphenoid sinus.

Explanation of other options:

Towne's view (Option B): Towne's view is used primarily for imaging the skull, particularly the occipital region, and is not specifically for the maxillary sinus.

Law's view (Option C): Law's view is used to assess the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and not for the maxillary sinus.

Stenver's view (Option D): Stenver's view is used to image the petrous portion of the temporal bone and is not ideal for visualizing the maxillary sinus.

option_b: Osteoma are the most common benign tumour of paranasal sinuses

question_text: A patient presents with a cyst like swelling in the superiomedial side of the eye. There is no pain when it is pressed. This entity affects which paranasal sinus most commonly?
explanation:
The given description is suggestive of a mucocele.

Mucocele of paranasal sinuses -

  • Frontal sinus is most commonly affected followed by ethmoidal, maxillary & sphenoidal.
  • Treatment of choice is FESS.

Frontal mucocele

question_text: Most common site of osteomas among the paranasal sinuses?
explanation:
Osteomas are most commonly seen in the frontal sinus followed by ethmoid and maxillary sinuses. They may remain asymptomatic, being discovered incidentally on X-rays.

Treatment is indicated when they become symptomatic.

question_text: The frontal sinus can be viewed by taking an X-ray at a specific angle, which is depicted in the image below. What is the name of the view depicted?
explanation:
Explanation:

Caldwell's view (Occipitofrontal view) is the standard X-ray projection for visualizing the frontal sinuses. The patient is positioned with the forehead and nose touching the plate, and the X-ray beam is angled 15-20° caudally. This projects the petrous ridges below the orbits, providing an unobstructed view of the frontal and ethmoid sinuses.

Explanation of other options:
Towne's view (Option B): An anteroposterior view with ~30° caudal tilt used to visualize the occipital bone, petrous pyramids, and foramen magnum, not the frontal sinuses.
Law's view (Option C): A lateral oblique view used to image the mastoid air cells.
Stenvers view (Option D): An oblique view used to image the petrous part of the temporal bone and internal auditory canal, typically for evaluating conditions like acoustic neuroma.

Key Takeaways:

  • Caldwell's view is the primary X-ray projection for assessing the frontal sinuses.
  • Different radiographic views are optimized for visualizing specific skull structures.

question_text: The x-ray shown below is done to view the frontal sinus. What is the common name of the view:
explanation:
The common name of the X-ray view shown to view the frontal sinus is option a: Caldwell's View.

  1. Caldwell's View: This X-ray view is obtained by positioning the patient with the chin resting on the cassette and the head tilted backward. The X-ray beam is directed through the nose and towards the film. This view allows visualization of the frontal sinuses.
  2. Water's View: Water's View is an X-ray view obtained for maxillary sinus evaluation. It involves positioning the patient with the occiput resting on the cassette, and the X-ray beam is directed through the open mouth. It provides a superior view of the maxillary sinuses.
  3. Pierre's View and d. Towne's View: Pierre's View and Towne's View are not related to frontal sinus imaging. Pierre's View is used to visualize the zygomatic arch
  4. Towne's View is used to visualize the skull base, particularly the occipital bone.

question_text: Which site is most commonly obstructed by a nasal polyp arising from the maxillary sinus?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The most common location for an obstruction caused by a nasal polyp originating from the maxillary sinus is the middle meatus.
  • Nasal polyps are benign, non-cancerous growths that develop in the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses due to chronic inflammation, often associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, or allergies.
  • When arising from the maxillary sinus, these polyps typically expand into the middle meatus, which is the drainage pathway of the maxillary sinus.
  • Obstruction at this site can lead to blocked sinus drainage, recurrent sinus infections, nasal congestion, and difficulty breathing.

question_text: The marked structure opens into which of the following spaces ?
explanation:
The marked structure in the image points to the sphenoid sinus. The sphenoethmoidal recess is a small, anatomical space located in the upper part of the nasal cavity where the sphenoid sinus and the ethmoid sinus meet. It is an important region in the nasal cavity and plays a role in the drainage and ventilation of these paranasal sinuses.

  • Option B. Superior Meatus: The superior meatus is a space in the nasal cavity located below the superior nasal concha. The sphenoid sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess, which is adjacent to the superior meatus.
  • Option C. Middle Meatus: The middle meatus is another space in the nasal cavity located below the middle nasal concha. It is a critical area for the drainage of several paranasal sinuses, including the anterior ethmoidal sinus, frontal sinus, and maxillary sinus. The sphenoid sinus does not open directly into the middle meatus.
  • Option D. Inferior Meatus: The inferior meatus is a space in the nasal cavity located below the inferior nasal concha. It serves as the opening for the nasolacrimal duct, which drains tears from the eyes to the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinus does not open directly into the inferior meatus.

question_text: What is the area marked in the CT shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The marked structure in the image is osteomeatal complex which is a final common pathway for drainage of anterior sinus.

The OMC is not a single structure but rather a collection of several key anatomical landmarks working together. These include:

  • Uncinate process: A sickle-shaped bone that forms the anterior and inferior border of the hiatus semilunaris.
  • Ethmoid bulla
  • Hiatus semilunaris: lies between the free edge of the uncinate process and the ethmoid bulla; connects the middle meatus into the infundibulum laterally
  • Ethmoidal infundibulum: A channel that lies between the uncinate process and the lamina papyracea Maxillary ostium: The opening of the maxillary sinus into the ethmoidal infundibulum.
  • Middle Turbinate
  • Maxillary Sinus Ostium

Explanation of Other Options:

Columella (Option B)

It is an external, visible anatomical structure of the nose, the narrow strip of skin and cartilage that separates the two nostrils and forms the inferior part of the nasal septum.

The uncinate process is a part of the OMC but not the entire complex. It is a thin, curved bony structure that helps form the anterior boundary of the hiatus semilunaris.

Maxillary sinus (Option C)

The maxillary sinus is a large air-filled space adjacent to the OMC but not the area marked if the arrow is on the narrow drainage pathway.

Nasal valve (Option D)

The nasal valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway, located in the anterior nasal cavity. It is unrelated to the osteomeatal complex or sinus drainage.

Key Takeaway:

The osteomeatal complex is a vital anatomical drainage unit for multiple paranasal sinuses and is a common site of pathology in sinus infections.

question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo that last for several hours, along with tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in her right ear. Over the last few months, she has also noticed a progressive decline in hearing in the same ear. Physical examination reveals sensorineural hearing loss on the right side. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
• Meniere's disease is characterized by a triad of recurrent vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss.
  • Episodes of vertigo in Meniere's disease last for several hours and are often accompanied by a sensation of fullness in the ear.
  • Hearing loss is typically unilateral and progresses over time, as described in this patient.

Why not others:

  • A) Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): Causes brief vertigo triggered by head movement, usually lasting seconds to minutes. It does not involve tinnitus, ear fullness, or sensorineural hearing loss.
  • B) Acoustic neuroma: Causes gradual hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance, but vertigo is less frequent and milder. Recurrent vertigo episodes and ear fullness are more indicative of Meniere's disease.
  • D) Labyrinthitis: Causes continuous symptoms following an infection, including hearing loss and vertigo, but is usually associated with fever and more profound hearing loss rather than recurrent episodes.

Key Takeaways:

  • Meniere's disease presents with recurrent vertigo, tinnitus, and sensorineural hearing loss, typically with a feeling of fullness in the affected ear.
  • Other options (BPPV, acoustic neuroma, labyrinthitis) do not fit the pattern of recurrent episodes or the combination of symptoms seen in Meniere's disease.

Tags: Fmge aug 2020

Tag: Special senses

Level: Must know

Reference: Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 517

question_text: A 40-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of vertigo, nausea, and vomiting that began after a recent upper respiratory infection. She describes feeling unsteady and reports that her symptoms worsen with head movement. On examination, she has horizontal nystagmus but no hearing loss or tinnitus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Vestibular neuritis typically occurs after a viral infection, leading to sudden onset of symptoms such as severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting.
  • The mechanism involves inflammation of the vestibular nerve, disrupting the balance signals sent to the brain.
  • Patients often report feeling unsteady and experience horizontal nystagmus on examination, a key sign indicating vestibular dysfunction.
  • Key differentiators:
    • There is an absence of hearing loss or tinnitus, which distinguishes it from conditions like labyrinthitis (which presents with both vestibular and auditory symptoms) and Meniere's disease (which includes fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus).
    • Symptoms typically worsen with head movements, reflecting the vestibular system's role in maintaining balance.

Why not others:

  • A) Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): BPPV involves brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head positions (like rolling over in bed). The sustained nature of this patient's symptoms and lack of positional triggers make BPPV less likely.
  • B) Meniere's Disease: This condition is characterized by episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sensation of fullness in the ear. The absence of these auditory symptoms in this case strongly argues against Meniere's disease.
  • C) Labyrinthitis: Labyrinthitis presents with inflammation of the inner ear structures, typically following an infection, causing both vertigo and hearing loss. The lack of auditory symptoms, particularly hearing loss or tinnitus, suggests that labyrinthitis is not the correct diagnosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • The presence of sudden vertigo, nausea, and horizontal nystagmus following a viral illness strongly supports a diagnosis of vestibular neuritis.
  • Other conditions either involve auditory symptoms or have specific positional triggers, reinforcing that vestibular neuritis is the most fitting diagnosis.

question_text:
A 55-year-old woman presents to the clinic with complaints of dizziness and balance issues. She describes feeling as though she is spinning when she is stationary. Neurological examination reveals nystagmus and difficulty maintaining her balance while standing. An MRI shows no significant findings, but she is suspected to have vestibular dysfunction.
Vestibular system is involved in
option_b: Processing visual information for spatial orientation
option_c: Integration of balance and posture information
option_d: Regulation of emotional responses to stimuli
explanation:
Integration of balance and posture information:

  • Role: The vestibular nuclei are essential for integrating sensory information related to balance and posture from the inner ear and other sensory modalities.
  • The signals are integrated by the brain to help control eye movements, stabilize vision, and adjust the body's posture to maintain equilibrium.
  • Function: This integration helps maintain stability and equilibrium, particularly during movement.
  • Its dysfunction will lead to above mentioned
  • Symptoms in the question.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Coordination of voluntary motor movements:
    • Explanation: While the vestibular system interacts with motor pathways, the primary control of voluntary movements is handled by the cerebellum and basal ganglia.
  • B) Processing visual information for spatial orientation:
    • Explanation: The vestibular nuclei assist with spatial orientation but do not primarily process visual information; that function is managed by visual centres in the brain.
  • D) Regulation of emotional responses to stimuli:
    • Explanation: Emotional responses are primarily controlled by regions such as the limbic system, not by the vestibular nuclei, which are focused on balance and spatial orientation.

Key Takeaways:

  • The vestibular system is critical for the integration of balance and posture information, enabling stability during movement.
  • Understanding vestibular dysfunction can help differentiate it from other neurological issues affecting balance and coordination.

question_text: A patient presents to her GP with recurrent nosebleeds and also complains of facial fullness and facial pain. Over the past 2 months she has developed progressive shortness of breath and on one occasion she coughed up some blood. What would be the most appropriate test to perform?
explanation:
The mostly likely diagnosis in this case is Wegeners granulamotosis. Sinusitis is the commonest ENT manifestation of this auto immune disorder. Septal perforation (bony and cartilaginous), saddle nose deformity with epistaxis is commonly seen. The multi-system involvement leads to pulmonary symptoms. The biopsy from the nose reveals necrotising vasculitis in this case. ANCA(Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) testing is further helpful for the diagnosis.

question_text: 49 year old resident of coastal parts of southern state of India has presented with recurrent epistaxis. He is a catlle bredder and uses ponds for bathing cows. option_c: Russell bodies and Mikulicz cells are classical histopathological features
option_d: Can also have similar lesions in oral and genital mucosa
explanation:
This is a case of Rhinosporidiosis.

  • Caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi – aquatic protozoan
  • Most cases from South India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan.
  • The disease is transmitted through contaminated water of ponds

CLINICAL FEATURES -

  • Mostly affects nose and nasopharynx
  • Other sites such as lip, palate, conjunctiva, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, bronchi, skin, vulva and vagina may also be affected.
  • Mulberry like polypoidal mass in the nose
  • The mass is very vascular and bleeds easily on touch. Its surface is studded with white dots representing the sporangia.

DIAGNOSIS: Biopsy

TREATMENT:

  • Complete excision of the mass with a cutting diathermy and cauterization of its base.
  • Medical management: Dapsone is a useful drug to prevent recurrence

Option C - Russell bodies and Mikulicz cells are classical histopathological features of Rhinoscleroma.

question_text: In a patient of resistant epistaxis from left nasal cavity, the bleeding could not be controlled even after the ligation of external carotid artery. What is the possible source of bleeding in this patient?
explanation:
Think about the blood supply of nose.

80 % is from external carotid artery (ECA).

20 % is from Internal carotid artery (ICA) via the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries.

Since ECA has been tied, only remaining circulation is from ethmoidal arteries. They are exposed in the medial wall of the orbit by an external ethmoid (Lynch) incision.

Sphenopalatine artery (branch of ECA) is the most common source of epistaxis in hypertensive patients.

question_text: Septodermoplasty is a surgery done for the management of recurrent epistaxis in which of the following conditions?

question_text: Which of the following is not ligated in case of epistaxis control?
explanation:
Internal carotid artery is a very important source of blood supply to the brain. It is never ligated for control of epistaxis due to the risk of serious cerebral complications and mortality.

The following arteries are ligated for control of epistaxis.

  • Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL) is done first.
  • If uncontrolled, ligation of maxillary artery is done.
  • Then ligation of external carotid artery above the origin of superior thyroid artery should be done.
  • If still uncontrolled, ligation of ethmoidal arteries is done.

question_text: A 62 year old man comes to emergency at 4.00 am with severe epistaxis and high blood pressure (180/110mm Hg). Management of hypertension is started. But the epistaxis could not be controlled on anterior nasal packing and posterior nasal packing. What is the next best management of this patient?
option_c: Foley's catheter placement in the nose and inflate the bulb
explanation:
Next Best Management for Severe Epistaxis with High Blood Pressure:

B) Endoscopic ligation of Sphenopalatine artery:

  • In the given situation, the patient has severe epistaxis and high blood pressure.
  • If anterior and posterior nasal packing are ineffective, the next step is targeted intervention.
  • Sphenopalatine artery ligation is a minimally invasive procedure.
  • This procedure is performed by an ENT specialist.
  • Sphenopalatine artery supplies the nasal mucosa.
  • Endoscopic ligation involves accessing and tying off the artery to stop bleeding at the source.
  • It's an effective approach for controlling hypertensive epistaxis.
  • Preferred method: TESPAL (Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation).
  • Sphenopalatine artery is ligated near the sphenopalatine foramen, close to the posterior end of the middle turbinate.
  • Especially useful for posterior epistaxis.

Other Options:

  • A) Ligation of External carotid artery: More invasive and considered after less invasive methods fail.
  • Sequential ligation: Sphenopalatine artery -> Maxillary artery -> External carotid artery -> Ethmoidal artery.
  • C) Foley's catheter placement: Alternative to posterior nasal pack, less effective.
  • D) Electrocauterisation of Little's area: Early measure for anterior epistaxis, less effective for hypertensive epistaxis (usually posterior bleeding).

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no – 208-210

question_text: A 35 year old male presents with epistaxis conservative management was done to stop the bleeding but it failed which will be the next step of management
explanation:
Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (ESPAL) is an effective intervention for severe or refractory epistaxis when conservative management fails. It involves the ligation of the sphenopalatine artery, which is the main source of blood supply to the anterior nasal septum.

Other options:

B. Maxillary artery: While the maxillary artery is the source of blood supply to the sphenopalatine artery, ligating the maxillary artery is an extensive and invasive procedure not typically performed for epistaxis.

C. ICA (Internal Carotid Artery): The internal carotid artery is a major blood vessel supplying the brain.

D. ECA (External Carotid Artery): This artery supplies blood to the face and scalp. It is not as likely to be the source of epistaxis.

question_text: Given below is the CECT showing an enhancing mass in the nose, sphenopalatine fossa and infratemporal fossa. The patient is 18-year-old male presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and swelling of cheek. He should be managed by all of the following except?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation and CT scan findings, it can be said that the diagnosis in this case isJuvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.
  • It is the most common benign lesion of the nasopharynx. It is almost exclusively seen inyoung males.
  • Clinical presentationincludes recurrent epistaxis, unilateral nasal obstruction,Frog face deformity.
  • Main investigation in this condition isCT PNS with brain cuts with contrast.
    • Biopsy is contraindicated in this condition due to the highly vascular nature of the mass. (Option D)
  • Treatment includessurgical excision,various surgical approaches includes:
    • Endoscopic approach (Option A)
    • Medial maxillectomy by lateral rhinotomy approach
    • Transpalatine & sub palatine approach
    • Infratemporal approach
    • Trans maxillary approach.
  • Since it is a very vascular tumourPreoperativeembolizationto the feeding vessel is also indicated in this condition. (Option C)
  • Radiotherapyis only indicated after surgical excision only in intracranial cases to achieve clearance. Not given Preoperatively. (Option B)

Key Takeaway:

Juvenile Angiofibroma -

  • Biopsy C/I & Pre Operative Embolization done: Due to Highly Vascular Tumor.
  • Surgical Excision Mainstay
  • Radiotherapy for Intracranial extension only Post Surgery.

question_text: A 22-year-old male presents with recurrent epistaxis. CECT imaging showed findings as shown. Which of the following statements is true regarding the likley cause of epistaxis?
option_c: Bleeding is from the adjacent invading blood vessels
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The CECT image demonstrates anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, known as the Holman-Miller sign.
  • This finding is characteristic of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma and is supported by the clinical features of young age and recurrent epistaxis.
  • Recurrent bleeding occurs because its highly vascular and the blood vessels in the tumour lack a muscular layer and therefore cannot contract effectively to reduce bleeding after injury.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

  • Most common benign tumours of nasopharynx predominantly seen in adolescent males.
  • Tumour is seen almost exclusively in males in the age group of 10-20 years.
  • JNA typically originates in the pterygopalatine fossa, a space behind the maxilla, and can extend into the infratemporal fossa and towards the cheek.
  • A highly vascular tumour, with the dominant blood supply to the tumour usually being internal maxillary artery.

Clinical features

  • Profuse, recurrent and spontaneous epistaxis.
    • The most common presentation.
  • Progressive nasal obstruction and denasal speech (rhinolalia clausa)
  • Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion due to obstruction of eustachian tube.
  • Mass in the nasopharynx.
    • Tumour is sessile, lobulated or smooth and obstructs one or both choanae.
    • It is pink or purplish in colour with firm consistency is firm but digital palpation should never be done until at the time of operation.
  • Extension of the tumour into the orbit can lead to proptosis (protrusion of the eye), resulting in a frog face deformity.

Diagnosis

  • CECT
    • Invetsigation of choice
    • Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign:
      • Pathogonomic sign of angiofibroma.
    • Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of maxillary sinus,.
  • Carotid angiography
    • Shows the extent of tumours, its vascularity and feeding vessels which mostly come from the external carotid system.
  • Biopsy of the tumor is contraindicated due to its high vascularity and risk of severe bleeding.

Treatment

  • Surgical excision is the treatmnet of choice.
  • Pre-operative embolization of the internal maxillary artery by an interventional radiologist is often performed to reduce blood loss during surgery.
  • Radiotherapy is generally reserved for cases with intracranial extension or residual/recurrent disease that is not amenable to further surgery.

question_text: Which artery is most affected when a child has bleeding from the nose?

The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, is the most frequent source of epistaxis.

question_text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the Little's area?
option_a: Kiesselbach's plexus is present in the Little's area
option_b: It is situated at the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum
option_d: Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Kiesselbach's plexus, also known as Little's area, is a highly vascularised region in the anteroinferior portion of the nasal septum. (Option B ruled out)
  • It comprises a network of arteries formed by anastomoses of branches from the internal carotid artery and the external carotid artery which supply the nasal septum.

Vessels involved Kiesselbach's plexus: Formed by four arteries ((Option D ruled out))


Clinical Significance:

  • Anterior epistaxis occurs most often in children and young adults, usually due to trauma (nose-picking), dry air, infections, or irritants. (Option C ruled out)
  • Epistaxis in this area is typically mild and self-limiting and can be controlled with local pressure or simple cauterization.

question_text: A 40-year-old male patient presents with right sided nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis. On examination, a mulberry mass with white dots is seen in the right nostril. Which of the Following is true about this disease?

Rhinosporidiosis

question_text: Sunil, 7 year old child has presented at midnight to emergency with the history of putting a disc battery of his father's wrist watch in his nose few hours back. What would be the ideal management?
option_d: Next day removal of foreign body in elective operation theatre
explanation:
Disc batteries contain alkali - sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and mercury which leaks through them to cause injury. It is observed that a disc battery causes damage to mucosa in 1 hour.

Hence disc battery should be urgently removed from the nose.

Xylometazoline nasal drops decongest the nose and are used in management of rhinosinusitis.

Anterior nasal packing is used in management of epistaxis.

Next day removal of foreign body is not suggestive for disc batteries.

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no - 409

question_text: A 12 year old boy has presenting with recurrent episodes of profuse epistaxis and reddish nasal mass is seen filling nasal cavity. What is investigation best avoided in this patient?
explanation:
Angiofibroma is a highly vascular tumor and its blood vessels lack elastic tissue and muscle fibres and hence cannot contract. So biopsy of the tumor results in massive hemorrhage and is avoided.

CECT is now the investigation of choice for angiofibroma - It shows the extent of tumour, bony destruction or displacements.

Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign, is pathognomic of angiofibroma – It is the anterior displacement of posterior wall of maxillary sinus(red arrow).

Carotid angiography shows the extent of tumours, its vascularity and feeding vessels which mostly come from the external carotid system.  

Magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) is complementary to CT scans and shows any soft tissue extensions.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 292

Scott Brown’s otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition, Volume 1, Page: 1266

question_text: A 13 year old boy has presenting with recurrent episodes of profuse epistaxis and reddish nasal mass is seen filling nasal cavity and is having proptosis of eye. What is the possible diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a case of Angiofibroma.

Angiofibroma is the most common benign tumour of nasopharynx seen in adolescent males. It originates from sphenopalatine foramen. It’s a highly vascular tumour.

question_text: A 15 year old male child presents with right sided nasal mass and profuse epistaxis with hyponasality of voice, findings suggestive of conductive hearing loss and cheek swelling. What is the possible diagnosis
explanation: Angiofibroma is a pink, firm, 1- to 2-mm dome-shaped papule most commonly located over the nasal bridge and cheeks and is a benign tumor made of blood vessels and connective tissue that can appear as small, red bumps on the face, particularly on the cheeks and nose.
