question_text: Which is the most common source of bleeding during tonsillectomy?
explanation:
Paratonsillar vein: After tonsillectomy (tonsil surgery), postoperative bleeding can occur, and the bleeding source is commonly the paratonsillar vein (peritonsillar vein). The paratonsillar vein is located near the tonsils and can be a site of bleeding following tonsil surgery. Post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage is a known complication, and the bleeding often originates from this vein.

B. External palatine vein: This is a less likely source of bleeding because it is located further away from the tonsils.

C. Ascending pharyngeal artery: This is less likely to cause bleeding because it is located further away from the tonsils and is a larger vessel.

D. Facial artery: This is less likely to cause bleeding because it is located further away from the tonsils and is a larger vessel.

question_text: A 6-year-old unimmunized child is brought to the ER with fever, cough, and difficulty in breathing. On examination, there is a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils which bleeded on attempts to remove, along with marked cervical lymphadenopathy producing a bull-neck appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described clinical presentation is most consistent with diphtheria, a bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

  • A hallmark feature of diphtheria is the greyish pseudomembrane that adheres firmly to the underlying tissue and bleeds upon removal.
  • Swelling of the neck due to bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue oedema is a classic sign of diphtheria, which leads to bull-neck appearance.
  • Fever, cough, and difficulty breathing are the common systemic and respiratory symptoms of diphtheria.
  • Diagnosis can be aided by Albert stain.
  • The lack of vaccination increases susceptibility to diphtheria, which is preventable through the DPT vaccine.

Common causes of membrane over the tonsils:

  • Moniliasis (Candidiasis)
  • Diphtheria (pseudo membrane)
  • Vincent's angina (pseudo membrane)
  • Infectious mononucleosis
  • Malignancy of tonsil
  • Trauma
  • Aphthous ulcers
  • Leukemia
  • Agranulocytosis

Explanation of other options:

Infectious mononucleosis (Option A): While it may cause tonsillar swelling and pharyngitis, it does not cause a pseudomembrane over the tonsil or bull-neck appearance.

Tonsillitis (Option B): Tonsillitis can cause fever and difficulty swallowing, but it does not produce a pseudomembrane or bull-neck swelling. It is usually due to bacterial (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes) or viral infections.

Candidiasis (Option D): Oral candidiasis can cause white patches on the mucosa, but these are easily scraped off without bleeding, unlike the pseudomembrane in diphtheria.

  • Beta lactam and macrolides should be started immediately .

Key Takeaway:

Diphtheria Characteristics

  • Unimmunised Child
  • High Fever, Sore Throat with Pseudomembrane which bleeds on removal.
  • Managed with Betalactam & Macrolides

Differentials of Whitish Membrane over tonsil :

  • Diphtheria - High Fever Sore Throat with Pseudomembrane which bleeds on removal.
  • Vincent's Angina - Low Grade Fever. Ulcerative Growth
  • Candida - Can be Rubbed off.
  • Oral Hairy leukoplakia - Can't be Rubbed off.

question_text: A 7-year-old male patient presented with complain of repeated throat infection since 3 years. On examination his oropharynx showed enlarged bilateral tonsils. Picture given below. All are the following are the contraindications of tonsillectomy except?
explanation:
Explanation:

Contraindications of tonsillectomy includes:

  • Bleeding disorders (Option A)
  • Polio epidemic: since the polio virus gets concentrated in the lymphoid tissues of the tonsils and adenoids, tonsillectomy can lead to entry of virus into the bloodstream, triggering paralytic polio. (Option B)
  • Cleft lip and palate: They are relative contraindications as these patients are at risk for velopharyngeal insufficiency getting unmasked post-surgery. (Option C)
  • Acute upper respiratory tract infection and tonsillitis: chances of Haemorrhage and septicemia is high. Surgery is postponed for three weeks.

Key Takeaway:

Tonsillectomy Contraindications : ABCDEF

  • Active infection/ Acute exacerbation, Aneurysm of internal carotid artery, Age below three years, Active menstruation.
  • Bleeding and clotting disorders.
  • Cervical spine pathology
  • Diphtheritic tonsillitis. Drugs: Patients under aspirin, oral contraceptives, etc.
  • Endemic of polio
  • Failure to control systemic diseases like hypertension, diabetes, bronchial asthma, LRTI, etc.

question_text: A child with a history of recurrent tonsillitis presents to the clinic for undergoing elective tonsillectomy. He does not have any symptoms now. While examining the patient which of the following would you find?
option_c: No lymph node enlargement as lymph nodes are only involved during acute attacks.
explanation:
This is a case of chronic tonsillitis.

Enlargement of jugulodigastric lymph nodes is a reliable sign of chronic tonsillitis.

During acute attacks, the nodes enlarge further and become tender.

Other features of chronic tonsillitis include -

  • Tonsils may show varying degree of enlargement. Sometimes they meet in the midline(chronic parenchymatous type).
  • There may be yellowish beads of pus on the medial surface of tonsil(chronic follicular type).
  • Tonsils are small but pressure on the anterior pillar expresses frank pus or cheesy material(chronic fibroid type).
  • Flushing of anterior pillars compared to the rest of the pharyngeal mucosa.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 308

question_text: 30-year-old male patient underwent tooth extraction. Now he presents with fever and trismus. Examination reveals that the tonsils are pushed medially. There is also swelling on the neck at upper border of sternocleidomastoid. Trismus in this case is due to which muscle?

Explanation:

  • Medial pterygoid muscle lies just opposite to the parapharyngeal space laterally. It being attached to the medial aspect of mandible. (Option A, & D)

Key Takeaway:

  • Inparapharyngeal space abscess,trismus is mainly because of spasm ofmedial pterygoid due to close anatomical proximation.

question_text: Which among the following conditions does not result in the development of a grey-white membrane over the tonsils ?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ludwig's angina does not produce a grey-white membrane over the tonsils.

  • Ludwig's angina is a deep neck space infection involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces.
  • Source infection: Usually dental caries or dental infection (often of the lower molars).
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Starts with a dental infection.
    • Midline chin swelling.
    • Trismus (difficulty in opening mouth).
    • Sometimes respiratory distress if the swelling is significant and pushes the tongue upwards.

Explanation of other options:

Streptococcal tonsillitis (Option A): Although rare, severe forms can lead to exudative tonsillitis, with grey-white deposits on the tonsils. However, this is not as adherent or classic as the membrane seen in diphtheria.

Diphtheria (Option B): Diphtheria is a hallmark condition associated with the formation of a grey-white pseudomembrane over the tonsils, which is firmly adherent and bleeds upon removal.

Infectious mononucleosis (Option D): Caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, it can produce white or greyish exudates on the tonsils, especially in severe cases, alongside fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.

question_text: Which of the following condition Does not cause whitish membrane I'm the tonsils?
explanation:
Membrane formation is not seen in Ludwig s angina. Ludwig angina causes firm painful swelling over submandibular and sub mental region.

  • Streptococcal tonsillitis is also called as Acute membranous tonsillitis. It is the most commonest cause of tonsillitis.
  • Diptheria also causes whitish membrane over tonsils. This membrane is firmly adherent to tonsil and bleeds on removal from the tonsil.
  • Infectious mononucleosis is also one of the cause of white membrane formation over tonsil.

explanation:
• Unlike acute tonsillitis, Diphtheria is abrupt in onset, diphtheria is slower in onset with less local discomfort, the membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils, on to the soft palate and is dirty gray in color.

question_text: Which of the following is the most important artery supply of tonsils:
explanation: The ascending palatine artery is the most important artery supplying the tonsils. It arises from the facial artery and provides the main blood supply to the tonsils. The other arteries listed also contribute to the blood supply of the tonsils but are not considered the most important.

question_text: A young male, who is a professional trumpet player, presents with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, compression of the swelling produces a gurgling sound. The neck X-ray was inconclusive, so a CT scan of the neck was performed (image provided). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a trumpet player presenting with a neck swelling that produces a gurgling sound on compression, the most likely diagnosis is a laryngocele. The given CT scan shows a characteristic air-filled structure adjacent to the larynx, confirming the diagnosis.

Laryngocele

  • A laryngocele is an air-filled dilation of the laryngeal saccule that may communicate with the laryngeal lumen.
  • It is commonly seen in individuals performing activities that increase intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure, such as trumpet players or wind instrument musicians.
  • Classification:
    • Internal laryngocele: Confined to the larynx.
    • External laryngocele: Extends outside the larynx into the neck.

Clinical features

  • Neck swelling, which may produce a gurgling sound on compression due to air or fluid within the sac.
  • Hoarseness

Diagnosis

  • Bryce's sign: Air escape sound on pressing the neck swelling.
  • Imaging:
    • CT scan: Gold standard, shows a well-defined air-filled structure adjacent to the larynx.
    • X-ray with Valsalva maneuver: Air-filled neck swelling becomes more prominent.

Management: Surgical excision is the treatment of choice to remove the sac and prevent recurrence.

Explanation of other options:

Pharyngeal pouch (Option A): Pharyngeal pouch, also known as the Zenker's diverticulum , typically presents with dysphagia, regurgitation of food, and aspiration, not a gurgling sound on neck compression. Moreover, it is located in the sterior pharyngeal wall, not adjacent to the larynx as seen in a laryngocele.

Tracheoesophageal fistula (Option C): Tracheoesophageal fistula is a congenital connection between the trachea and oesophagus, usually diagnosed in infancy.
In adults, it does not present as a neck swelling with a gurgling sound. On CT imaging, it would show a direct connection between the trachea and oesophagus.

Tonsillar swelling (Option D): Tonsillar swelling usually results from infection or tumours of the tonsils. It does not produce a gurgling sound on neck compression, nor does it show the air-filled structure adjacent to the larynx seen on CT imaging in laryngocele.

question_text: A 9-year-old female patient had chronic tonsillitis. She was advised Coblation assisted tonsillectomy. The intraoperative picture is given below. What is the principle of coblation technology?

  • Cryotherapyuses extremely cold temperature. And repeated freezing and thawing cycles. (Option B)

Coblation band converts the conductive saline solution into an ionized plasma layerresulting in molecular thermal dissection with minimal transfer of thermal energy.

question_text: A child, following tonsillectomy, ate a packet of chips, 2 days after surgery, and now came to the hospital with bleeding. What is the next ideal step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bleeding 2 days after surgery indicates secondary haemorrhage, commonly caused by infection or slough separation. In this case, hard food disturbed the slough casing bleeding and minor bleeding are managed conservatively with antibiotics and a soft/semi-solid diet.

Post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage

  • Primary hemorrhage:
    • Occurs during surgery; main source is the paratonsillar vessels.
    • Bleeding is controlled with pressure, ligation, or electrocautery.
  • Reactionary hemorrhage:
    • Occurs within 24 hoursdue to slippage of a ligature.
    • It is a surgical emergency requiring clot removal, vessel re-ligation under general anaesthesia, IV fluids, and possible blood transfusion.
  • Secondary hemorrhage:
    • Occurs 5-10 days after surgery, usually from infection or premature slough separation, and is typically
    • Managed with hospital admission, IV antibiotics, and a semi-solid diet.

question_text: A post tonsillectomy child was lying in the ward he started bleeding in the ward which of the following should be done
option_a: Take to OT and remove the clot and re-ligation
option_b: Take to OT and pressure packing
explanation: Take to OT, remove the clot and re-ligation: In the given question as the hemorrhage occurs within a period of 24hrs known as Reactionary hemorrhage which can be controlled by simple measures like removal of the clot, application of pressure or vasoconstrictor. Presence of the clot prevents the clipping action of the superior constrictor muscle on the vessels which pass through it. If above measures fail, ligation or electro-coagualtion of the bleeding vessels can be done under general anaesthesia.

question_text: A 14-year-old male presents with a recurrent history of epistaxis and associated with nasal block and excessive nasal discharge. On examination, a solid purplish growth was observed on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. What is the probable underlying cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical history of recurrent epistaxis and nasal obstruction, along with a mass in the posterior nasopharynx in a child is likely suggestive of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

  • A benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour occurring predominantly in adolescent males.
  • Site of origin:
    • Posterior nasal cavity, near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen, where the sphenoid and palatine bones meet.
  • Gross Appearance
    • Reddish-purple, lobulated, sessile mass covered by mucosa; lacks a capsule despite being benign.
  • Microscopic Appearance
    • Vascular Tissue: Endothelium-lined spaces with incomplete/absent muscle coats, leading to bleeding; peripheral vessels are thin-walled, central vessels hyperplastic.
    • Stromal Cells: Stellate or spindle-shaped cells that produce collagen, affecting tumor firmness.
  • Immunohistochemistry
    • Fibroblasts, collagen, myofibroblasts, mast cells, and occasionally giant cells are present.
    • Reactivity to smooth muscle actin and beta-catenin, suggesting beta-catenin's role in growth.

Explanation of other options:

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Option A): This malignant tumour usually occurs in older adults and is rare in this age group. It often presents with neck lymphadenopathy, nasal obstruction, or ear symptoms but is unlikely to present with a solid, vascular growth in a young male.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option B): This is a malignant soft tissue tumour that can occur in the nasopharynx but is rare and less likely to cause repeated epistaxis without systemic signs like weight loss or fatigue.

Pyogenic granuloma (Option C): This is a vascular lesion but typically occurs on the nasal septum or oral mucosa, not in the nasopharynx. It is usually smaller, friable, and more superficial.

question_text: Which of the following is incorrect about juvenile angiofibroma
explanation:
Explanation:

Biopsy done under local anesthesia is the incorrect statement.

Definition and Epidemiology:
 Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males aged 10-20 years. It arises from the posterior nasal cavity near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen. The tumor originates from a hamartomatous vascular nidus that proliferates under the influence of testosterone, making it a hormone-dependent tumor.

Clinical Features:
 The tumor can expand into the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pterygomaxillary fossa, infratemporal fossa, orbit, cheek, or even intracranial space, producing characteristic signs and symptoms:

  • Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous epistaxis - the most common symptom
  • Progressive nasal obstruction and denasalized speech due to mass effect in the postnasal space
  • Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion from Eustachian tube blockage
  • Nasopharyngeal mass that may appear sessile, lobulated, or smooth
  • Additional features: broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis, cheek swelling, and possible involvement of cranial nerves II, III, IV, and VI
  • In advanced cases, frog-face deformity may develop

Diagnosis:
 Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical examination and imaging studies.

  • Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice.
  • A pathognomonic sign is the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, known as the Holman-Miller sign (Antral sign).

Surgery is the treatment of choice.

question_text: A 17 year old male patient presented to ENT OPD with the history of nasal obstruction and severe nasal bleeding. The nasal endoscopy picture shows a mass in the choana as given in the image. What is the possible diagnosis?
explanation: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a rare highly vascular tumor within the posterior nasal cavity found almost exclusively in adolescent boys. The most common presentation is an adolescent male with chronic unilateral nasal obstruction. Also, painless, unprovoked epistaxis is common. Other presenting complaints consist of headache and rhinorrhea, and when the mass is large and invasive, proptosis, visual disturbance, cranial nerve palsy. On physical exam, a mass is generally visible within the nasal cavity.

question_text: Rhinolalia clausa occurs in all of the following except:
explanation:
Explanation:

Rhinolalia clausa is not seen in cleft palate. Instead, a cleft palate causes velopharyngeal insufficiency, leading to hypernasal speech (rhinolalia aperta) due to excessive nasal resonance, rather than the nasal obstruction characteristic of rhinolalia clausa.

Rhinolalia clausa

  • Rhinolalia clausa or hyponasality is the lack of nasal resonance for sounds that are normally resonated in the nasal cavity, such as m, n, and ng.
  • It manifests as a nasal or blocked voice caused by obstruction of the nasal passages or nasopharynx.
  • Common causes of hyponasality
    • Common cold
    • Nasal allergy
    • Nasal polyp
    • Nasal growth
    • Adenoid hypertrophy
    • Nasopharyngeal mass (Option A, B, D ruled out)

question_text: A 12-year-old male presents with recurrent, profuse nasal bleeding and right-sided nasal obstruction. Endoscopy reveals a globular, vascular mass in the right nasal cavity occupying the posterior choanae and nasopharynx. A CT scan shows anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation :

The combination of clinical and radiological findings is pathognomonic for a Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

Angiofibroma:

  • The most common benign tumor of the nasopharynx
  • Arises from the sphenopalatine foramen
  • Exclusive in adolescent males

Clinical features

  • Presents with profuse epistaxis and nasal obstruction, hyponasality( Rhinolalia clausa)
  • On examination, a red and fleshy mass was seen in the nasal cavity
  • As Eustachian tube obstruction occurs, serous otitis media can occur, and the patient can present with conductive type hearing loss

The tumor can spread into

  • Laterally- pterygopalatine fossa, causing pressure over the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, causing it to bow anteriorly, called the Holman Miller sign or Antral sign, seen in contrast CT
  • Orbit- through the inferior orbital fissure, causing proptosis, diplopia, with involvement of II, III, IV, and VI cranial nerves, depending on the extent of the tumor
  • Infratemporal fossa- through the pterygomaxillary fissure, and appears as cheek swelling
  • Intracranial extension can occur

Nasal bridge broadening, proptosis, and cheek swelling give rise to frog face deformity

Explanation of other options:

Antrochoanal polyp (Option B): While this also presents as a unilateral nasal mass, it is an inflammatory polyp that is typically pale and avascular. It causes nasal obstruction but does not typically cause profuse bleeding. On CT, it opacifies and expands the maxillary sinus ostium, but does not cause the characteristic bony bowing seen in JNA.

Rhinoscleroma (Option C): This is a chronic granulomatous bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It leads to hard, nodular infiltrations ("woody" feel) of the nasal mucosa, not a distinct globular, vascular mass.

Rhinosporidiosis (Option D): This is a chronic fungal infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi that presents as a friable, polypoidal, "strawberry-like" mass that bleeds easily on touch, but it does not cause the specific bony erosion pattern of JNA.

question_text: A 20-year-old male patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent bleeding for the past 1 year. Trans nasal endoscopic results are shown below. A contrast-enhanced CT revealed a mass extending from the posterior choana to the nasopharynx. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

The presentation of a young male with unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, and imaging showing a vascular mass extending into the nasopharynx is classic for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). It is a benign but highly vascular tumor arising from the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity near the sphenopalatine foramen.

Clinical Features of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA):

  • Nasal and Nasopharyngeal Symptoms
    • Recurrent, profuse epistaxis due to fragile thin-walled vessels.
    • Progressive nasal obstruction causing a nasal, hyponasal voice.
    • Secondary nasal discharge from sinus obstruction or infection.
  • Otologic Symptoms
    • Conductive hearing loss from Eustachian tube obstruction.
    • Otitis media with effusion and possible ear pain.
  • Ophthalmic and Neurological Symptoms
    • Proptosis from orbital invasion.
    • Diplopia due to cranial nerve compression (III, IV, VI).
    • Other cranial nerve palsies (II, V, IX, X).
  • Facial Features
    • Broadening of nasal bridge or cheek swelling from tumor extension.
    • "Frog-face deformity"in advanced cases with bilateral proptosis and facial distortion.
  • Demographics
    • Occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males (10-20 years).
    • Very rare in females.
  • Endoscopic Appearance
    • Smooth or lobulated reddish-purple mass in nasopharynx.
    • Firm in consistency but must not be palpated due to high bleeding risk.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Antrochoanal polyp (Option B): Arises from the maxillary sinus (antrum) and extends posteriorly into the choana. It presents with nasal obstruction but typically does not cause recurrent severe epistaxis or such vascular mass extension into the nasopharynx.

Rhinoscleroma (Option C): Chronic granulomatous condition caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (Frisch bacillus). It progresses through three stages-catarrhal, granulomatous, and sclerotic. Patients develop nasal obstruction, discharge, and deformity, but recurrent severe epistaxis and a vascular nasopharyngeal mass are not characteristic. Histology shows Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies.

Concha bullosa (Option D): This is an anatomical variation where the middle turbinate is pneumatized (air-filled). It may cause obstruction but does not present with epistaxis or extension into the nasopharynx.

Key Takeaway
Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) should be suspected in a young male presenting with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis, especially when imaging shows a vascular mass extending into the nasopharynx.

question_text: The investigation shown in the picture is used in which of the following diseases?
explanation:
• A CT scan of the head with contrast enhancement is the investigation of choice.
  • It shows the extent of the tumour, bony destruction or displacement.
  • Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, often called the antral sign or Holman-Miller sign, is pathognomonic of angiofibroma.
  • MRI helps assess soft tissue extensions (intracranial, infratemporal fossa, orbit).
  • Carotid angiography defines tumour vascularity and feeding vessels, mainly from the external carotid.
  • Embolization is done before surgery to reduce intraoperative bleeding (ideally within 24-48 hrs).
  • Blood should be arranged even after embolization (2-3 units in reserve).
  • Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a highly vascular tumour seen in adolescent males.
  • Classical radiologic feature: Holman-Miller sign
  • Surgery is the mainstay of treatment; pre-op embolization is critical.

Explanation of other options:

Capillary Haemangioma of the septum (Option B): Usually diagnosed clinically or with nasal endoscopy. Not associated with the Holman-Miller sign.

Cancer of the Maxillary sinus (Option C): CT may show destruction but not the characteristic anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary wall.

D) Inverted Papilloma of Nose (Option D): Appears as a soft tissue mass on imaging but lacks the typical vascular and bony features of angiofibroma.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Holman-Miller sign is diagnostic of JNA on contrast-enhanced CT.
  • Embolization must be followed by timely surgery (within 24-48 hours).
  • JNA is a vascular tumour requiring special perioperative planning.

Reference:

Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 7th Edition, Page Numbers: 292-293

question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with nonaxial proptosis of the left eye. He reports a remote history of a road traffic accident that occurred 15 years ago. Based on the findings in the accompanying CT scan, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis based on clinical features and CT is frontal mucocele.

  • A mucocele is a cyst-like structure that forms when the lining of a sinus cavity becomes inflamed or blocked.
  • When a mucocele forms in the frontal sinus, it can cause proptosis (bulging) of the eye.
  • This commonly occurs as a result of obstruction to the frontal ostium due to chronic disease of the frontal recess or due to postsurgical/ traumatic fibrosis, causing blockage.
  • Symptoms of a frontal mucocele include:
    • Proptosis (bulging) of the eye
    • Headache or facial pain
    • Vision changes or double vision
    • Nasal congestion or discharge
    • Sinus pressure or pain
    • Swelling or tenderness in the forehead

Explanation for other options:

Frontal meningioma (Option B):

  • A meningioma is a tumour that arises from the lining of the brain or spinal cord.
  • When a meningioma forms in the front of the head, it can cause eye proptosis.
  • However, meningiomas are relatively uncommon in young adults, and a history of trauma may not be associated with developing a meningioma.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option C):

  • Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a rare and benign tumour, typically in adolescent males.
  • It arises from the back of the nose or upper throat and can cause eye proptosis as it grows.
  • However, the history of trauma 15 years prior is not usually associated with developing a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Pseudotumor of the orbit (Option D):

  • Pseudotumor of the orbit, also known as an idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome, is a condition in which the tissues around the eye become inflamed and swollen, causing eye proptosis.
  • The cause of the pseudotumor of the orbit is unknown, but it is thought to be related to an abnormal immune response.
  • While a history of trauma is not typically associated with developing pseudotumor of the orbit, the condition can occur at any age.

question_text: The main vessel involved in bleeding from juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
explanation:
• The main feeding vessels of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma are the terminal branches of Maxillary Artery( which is a branch of External Carotid Artery)
  • This artery is subjected to pre-operative embolization to reduce the blood loss during surgery.
  • Resection of tumour should not be delayed beyond 24–48 h of embolization to avoid revascularization from the contralateral side.

In very large tumors or those with intracranial extension, bloody supply may come from branches of Internal Carotid Artery. But these are not embolized.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 292

question_text: What is the ideal surgical approach for limited Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma(Radkowski Stage 1)
explanation:
Limited Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma(Fisch stage 1) –

  • In this the tumor is limited to the nose and the nasopharyngeal area.
  • Transpalatal endoscopic approach is the best for such tumors.
  • If unavailable, Wilson's transpalatal approach can be used.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 294

question_text: All of the following are true about juvenile angiofibroma except
option_a: The nidus of fibrovascular tissue for origin of angiofibroma is due to incomplete regression of first branchial artery.
option_b: Weber Fergusson's transmaxillary approach is ideal for angiofibroma limited to nose & nasopharynx
option_c: The tumor is seen 24 times more commonly in patients of adenomatous polyposis of colon
option_d: C-myc is a proto oncogene found in large angiofibromas
explanation:
Tumours confined to nasopharynx can be approached through transnasal endoscopic approach or Wilson’s transpalatal approach.

But tumours extending to cheek would need trans-maxillary approach using Weber Fergusson incision.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 295

question_text: All are applicable to Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma except
explanation:
Angiofibroma is the most common benign tumor of nasopharynx.

Site of origin is the superior margin of sphenopalatine foramen.

This tumor is seen in young adolescent boys (12-14 years).

The tumor is highly vascular as the blood vessels of this tumor do not have muscular layers. Therefore, if once cut they do not contract or retract. So, it always presents with profuse epistaxis and biopsy is contraindicated for this tumor.

Angiofibroma is a hormone sensitive tumor therefore preparative estrogen/flutamide shrinks the tumor

It is a locally invasive tumor. It can extend into :

  1. Nose
  2. Sinuses (Nasal mass and epistaxis)
  3. Cheek (the tumor grows into pterygopalatine fossa behind the maxilla and enters the infratemporal fossa to present as cheek swelling. In its expansion into pterygopalatine fossa, it pushes the posterior wall of maxilla forwards. This finding on radiology is called ‘ HOLLMAN MILLER’ or ANTRAL sign)
  4. Orbit – orbital involvement will lead to proptosis, which is called ‘ FROG FACE DEFORMITY’.
  5. Brain(middle cranial fossa, anterior cranial fossa)

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Pg. no. 289

question_text: What is the staging system used for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma?
explanation:
Explanation:

Radkowski's system classifies Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma based on tumor extent seen on imaging.

  • Several methods exist for staging Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) to guide surgery and treatment.
  • The Radkowski and Andrews-Fisch systems are widely used, as both correlate with tumor extent, surgical approach, recurrence, and outcomes.

Radkowski Staging System: Most popular and widely used

Explanation of other options:

TNM staging (Option B): TNM staging is not used for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma

Ann Arbor staging system (Option C): Ann Arbor staging system is used for classification of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Duke's staging (Option D): Duke's staging system applies to the classification of colorectal cancer.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545240/

question_text: Identify the sign show in the image?
option_a: Holman miller sign - JNA Sphenopalatine foramen / Nose of Nasopharynx
explanation:

question_text: A 12-year-old child with a history of recurrent bleeding undergoes an endoscopic examination, which is given below. What is the investigation of choice (IOC) for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given endoscopic image shows a highly vascular, lobulated, reddish mass in the nasopharynx, which is suggestive of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA). This condition is a benign but highly vascular tumor seen in adolescent males and presents with recurrent epistaxis and nasal obstruction.

Investigation of Choice (IOC):

Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) is the preferred imaging modality for JNA as it:

  • For a highly vascular nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis, CECT is the investigation of choice for diagnosing juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA).
  • Identifies tumor extent and bony erosion.
  • Helps in staging and surgical planning.
  • Shows an intensely enhancing mass in the nasopharynx without significant necrosis.

Explanation for other options:

Biopsy (Option B): is incorrect because JNA is highly vascular, and biopsy may cause profuse bleeding, making it contraindicated.

X-ray (Option C): is incorrect because it has low sensitivity and may only show an indirect sign like bony erosion of the pterygoid plates.

MRI (Option D): is incorrect because while MRI is useful for soft tissue delineation, CECT is preferred for preoperative vascular mapping and bony involvement.

question_text: A 50-year-old male presents with right-sided serous otitis media and a history of cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In an elderly patient presenting with serous otitis media and cervical lymphadenopathy, the most likely diagnosis is nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

  • Nasopharyngeal cancer is a multifactorial disease most common in China.
  • Mostly affects people aged 50 to 70 years, although younger patients can also be affected.
  • Aetiology
    • Epstein-Barr (EB) virus is closely associated with nasopharyngeal cancer.
    • Genetics, particularly HLA-A2 and B47, also play a supportive role.
    • Air pollution, smoking of tobacco and opium, nitrosamines from dry salted fish, smoke from burning of incense and wood have all been incriminated.
  • Most common site of origin: Fossa of Rosenmuller.
  • Nasopharynx is rich in lymphatics and an early lymphatic spread is seen in cervical nodes.

Clinical features

  • Cervical lymphadenopathy
    • The most common presentation is metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy (secondary neck node).
  • Hearing loss
    • The second most common presentation is unilateral conductive hearing loss due to the blockage of the eustachian tube opening, leading to unilateral glue ear (serous otitis media).
  • Ophthalmoneurologic symptoms
    • Multiple cranial nerve palsies may occur in nasopharyngeal carcinoma because the nasopharynx lies just below the skull base.
    • The tumor can spread into the cranial cavity through the foramen lacerum.
    • The sixth cranial nerve is most commonly affected, followed by the fifth nerve.
  • Trotter's triad
    • Neuralgia in the temporal parietal area (fifth nerve involvement)
    • Palatal paralysis (tenth nerve involvement)
    • Unilateral conductive hearing loss (glue ear).

Diganosis

  • Nasal pharyngoscopy to visualise the nasopharynx, follwed by biopsy and histopathological confirmation.

Treatment

  • The treatment of choice is chemo-radiation (radiotherapy plus chemotherapy). NPC is a radio-sensitive tumor.
  • Chemotherapy often involves cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil.

Explanation of other options:

Angiofibroma (Option A): Angiofibroma is seen in the juvenile age group and presents with recurrent epistaxis.

Adenoid hypertrophy (Option C): Adenoid hypertrophy is seen in children and presents with mouth breathing, nasal obstruction and recurrent ear infections, but is not associated with cervical lymphadenopathy

Peritonsillar abscess (Option D): A peritonsillar abscess is a collection of pus in the peritonsillar space, located between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle. It most commonly affects adults and presents with severe throat pain, odynophagia, hot-potato voice, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

question_text: Identify the structure marked in the given endoscopic view of the nasopharynx.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The marked structure in the endoscopic image is the fossa of Rosenmüller.
  • It is a common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is located posterior to the torus tubarius on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.
  • On endoscopic examination, it appears as a deep recess lateral to the Eustachian tube opening.

Nasopharynx

  • The nasopharynx is the uppermost part of the pharynx, located posterior to the nasal cavities, extending from the base of the skull to the soft palate (level of the hard palate).
  • It is functionally a posterior extension of the nasal cavity and is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

Walls of the Nasopharynx

  • Roof: Formed by the basisphenoid and basiocciput.
  • Posterior wall: Formed by the arch of the atlas, covered by prevertebral muscles and fascia.
  • Floor: Formed anteriorly by the soft palate, posteriorly deficient.
  • Anterior wall: Formed by the posterior nasal apertures (choanae), separated by the posterior border of the nasal septum.
  • Lateral walls:
    • Each wall contains the pharyngeal opening of the Eustachian tube, about 1.25 cm behind the inferior turbinate.
    • Bounded above and behind by the torus tubarius, raised by the cartilage of the tube.
    • Posterior and superior to torus tubarius lies the fossa of Rosenmüller, a common site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
    • A salpingopharyngeal fold extends from the lower torus tubarius to the lateral wall, raised by the salpingopharyngeus muscle.

Important Structures in the Nasopharynx

question_text: Which is the most common site for head and neck cancer in India?

  • In India, the oral cavity is the most common site for head and neck cancer.

  • Poor oral hygiene and HPV infection are also contributory factors.

Explanation of other options:

Hypopharynx (Option D): Hypopharyngeal cancers are associated with smoking and alcohol use but are less frequent than oral cavity cancers in the Indian population.

question_text: A patient presents with a persistent red lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following viral infections is most strongly associated with this malignancy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity is associated with human papillomavirus.

  • Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) constitutes up to 80% of SCCs in this region, most commonly involving the tonsils, base of tongue, and pharynx, and is frequently associated with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly HPV-16.
  • The incidence of HPV-associated SCC of the oropharynx has more than doubled in recent decades, and these tumours often arise in the reticulated epithelium of the tonsillar crypts, presenting as nonkeratinizing, basaloid cell proliferations in nests and cords accompanied by sheets of lymphocytes, as shown below.
  • Clinically, HPV-associated SCCs may lack obvious mucosal lesions but are notable for significant cervical lymphadenopathy, and p16 protein overexpression is a useful marker for diagnosis, with PCR or in situ hybridization serving as confirmatory tests.
  • In contrast, keratinizing SCCs, more often linked to smoking and alcohol, usually originate as dysplastic lesions that may progress to full-thickness dysplasia (carcinoma in situ) before invading the underlying stroma.
  • They can vary from well-differentiated to anaplastic forms, and histologic differentiation does not correlate with behaviour. These tumours tend to infiltrate locally before metastasising, with cervical lymph nodes as common sites for local spread, and lungs, liver, and bones as frequent sites for distant metastases.
  • Long-term outcomes are generally better in HPV-positive cases.
  • A significant concern in SCC of the oropharynx is field cancerization, where patients, particularly those with classic SCC, face a high risk of developing new primary tumours due to widespread mucosal carcinogen exposure.

Explanation of other options:

Epstein–Barr virus (Option A): Hairy leukoplakia is an EBV-associated oral lesion typically seen on the lateral border of the tongue in immunocompromised individuals, notably those with HIV, but also in cases of cancer therapy, transplant-related immunosuppression, and advanced age. It appears as white, confluent,  hyperkeratotic patches that cannot be scraped off, with histology showing hyperparakeratosis, acanthosis with balloon cells, and detectable EBV RNA and proteins in lesional cells. Malignancies associated with EBV include nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and other B-cell lymphomas.

Cytomegalovirus (Option B): In immunocompetent individuals beyond the neonatal stage, CMV infection most often presents as an infectious mononucleosis syndrome, characterised by fever, atypical lymphocytosis, lymph node enlargement, and hepatitis with hepatomegaly and abnormal liver function test results.

Herpes simplex virus (Option C): Oral herpes, most often due to HSV-1, commonly presents in children as acute gingivostomatitis and in adults as acute pharyngitis, with vesicles and ulcerations that may be accompanied by fever, lymphadenopathy, and anorexia. Lesions range from small vesicles to large bullae containing clear fluid, which rupture to form painful shallow ulcers. Histology shows intracellular and intercellular oedema with intranuclear viral inclusions or multinucleated giant cells, demonstrable by the Tzanck test.

question_text: Which is the narrowest part of the adult larynx airway?
explanation:
Explanation:

The adult laryngeal airway is divided into three regions: supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis.

  • The glottis, which includes the true vocal cords and the space between them, is the narrowest part of the adult airway.
  • In contrast, the pediatric airway has its narrowest point at the cricoid cartilage (subglottis).
  • Knowledge of the narrowest airway region is crucial for airway management, endotracheal intubation, and recognizing potential sites of obstruction.

Explanation of Other Options:

Supraglottis (Option A): Includes epiglottis, arytenoids, false cords, and ventricles; wider than the glottis.

Subglottis (Option C): Area below the vocal cords to the cricoid; narrowest in children.

Trachea (Option D): Continues below the subglottis; larger than glottis in adults.

question_text: Croup can be caused by which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) is an acute viral infection of the upper airway that causes inflammation and narrowing of the subglottic region of the larynx and trachea, leading to a characteristic barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness. It commonly affects children between 6 months and 3 years of age, with a higher incidence in boys and during the late fall and winter months.

Etiology: The most common cause is Parainfluenza virus type 1, followed by types 2 and 3. Other viruses include Influenza virus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), Adenovirus, and Measles virus.

Pathophysiology: Viral infection leads to inflammation and edema of the laryngeal, tracheal, and bronchial mucosaespecially the subglottic area. This narrowing increases airway resistance during inspiration, producing stridor.

Clinical Features: Croup typically begins with nonspecific upper respiratory symptoms (coryza, low-grade fever, and sore throat), progressing to barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor. Symptoms worsen at night and may be associated with varying degrees of respiratory distress.

Diagnosis:

Usually clinical, based on characteristic symptoms.

Neck X-ray (AP view) may show the "steeple sign" tapering of the subglottic tracheal shadow.

Treatment:

  • Mild cases: Humidified air, hydration, and reassurance.
  • Moderate to severe cases: Nebulized epinephrine for rapid relief and systemic corticosteroids (dexamethasone or budesonide) to reduce airway inflammation.
  • Severe airway obstruction: Hospitalization and oxygen support may be needed.

Explanation of other options:

Streptococcus (Option A): May cause bacterial tracheitis, which is a different, more severe condition.

Hemophilus Influenza (Type B) (Option B): The classic cause of Acute Epiglottitis, a medical emergency distinct from croup.

N.Gonorrhoea (Option D): It causes sexually transmitted infections and neonatal conjunctivitis, not croup.

Key Takeaways:

  • Croup = Viral (Parainfluenza, Influenza, RSV).
  • Epiglottitis = Bacterial (H. influenzae type B).

question_text: Dohlman's procedure is performed for which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Dohlman's procedure is a minimally invasive endoscopic technique used for the treatment of Zenker's diverticulum - a pharyngoesophageal pouch resulting from cricopharyngeal muscle dysfunction. The procedure involves an endoscopic diverticulotomy, in which the cricopharyngeal bar is divided to facilitate smooth passage of food into the oesophagus."\

Zenker's Diverticulum

  • A false diverticulum caused by herniation of the pharyngeal mucosa through Killian's dehiscence.
    • Killian's dehiscence is a weak area between the oblique and transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus muscle.
  • Pathophysiology: Dysfunction of the cricopharyngeal muscle leads to increased intraluminal pressure during swallowing, resulting in posterior outpouching (diverticulum) of mucosa.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Dysphagia
    • Regurgitation of undigested food
    • Halitosis
    • Aspiration pneumonia due to regurgitation into the airway
  • Diagnosis:
    • Barium swallow X-ray: Demonstrates a posterior pharyngeal pouch arising from Killian's dehiscence.
  • Treatment:
    • Endoscopic diverticulotomy (Dohlman's procedure): Preferred for small to moderate pouches.
    • Open diverticulectomy: Indicated for large diverticula or recurrent cases.

Explanation of other options:

Meckel's diverticulum (Option A): Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct located in the small intestine. It is treated surgically by Meckel's diverticulectomy, not by Dohlman's procedure.

Bochdalek hernia (Option C): A congenital diaphragmatic hernia resulting from the failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close. Management involves surgical repair of the diaphragmatic defect, not Dohlman's procedure.

Menetrier's disease (Option D): Menetrier's disease is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy characterized by protein loss and excessive mucus secretion. Treatment includes medical management and, in severe cases, gastrectomy.

question_text: Which vitamin deficiency leads to Laryngismus stridulus?
explanation:
Explanation:

Laryngismus stridulus is associated with Vitamin D deficiency as in rickets.

  • Laryngismus stridulus is a condition in which stridor (a high-pitched, wheezing sound during breathing) is caused by spasmodic contraction of the adductor muscles of the larynx.
  • It is usually a manifestation of a broader disorder, namely tetany or spasmophilia, often secondary to rickets.
  • Thus, it can result from calcium or vitamin deficiency.

Explanation of other options:

Vitamin K (Option A): Vitamin K is involved in blood clotting; its deficiency causes bleeding disorders like hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Vitamin E (Option B): Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant and is not associated with laryngospasm.

Vitamin A (Option D): Vitamin A is essential for epithelial integrity and vision. Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia and keratomalacia, not laryngismus.

question_text: A child presented with stridor, barking cough and difficulty in breathing since 3 days. He also had low grade fever with increased leukocyte count. All of the following are true except:
option_a: On X-ray, sub glottic stenosis is seen
option_b: Boys are affected more than girls
option_c: Antibiotics are the main stay of treatment
explanation:
This is a case of acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup).

Treatment includes:

  • Hospitalization & IV fluids
  • I/v steroids : to reduce edema especially when child is in distress
  • Humidified air to soften crusts
  • Racemic Adrenaline via a respirator - Bronchodilator
  • Intubation / tracheostomy may be needed

Antibiotics are only given to prevent secondary infection. Croup is usually caused by viral infections, and antibiotics are not the mainstay of treatment. Supportive care, such as humidified air, hydration, and sometimes corticosteroids, is more commonly used. Antibiotics are not effective against viral infections.

Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no – 339, 340

question_text: Which of the following treatment options is not recommended for a 4-year-old boy presenting with low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and barking cough for the past 5 days? The examination shows a hoarse voice, a moderately inflamed pharynx, and a slightly increased respiratory rate. The chest x-ray reveals subglottic narrowing resembling a steeple.
explanation:
Explanation:
The clinical picture barking cough, stridor, hoarseness, and the steeple sign on X-ray is classic for viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus. Antibiotics like cefotaxime have no role in the treatment of uncomplicated viral croup.

The management of this condition involves a multi-faceted approach.

  • Antibiotic therapy, typically with Ampicillin at a dosage of 50 mg/kg/day, is administered to target bacterial pathogens such as influenzae.
  • Humidification is employed to loosen and clear obstructive crusts and thick secretions from the tracheobronchial tree.
  • Steroids are added to the regimen to reduce inflammatory edema, while racemic epinephrine is used for its bronchodilatory effects to relieve airway constriction. If the obstruction persists or worsens beyond 72 hours despite these measures, intubation or tracheostomy must be considered to secure the airway.

Explanation of other options:
Nebulized racemic epinephrine (Option A): Used for moderate to severe croup to provide temporary relief of airway edema via vasoconstriction.
Helium oxygen mixture (Heliox) (Option C): Can be used in severe croup to reduce airway turbulence and work of breathing due to its low density.
Intramuscular dexamethasone (Option D): A single dose of corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) is the cornerstone of treatment for all severities of croup to reduce inflammation and edema.

Key Takeaways:

  • Croup is a viral illness; antibiotics are not indicated unless there is strong evidence of a secondary bacterial infection (e.g., bacterial tracheitis).
  • Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment.

question_text: A neonate with a history of respiratory difficulty and stridor since birth has been evaluated by microlaryngobronchoscopy. The laryngeal image is shown in the picture. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Subglottic Hemangioma: Though congenital, a patient is asymptomatic till 3-6 months of age when the haemangioma begins to increase in size. About 50% of the children have associated cutaneous haemangiomas. Patient may present with a stridor but has a normal cry. Agitation of the patient or crying may increase airway obstruction due to venous filling. Direct laryngoscopy shows reddish-blue mass below the vocal cords. Biopsy is sometimes, not always, associated with hemorrhage. Some patients have associated mediastinal haemangioma.

Depending on individual case, the treatment is:

  1. Tracheostomy and observation, as many haemangiomas involute.
  2. Steroid therapy. Dexamethasone 1 mg/kg/day for 1 week and then prednisolone 3 mg/kg in divided doses for 1 year.
  3. CO2 laser excision, if the lesion is small.

question_text: A 3 year old child has been brought to paediatric emergency with the history of fever, respiratory difficulty, stridor and drooling of saliva since yesterday. The child is in a very critical situation with Sp02 level of 80 %. What would be your immediate management?

explanation:
This is a case of acute epiglottitis.

It is an acute inflammatory condition confined to supraglottic structures, i.e. epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds and arytenoids. There is marked oedema of these structures - which may progress rapidly and prove fatal unless relieved immediately.

Acute Epiglottitis is an airway emergency.

In any airway problem, the first treatment is to establish the airway first.

Indirect laryngoscopy is avoided for fear of precipitating complete obstruction. It is better done in operation theatre where facilities for intubation are available.

question_text: A 1-month-old child presented with complain of weak cry since birth and biphasic stridor. His examination findings are given in the picture below. Which of the following statements about this condition is not true?

question_text: A 3-year-old child presented with hoarseness voice and stridor. Following a normal vaginal delivery, this child received all the routine immunization. Endoscopic picture of larynx is given below. Most probable diagnosis is:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosisis the most common benign tumour seen in children 2 to 5 years of age. It is caused by the human pailloma virus (HPV), subtypes 6 and 11, HPV 11 being more aggressive.
  • Transmission to neonate occurs through contact with mother's birth canal during vaginal delivery.
  • The papilloma starts at the true vocal cords, as seen in the endoscopic picture, and later on spreads to involve the whole of the larynx. They are multipleand even reach the mouth, pharynx, trachea and lower respiratory tract.
  • Managementinvolves microlaryngoscopic excision/ debulking by microdebrider, CO2 laser, cup forceps or cryosurgery. The most accepted and gold standard means is the microdebrider.
  • Chances of recurrence are very high, so repeated excision is required. In the postoperative period, alpha interferon, bevacizumab, and cidofovir have been shown to decrease the chance of recurrence.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding laryngomalacia is true?
option_c: The most common cause of stridor in newborn
option_d: Surgical management is required in most children
explanation:
Explanation:

  • It is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx and the most common cause of stridor in newborns.
  • Also known as congenital laryngeal stridor.
  • It is characterised by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx, which is sucked in during inspiration, producing an inspiratory stridor and sometimes cyanosis. (Option A ruled out)
  • The stridor increases with crying and breastfeeding due to increased negative pressure causing more supraglottic collapse.
  • The stridor improves in the prone position because the floppy supraglottic structures fall away from the vocal cords, increasing the breathing space. (Option B ruled out)
  • The condition manifests at birth or soon after with stridor, and usually resolves by 1-2 years of age.
  • Direct laryngoscopy shows elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself (omega-shaped Ω), floppy aryepiglottic folds and prominent arytenoids.

Management

  • Mostly, treatment is conservative.
    • 90% of babies improve by 12 to 18 months of age. (Option D ruled out)
  • Severe laryngomalacia may necessiate the need for supraglottoplasty or epiglottoplexy.

question_text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a barking cough and noisy breathing. An anteroposterior neck X-ray reveals a steeple sign. Which type of stridor is most commonly associated with this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of barking cough, noisy breathing, and a steeple sign on X-ray in a 2-year-old child is indicative of croup, which typically presents with biphasic stridor.

Croup

  • Also known as laryngotracheobronchitis, it is an inflammation of larynx, trachea, and bronchi.
  • Commonly caused by parainfluenza virus.
  • Typically affects infants and yound children aged 3 months to 3 years.

Clinical presentation

  • Low grade fever
  • Barking cough: Due to bronchospasm.
  • Biphasic stridor: Due to the subglottic involvement.

Diagnosis

  • Anteroposterior soft tissue xray of neck shows th steeple sign due to subglottic stenosis resembling the steeple of a church.

Management

  • Antibiotics against secondary infections due to Gram-positive cocci and H. influenzae.
  • Humidification helps to soften crusts and tenacious secretions which block tracheobronchial tree.
  • Steroids may be useful to relieve oedema.
  • Adrenaline, racemic adrenaline administered via a respirator is a bronchodilator and may relieve dyspnoea and avert tracheostomy.
  • Intubation/tracheostomy is done, if respiratory obstruction increase in spite of the above measures.

Explanation of other options:

Inspiratory Stridor (Option A): Typically occurs in inflammatory or obstructive conditions above the vocal cords (supraglottic) as seen in laryngomalacia.

Expiratory Stridor (Option B): Associated with subglottic or lower airway involvement, such as inflammation in the trachea or bronchi.

question_text: In a 2-year-old child with a sudden onset of noisy breathing, which type of stridor is most likely to be represented by the image below?

  • The key clinical feature is inspiratory stridor, caused by dynamic upper airway obstruction during inspiration.

Laryngomalacia

Stridor:

An abnormal, noisy breathing sound caused by turbulent airflow through a narrowed portion of the airway.

question_text: An infant was brought to the OPD with complaints of noisy breathing, the stridor was reported to worsen on lying supine. The image of the airway is given below. What type of stridor is the patient suffering from?
explanation:
Laryngomalacia sis inspiratory stridor

  • In this case, the improvement of stridor when the infant lies supine suggests that the obstruction may be positional in nature.

Other Options:

  • Biphasic stridor involves both inspiratory and expiratory components and is typically associated with fixed anatomical obstructions in the airway.
  • Positional stridor suggests that the stridor is related to the infant's position and can occur during specific body positions or activities.

question_text: Which of the following organisms is not a known cause of croup?

Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis)

  • Croup is a viral infection of entire airway (larynx, trachea and bronchi), although the subglottis the most common affected.
  • Most commonly due to Parainfluenza viruses (Types 1 and 2), followed by RSV, Influenza, and Adenovirus. (Option A, B, D ruled out)
  • Commonly affects children aged 3 months to 3 years.

    • Biphasic stridor due to subglottic involvement. Inspiratory more than expiratory.
    • Low-grade fever
    • Respiratory distress

question_text: A child presents with noisy breathing. On examination, inspiratory stridor is noted, and the laryngeal findings are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Laryngoscopy reveals an omega-shaped epiglottis, which, along with the clinical presentation of inspiratory stridor in a child, is characteristic of laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia

  • Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital anomaly of the larynx and the leading cause of stridor in newborns.
  • It is also referred to as congenital laryngeal stridor.
  • The condition is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic structures, particularly the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds.
  • During inspiration, these structures collapse inward, leading to inspiratory stridor and, occasionally, cyanosis.

Clinical Features:

  • Inspiratory stridor, appearing at birth or soon after.
  • Stridor worsens with crying or feeding due to increased negative intrathoracic pressure.
  • But improves in the prone position, as the floppy supraglottic tissues fall forward, increasing airway space.
  • Usually resolves spontaneously by 12-24 months of age.

Laryngoscopic Findings:

  • Omega-shaped epiglottis
  • Floppy aryepiglottic folds
  • Redundant arytenoid mucosa collapsing into the airway during inspiration.

Management:

  • Conservative in most cases: 90% resolve by 12-18 months of age.
  • Surgical intervention (supraglottoplasty or epiglottoplexy) is indicated for severe cases with feeding difficulty, cyanosis, or growth failure.

Explanation of other options:

Vocal cord paralysis (Option A): Vocal cord paralysis presents with biphasic stridor and a weak or breathy cry, unlike laryngomalacia, which causes purely inspiratory stridor with a normal cry.

Subglottic stenosis (Option B): Subglottic stenosis also typically produces biphasic stridor and is commonly associated with a history of prolonged intubation, which is not seen in laryngomalacia.

Laryngeal papilloma (Option C): Laryngeal papilloma leads to progressive hoarseness and voice changes due to involvement of the vocal cords, whereas laryngomalacia primarily causes stridor without affecting the voice.

question_text:
Stridor in a newborn is commonly seen in which of the following conditions?
1.Laryngomalacia
2.Subglottic stenosis
3.Laryngeal papilloma
4.Hemorrhagic polyp
explanation:
Explanation:

Subglottic stenosis and Laryngomalacia are the causes of stridor in neonates.

Stridor is an abnormal, harsh respiratory sound caused by turbulent airflow through a narrowed segment of the airway. It can occur during inspiration, expiration, or both.

  • Inspiratory stridor: Typically results from obstruction above the vocal cords, such as in the supraglottic region or pharynx. Common causes include laryngomalacia and retropharyngeal abscess.
  • Biphasic stridor: Heard during both inspiration and expiration, usually due to narrowing at the glottis, subglottis, or cervical trachea. Examples include laryngeal papillomas, bilateral vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.
  • Expiratory stridor: Occurs with obstruction of the lower airway, such as the thoracic trachea or bronchi, and is seen in conditions like tracheal stenosis or a bronchial foreign body.
  • Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis presents with stridor in children and not in neonates.
  • Haemorrhagic polyp may present with obstruction but not with stridor.

Key takeaway:

Noisy breathing/ Acute stridor

question_text: A patient with prolonged intubation complained of respiratory distress. Which of the following staging systems is used to stage the condition shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Cottom-Meyer classification is used for staging post-intubation tracheal stenosis, which can develop due to prolonged intubation, leading to respiratory distress. This classification helps assess the severity of tracheal injury and stenosis caused by mechanical ventilation.

Cotton-Meyer Classification of Subglottic Stenosis

  • Used to classify subglottic stenosis based on cross-sectional airway obstruction.
  • Originally developed for pediatric patients but now applied in adults.
  • Can be supplemented with letters (a-d) based on the number of laryngeal subsites involved.
  • Severe comorbidities or congenital abnormalities are marked with a '+' sign.
  • Idiopathic laryngotracheal stenosis (iLTS) commonly presents as Grade I-II stenosis.
  • iSGS (idiopathic subglottic stenosis) often occurs in women and presents with a higher grade of stenosis.

Radkowski classification (Option B): Incorrect because the Radkowski classification is used for tracheal injuries, but it is not the primary staging system for post-intubation tracheal stenosis.

TNM classification (Option C): Incorrect because TNM is a staging system used for cancers (such as lung cancer) and is not applicable to respiratory issues caused by prolonged intubation.

AJCC classification (Option D): Incorrect because the AJCC classification is primarily used for cancer staging and does not apply to conditions like tracheal stenosis caused by intubation.

Reference:

  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7139051/
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8892813/

question_text: Foreign body entry in the laryngeal inlet, prevented by cough reflex. Reflex is sluggish in alcohol ingestion and some other conditions. Which nerve is likely injured/damaged?
explanation:
Internal laryngeal nerve (ILN): Above the vocal cords, The sensory supply of the larynx is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve- a branch of superior laryngeal nerve. So as mentioned in the question when a foreign body enters in the laryngeal inlet coughing reflex occurs as a preventive measure. In cases of alcohol it affects the sensitivity of the laryngeal inlet as the ILN may be affected, leading to a sluggish reflex.

Option A: ELN (External laryngeal nerve): innervate the cricothyroid muscle and is not involved in the cough reflex.

Option C: RLN (Recurrent Laryngeal nerve): is responsible for the innervation of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx and the sensory innervation to the larynx below the vocal cords. It does not produce a cough reflex.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve: is responsible for the sensory innervation to the oropharynx and the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue but is not involved in the cough reflex.

KEY TAKEAWAY- Internal laryngeal nerve which is a branch of superior laryngeal nerve gives sensory supply to pyriform fossa and supraglottis.

question_text: A 6 year old male child comes to emergency with stridor and respiratory distress for last 6 hours. On Direct laryngoscopy, the vocal cords are found to be immobile and lying in median position. Which of the following would not be part of the management strategy of this patient?

question_text: Warthin's tumour is also called?
explanation:
Explanation:

Warthin's tumour is a benign salivary gland tumour, most frequently seen in the parotid gland. It is also referred to as adenolymphoma or papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum, owing to its characteristic histology.

Histological features:

  • Composed of oncocytic epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
  • Shows a bilayered epithelial lining.
  • Contains a prominent lymphoid stroma.

Clinical features:

  • Appears as a painless, cystic swelling.
  • More common in older men.
  • Strongly linked with cigarette smoking.

Pleomorphic adenoma (Option B): This is the most common benign salivary gland tumour, but it differs from Warthin's tumour in its microscopic appearance. It is termed a mixed tumour because it shows both epithelial structures (ductal/glandular elements) and mesenchymal-like areas, which may resemble myxoid tissue, cartilage, or even bone.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option C): This is a malignant salivary gland tumour, unlike the benign Warthin's tumour. It is made up of three main cell types - mucous-producing cells, squamous cells, and intermediate cells - and is known for its variable grade and clinical course.

Acinic cell carcinoma (Option D): This is also a malignant salivary gland tumour, originating from the acinar cells that normally produce serous secretions. It usually presents as a slow-growing mass but carries malignant potential, which sets it apart from benign entities like Warthin's tumour.

question_text: An 72-year-old man presents with painless swelling below the right ear that has been growing slowly for about a year. Physical examination confirms a cystic lesion. Fine- needle aspiration returns scanty brown fluid, which microscopically consists of a mixture of lymphoid cells and epithelial cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. A biopsy of the mass is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Warthin tumor is a benign neoplasm of the parotid gland, composed of cystic glandular spaces embedded in dense lymphoid tissue. This tumor is the most common monomorphic adenoma. Although the neoplasm is clearly benign, it can be bilateral (15% of cases) or multifocal within the same gland. Warthin tumor is the only tumor of the salivary glands that is more common in men than in women. These lesions generally occur after the age of 30, with most arising after age 50 years. Pleomorphic adenoma (choice c) has a biphasic appearance, which represents an admixture of epithelial and stromal elements. Acinic cell carcinoma (choice a) is an uncommon malignancy. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (choice b) is a slow-growing malignant neoplasm of the salivary gland, which invades locally and tends to recur after surgery.

question_text: A seven year old child patient has mild hearing loss along with nasal obstruction, crowding of upper teeth and dull voice. The otoscopy examination finding is given in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

GLUE EAR (OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION-OME)

It is most common cause of hearing loss.

  • Glue ear is also called SEROUS OTITIS MEDIA or SECRETORY OTITIS MEDIA. (SOM)
  • Its new name is OME (OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION).
  • It is collection of sterile thick glue-like fluid in middle ear.

School age child complaining of

+/- Adenoid face

Examination

  2. Air bubbles trapped within glue.
  3. Retracted tympanic membrane.

question_text: Oropharyngeal picture of a patient with Trismus, hot potato voice and dysphagia is shown in the given image. What is the possible diagnosis?
explanation:
The clinical scenario suggests quinsy.

Quinsy/peritonsillar abscess –

Tonsil is pushed medially and uvula is deviated to other side. This is classical feature of quinsy. There is NO outer neck swelling in Quinsy. Patient has Trismus(due to spasm of medial pterygoid muscle), odynophagia, hot potato voice.

If similar history and examination findings are there along with neck swelling close to angle of mandible, then the diagnosis is parapharyngeal abscess.

question_text: A patient presented with fever, plummy voice and difficulty in swallowing. The oropharyngeal picture is shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
uvula is pushed to the other side and tonsil is pushed medially.It is a typical finding in peritonsillar abscess also known as quincy.

The oropharyngeal picture shown indicates the presence of a peritonsillar abscess. A peritonsillar abscess is a collection of pus located between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle. It can cause symptoms such as fever, severe sore throat, "hot potato" voice (muffled voice), and difficulty swallowing.

Other options:

B. Parapharyngeal abscess: A parapharyngeal abscess is a deep neck infection involving the spaces around the pharynx, and it would not typically present with the specific oropharyngeal appearance seen in the image.It presents with neck swelling or swelling near the angle of mouth

C. Retropharyngeal abscess: A retropharyngeal abscess is an infection located in the retropharyngeal space, but it would not produce the distinct bulging seen in the tonsillar area in the image.It produces swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall.

D. Ludwig's angina: Ludwig's angina is a severe infection involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces of the neck, which can cause significant swelling and elevation of the tongue, but it would not present with a peritonsillar appearance as seen in the image.

Peritonsillar abscess or quinsy presents with

question_text: A professional singer presents with difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice following thyroid surgery. There is no hoarseness. Which nerve is likely injured?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (ELN) supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses and elongates the vocal cords
  • This function is essential for modulating pitch, particularly for producing higher frequencies in professional voice users
  • Injury to the ELN, commonly during thyroid surgery, may not cause hoarseness but results in the inability to raise pitch or project the voice
  • Singers and other voice professionals are often the first to notice this subtle voice change
  • The ELN lies close to the superior thyroid vessels, putting it at risk during thyroid procedures
  • ILN and RLN injuries typically cause hoarseness or loss of voice, which is absent in this case (Option A & C ruled out)
  • Glossopharyngeal nerve involvement would affect swallowing and pharyngeal sensation, not pitch (Option D ruled out)

question_text: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most probable diagnosis in a teacher presenting with hoarseness of voice is a vocal nodule.
This is because vocal nodules are the most common benign lesions of the vocal cords in individuals who rely heavily on their voice, such as teachers, singers, and actors.

They develop due to vocal abuse or misuse, where repeated trauma to the vocal folds causes small, benign swellings to form.

Clinical Features

  • Hoarseness of voice
  • Voice fatigue after prolonged speaking
  • Difficulty producing high-pitched sounds

Explanation of Other Options:

Vocal polyp (Option A): Unlike vocal nodules, which are typically bilateral and symmetric, vocal polyps are usually unilateral, larger, and more vascular. They are often associated with acute voice trauma (e.g., shouting, sudden excessive vocal use) rather than chronic overuse. Patients may present with sudden hoarseness following a single vocal strain episode.

Vocal cysts (Option B): These are fluid-filled sacs that develop on the vocal folds, typically due to blockage of a mucous gland.

Reinke's edema (Option D): This condition involves swelling and fluid accumulation within the vocal folds, most often linked to chronic irritant exposure such as smoking or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). While it can also lead to hoarseness, it is less likely to be the underlying cause in a teacher presenting with voice changes, where vocal nodules are more common.

question_text: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complain of severe pain and hoarseness of voice. Endoscopic picture of larynx is given below, The picture shows mouse nibbled appearance of the vocal cords, what is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical features and pictures shown above the diagnosis in this case is TB laryngitis.

Primary TB laryngitis is very rare. It usually develops secondary to pulmonary TB.

Clinical features include odynophagia. Painful deglutition is due to inflammation of Epiglottis.

Signs: The earliest sign is hyperemia of vocal cords and posterior commissure.

Arytenoid becomes very swollen known as mammillated arytenoids.

There are multiple ulcers on the vocal cords giving it mouse nibbled appearance.

Epiglottis becomes very swollen giving it a turban Epiglottis appearance.

Management is anti tubercular therapy.

Key Takeaway:

TB Larynx - 2 P & 2 M

  • Posterior & Painful
  • Mouse Nibble Cords & Mammillated Arytenoids

question_text: A 35-year-old male patient presented with complaints of hoarseness of voice. He was a chronic smoker. His endoscopy examination reveals the following features. The picture given below. Which of the following statements about this condition is not true?
option_a: Involve whole of the membranous part of the vocal cords
option_b: Patient has a low pitch voice
option_d: Voice rest and Corticosteroids are the mainstay of management
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical picture and symptoms, the diagnosis in this case is Rienke's oedema.
  • This is a chronic and irreversibleoedema of the Rienke's space. It involves the submucosal space of the membranous true vocal cords along their free medial margin. (Option A)
  • It can occur due to any chronic irritation of larynx, most commonly due to smoking;hence also known as smoker's larynx. (Option C)
  • Other irritants such as voice abuse, acid reflux and postnasal drip can also cause this.
  • Patients present with a low-pitched voice, effortful speaking and hoarseness. (Option B)
  • Diffuse symmetrical pale swellingis seen on the free edges of both the vocal cords.
  • Management - Cessation of smoking, Voice therapy and Reduction glottoplasty if required.

question_text:
A 20 year old male patient has high pitch voice. His fiberoptic laryngoscopy is normal. The clinician has advised him for speech therapy in which he is asked to phonate while pulling the thyroid cartilage downwards and pressing it backwards.
What is the name of this manoeuvre for speech therapy?
explanation:
This is a case of Puberphonia.

  • Normally, childhood voice has a higher pitch.
  • When the larynx matures at puberty, vocal cords lengthen and the voice changes to one of lower pitch. This is a feature exclusive to males.
  • Failure of this change leads to persistence of childhood high-pitched voice and is called puberphonia
  • Treatment - pressing the thyroid prominence in a backward and downward direction relaxes the overstretched cords and low tone voice can be produced (Gutzmann’s pressure test).
  • Prognosis is good.
  • If patient is not relieved with speech therapy, then Type III thyroplasty is done.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8th Edition, pg. no – 367, 351

SPASMODIC DYSPHONIA

Aetiology is uncertain but one should exclude neurological conditions such as Parkinsonism, myoclonus, pseudobulbar palsy, multiple sclerosis, cerebellar disorders, tardive dyskinesia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Earlier disease was considered to be psychological in origin but psychotherapy was not found useful.

Treatment includes speech therapy with botulinum toxin injections.

question_text: A 20-year-old male patient presented with complaints of persistence of a boy-like high-pitched voice. All his friends have developed adult-like low-pitched voices. question_text: A 30-year-old female patient presented with complain of scratchy creaky voice. On examination, the vocal cords were found to be having Adductor Spasmodic dysphonia. All are true about this condition except?
