question_text: A 45-year-old teacher presents with complaints of progressive hoarseness and voice fatigue that worsens by the end of the day. She has no history of smoking or alcohol use. Flexible laryngoscopy findings are shown in the given image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The laryngoscopic image shows nodular lesions at the anterior-middle third junction of the vocal cords. In the context of hoarseness and vocal fatigue in a teacher, these findings are indicative of vocal nodules.

Vocal nodules

  • Also known as singer's or screamer nodes.
  • Most common cause of vocal abuse.
  • These nodules appear symmetrically on the free edge of vocal cord at the junction of anterior 1/3rdand the posterior 2/3, which is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus subject to maximum trauma.
  • Vocal nodules are the result of vocal trauma in form of misuse or abuse; mostly affects teachers, actors, singers.
  • A contributory risk factor is laryngopharyngeal reflux or gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Presenting complaints

  • Hoarsness
  • Vocal fatigue
  • Pain in neck on prolong phonation.

Treatment

  • Early cases of vocal nodules can be treated conservatively by speech therapy to teach proper vocal techniques.
  • If speech therapy is not an option, voice rest is the second-best treatment.
  • Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are also recommended due to the role of reflux.
  • Surgery is required for large nodules or nodules of long standing in adults.
    • They are excised with precision under operating microscope either with cold instruments or laser avoiding any trauma to the underlying vocal ligament.

Explanation of other options:

Reinke's oedema (Option B): It is characterized by bilateral diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. It results from vocal abuse (excessive talking or shouting) and smoking.

Vocal polyp (Option C): The etiology and site of vocal polyps are the same as vocal nodules, but the key difference from nodules is that vocal polyps are usually unilateral.

Keratosis larynx (Option D): Commonly results due to chronic irritation by smoking, tobacco chewing, excessive voice abuse, and reflux.  This presents as a whitish keratinous coating on the vocal cords.

question_text: What is the most common site of a ranula?
explanation:
Explanation:

A ranula is a mucus retention cyst that arises in the floor of the mouth. It results from obstruction or rupture of the sublingual gland duct, leading to saliva pooling in the surrounding tissues. Clinically, it presents as a bluish, dome-shaped, fluctuant swelling beneath the tongue. Larger ranulas can cause discomfort and may interfere with speech, mastication, or swallowing.

question_text: Which of the following symptoms is most characteristic of Reinke’s oedema?
option_c: Dysphagia of liquids more than solids
option_d: Dysphagia of solids more than liquids
explanation:
Explanation :

The hallmark symptom of Reinke's edema is diplophonia, often described as a 'double voice.' This occurs when the vocal cords vibrate irregularly, producing two different pitches simultaneously. The condition is strongly linked to chronic irritation of the vocal cords.

Aetiology / Risk Factors:

  • Chronic smoking (hence also called smoker's larynx).
  • Prolonged vocal abuse or strain.
  • Laryngopharyngeal reflux.
  • Endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Hoarseness and a low-pitched, rough voice.
  • Diplophonia (classic sign).
  • Swollen, translucent, fusiform vocal cords on laryngoscopy.
  • False vocal cord hypertrophy may obscure the true cords.

Management:

  • Microlaryngeal surgery (cord decortication) is performed in stages.
  • Voice rest post-surgery.
  • Speech therapy to restore proper voice function.

Explanation of Other Options:

Dysphonia (Option B):Refers to any general voice change and can occur, but it is not specific.

Dysphagia (Options C & D):Difficulty swallowing liquids or solids is notassociated with Reinke's oedema.

question_text: A 20 year old male patient have high pitch voice. His fiberoptic laryngocopy is normal. The clinician adviced him for speech therapy. What is the name of maneuver in this therapy?
explanation:
• Normally after puberty male develops a low pitch voice. Persistence of high pitch voice in males after puberty is called puberphonia.
  • The main treatment in puberphonia is speech therapy. In this therapy patient is asked to press the thyroid cartilage backwards this leads to shortening of vocal cords.
  • The patient is asked to continue this therapy for 3months. The name of this maneuver is called as Gutzmann maneuver.

question_text: Post complete laryngectomy all advised/done except?
explanation:
After a complete laryngectomy, the patient will need a way to produce speech. The most common methods are an electrolarynx, a tracheo-esophageal fistula, or esophageal speech.

Supra tracheal prosthesis / fistula is not a method of speech production that is used after a complete laryngectomy.

A. Electrolarynx: An electrolarynx is an electronic device held against the neck that produces sound when activated, providing an artificial voice.

B. Tracheo -Esophageal fistula (TEF): TEF is a surgical technique that creates a connection between the trachea (windpipe) and the esophagus. This allows air to be diverted into the esophagus, and the patient can use the upper esophageal sphincter to create speech sounds. It is a common method of post-laryngectomy voice rehabilitation.

D. Esophageal speech: Esophageal speech is a technique where the patient swallows air and then regurgitates it while shaping the mouth and pharynx to produce speech sounds.

question_text: Given below is the image of a patient who underwent laryngectomy. Which mode of speech is he using?
explanation: In the image, a laryngectomy has been performed, which means the patient's larynx (voice box) has been removed. In such cases, patients often use alternative methods to produce speech. Tracheoesophageal speech is a common method used by laryngectomy patients. It involves the surgical creation of a small opening between the trachea and the esophagus, through which air can be redirected from the lungs into the esophagus. By expelling air from the esophagus, patients can produce speech sounds and communicate.

question_text: A 45 year old female was operated for emergency appendectomy under general anesthesia. After surgery she is complaining of hoarseness of voice. What can be the most probable etiology?
explanation:
This patient was given general anaesthesia which implies that she has been intubated. Therefore intubation granuloma is the most probable cause of this situation. It is an iatrogenic entity.

Intubation granuloma

  • Due to injury to vocal processes of arytenoids due to rough intubation, use of a large tube or prolonged presence of tube between the cords.
  • Mucosal ulceration is followed by granuloma formation over the exposed cartilage.
  • Bilateral involving posterior thirds of true cords.
  • Present with hoarseness and if large, dyspnoea as well.
  • Treatment is voice rest and removal by microlaryngeal surgery.

REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no - 354

question_text: Voice problems in public appearances is :

question_text: A 43-year-old smoker presents to the ENT OPD with hoarseness of voice. Study the given image of laryngeal endoscopy and comment on the diagnosis.

INTUBATION GRANULOMA - bilateral following intubation.

question_text: A 47 year old with history of smoking for last 10 years has presented with hoarseness of voice for last 3 weeks. The fibreoptic laryngoscopy image has been shown in the given image. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
In vast majority of cases, laryngeal cancer originates in the glottic region. Free edge and upper surface of vocal cord in its anterior and middle third is the most frequent site

spread. Locally, the lesion may spread anteriorly to anterior commissure and then to the opposite cord; posteriorly to vocal process and arytenoid region; upward to ventricle and false cord; and downwards to subglottic region. Vocal cord mobility is unaffected in early stages.

Fixation of vocal cord indicates spread of disease to thyroarytenoid muscle and is a bad prognostic sign.

There are few lymphatics in vocal cords and nodal metastases are practically never seen in cordal lesions unless the disease spreads beyond the region of membranous cord.

symptoms. Hoarseness of voice is an early sign because lesions of cord affect its vibratory capacity. It is because of this that glottic cancer is detected early.

question_text:

question_text: A 5-year-old female child presented with complaints of hoarseness of voice. Her laryngoscopic endoscopy examination was done, and the image is given below. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
option_b: Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice
option_c: It is more common in 15 to 30 years of age.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical picture and symptoms, the diagnosis in this case is Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis.
  • It is the most common benign tumour seen in children. It is commonly seen between the ages of 2 and 5 years. (Option C)
  • It is caused by the human papilloma virus (HPV). HPV 6 and 11 strains are the common subtypes, HPV 11 being more aggressive. (Option A)
  • Transmission occurs from the mother to the child during vaginal delivery. It presents with hoarseness of voice and abnormal cry.
  • Malignant transformation can occur.Thus, it is considered a premalignant (Option D)
  • Treatment includes microlaryngoscopic removalusing laser or cold steel, or microdebrider. (Option B)

question_text: Biology after taking a long vigorous 8 hour class for 6 years began to have hoarseness in his voice. Which of the following condition is associated with this:
explanation:
The above picture depicts vocal nodules over both the vocal folds. History of a teacher with gradual hoarseness of voice also supports the diagnosis.

  • Vocal fold nodules are small bilateral swellings (less than 3 mm in diameter) that develop on the free edge of the vocal fold at approximately the mid-membranous portion
  • The etiology of vocal nodules is not known, but traditionally they are thought to be due to 'voice abuse' rather than overuse.

Voice abuse is characterized by forced voice production due to strain in the neck and shoulder region producing a harsh quality to the voice.

It may be precipitated by talking for prolonged periods in a loud voice as in teachers, repeated shouting and/or singing above one's natural range and occasionally repeated coughing and throat clearing.

  • The repeated trauma of the mid membranous portions leads to localized swelling and epithelial thickening.
  • The mainstay of treatment for persistent vocal nodules is voice therapy with the aim of modification of lifestyle and vocal behavior, providing information and guidance on voice care, producing the voice more effectively with less strain and coping strategies.
  • Surgery is reserved for those who fail voice therapy and remain symptomatic. If surgery is performed, the aim must be precise excision of the nodule alone with no exposure or damage to the underlying ligament

question_text: A 42 year old patient, singer by profession has been vigorously practicing for an important concert of his life.  He has subsequently developed hoarse voice. On fiberoptic laryngoscopy, he is found to have adduction of false vocal cords while phonating. What is the name of this clinical condition?
explanation:
This is a case of Dysphonia Plica Ventricularis (Ventricular Dysphonia) -

  • Here voice is produced by ventricular folds (false cords) which have taken over the function of true cords.
  • Voice is rough, low-pitched and unpleasant.
  • Indirect laryngoscopy - false cords are seen to approximate partially or completely.
  • It is of two types -
    1. FUNCTIONAL TYPE - Psychogenic. Here voice begins normally but soon becomes rough.
    2. Secondary to laryngeal disorders

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no - 366

question_text: A patient with hoarseness of voice was found to be having pachydermia laryngis. All of the following are true except:
option_a: It is a hyperkeratotic lesion present in the interarytenoid region

Pachydermia laryngis is not a premalignant condition

Pachydermia laryngis:

question_text: A 19 year old college going girl has presented to emergency with sudden loss of voice. Her cough sound is normal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Functional aphonia is a voice disorder that occurs when someone is unable to use their voice normally, despite being physically healthy. It can be caused by a number of factors, including:

  1. Improper breathing :The respiratory system powers the voice, so breathing problems can make it difficult to speak.
  2. Lack of coordination: Using the voice normally requires coordination between the respiratory system, larynx, throat, nose, and mouth.
  3. Underlying psychiatric condition :Functional aphonia can be a symptom of an underlying psychiatric condition.

There are two types of functional aphonia:

  • Habitual aphonia: Can be caused by any factor and may continue even after the cause is gone.
  • Psychogenic aphonia: Occurs when someone loses their voice in response to a traumatic or stressful life event.

Misophonia: A strong reaction to specific sounds.Misophonia may cause a reaction to sounds such as dripping water, chewing, snapping gum, or repetitive noises, such as pencil tapping or clicking sounds.

Phonasthenia is a voice disorder that refers to a functional weakness or fatigue of the voice.

question_text: A patient suffering from chronic recurrent heartburn, epigastric pain has developed a hoarse voice for the last one month. The laryngeal fiberoptic laryngoscopy has revealed the congestion and mamillation of mucosa in the interarytenoid area. What is the possible diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Chronic recurrent heartburn and epigastric pain are suggestive of gastro-oesophageal reflex.

GERD (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease) -> LPR -> posterior part of larynx constantly bathed by acid juices from the stomach -> chronic irritation of the affected area -> vocal nodules, pachydermia laryngis , reinke’s edema, keratosis larynx.

Pachydermia laryngis is heaping up of epithelium in the interarytenoid region. It is not premalignant.

Reinke’s edema is polypoid degeneration of vocal cord seen as bilateral, symmetrical, fusiform swelling of vocal cords on laryngoscopy.

Keratosis of larynx is a localized epithelial hyperplasia involving upper surface of one or both cords. It is premalignant.

Laryngeal pseudosulcus is not attached to the underlying tissues whereas a true vocal cord sulcus is adherent to underlying tissues of vocal cord. It refers to the appearance of a fold parallel to the free edge of the vocal cord.

Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no – 342, 354

question_text: A 72-year-old female smoker presents with a long history of hoarseness of voice, difficulty swallowing, and difficulty breathing. The patient was diagnosed with laryngeal cancer and underwent surgical management. The post-operative picture is shown below. Which of the following surgeries was most likely performed on the patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a permanent end tracheostomy, which is the definitive result of a total laryngectomy.

Indications of total laryngectomy:

  • Advanced laryngeal cancer (e.g., T4a stage with thyroid cartilage invasion).
  • Stage 3 or 4a tumours in patients unfit for chemoradiation.
  • Recurrent tumours after previous treatments.
  • Bilateral arytenoid involvement affects vocal cord mobility.

Permanent End Tracheostomy (Post-Total Laryngectomy)

  • Seen after total laryngectomy, performed for advanced laryngeal cancers when organ preservation is not feasible.
  • Entire larynx (including vocal cords, thyroid cartilage, and cricoid cartilage) is removed.
  • Pharynx is closed and the trachea is brought forward and sutured to the skin, creating a permanent stoma for breathing. This permanently separates the airway from the digestive tract.
  • Patients lose natural voice production, and require voice rehabilitation (esophageal speech, tracheoesophageal puncture, or electronic larynx).

Explanation of Other Options:

Partial laryngectomy (Option A): Involves removal of part of the larynx (e.g., hemilaryngectomy, supraglottic laryngectomy) with preservation of voice and no permanent tracheostomy. The picture does not match.

Standard tracheostomy (Option C): Involves creation of a temporary opening in the trachea for airway access. The upper airway remains intact, and tracheostomy tubes are usually present, unlike the permanent end stoma seen here.

Percutaneous tracheostomy (Option D): Minimally invasive tracheostomy done at the bedside, temporary and not equivalent to laryngectomy. It does not result in permanent separation of airway and digestive tract.

question_text: A 50 yrs old male chronic smoker complains of hoarseness for the past 4 months.  Microlaryngoscopy biopsy shows it to be keratosis of the larynx.  All the suggested treatment modalities for this condition, except
explanation:
Leukoplakia or keratosis of larynx is a premalignant epithelial hyperplasia involving the upeer surface of vocal cords. Treatment includes

  • Stripping of vocal cords followed by histology of tissue for any malignant change. Laser vaporizer can also be used.
  • Chronic laryngeal irritants should be eliminated.

Partial laryngectomy is done for T2 stage of carcinoma larynx.

Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no 354

question_text: Which of the subsequent laryngeal cartilages is least prone to calcification?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Epiglottis is least prone to calcification because it is composed of elastic cartilage, which resists calcification compared to hyaline cartilage.
  • Elastic cartilage maintains its flexibility and does not undergo the age-related ossification seen in other laryngeal cartilages.

Epiglottis:

  • Unpaired Elastic Cartilage
  • Shape: Leaf-shaped yellow elastic cartilage.
  • Location: Forms the anterior wall of the laryngeal inlet.
  • Attachments:
    • Connected to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament, dividing it into suprahyoid and infrahyoid Portions.
    • The petiole attaches it to the thyroid cartilage just above the vocal cords.
  • Anterior Surface:
    • Pre-epiglottic Space: Located in front of the epiglottis, between the anterior surface and the thyrohyoid membrane/upper thyroid cartilage. Filled with fat, it may be involved in supraglottic cancers or the base of tongue carcinomas.
  • Posterior Surface:
    • Tubercle of Epiglottis: A bulge that may obstruct the view of the anterior commissure during indirect laryngoscopy.
    • Contains pits for mucous glands and occasional perforations, which may facilitate cancer spread to the pre-epiglottic space.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Cancer Spread: Supraglottic cancers can invade the pre-epiglottic space through epiglottic perforations.
    • Non-Essential for Swallowing: The epiglottis can be safely amputated in cases of cancer or trauma without significant risk of aspiration.

Explanation of other options:

Thyroid (Option A): The thyroid cartilage is made of hyaline cartilage, which tends to calcify with age, especially after the third decade of life.

Cricoid (Option B): Like the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage is also composed of hyaline cartilage and is prone to calcification as part of the normal ageing process.

Arytenoid (Option C): The arytenoid cartilage consists of hyaline cartilage in its base and elastic cartilage in its apex, but the hyaline portion is susceptible to calcification over time.

Key Takeaways:

question_text: Laryngeal crepitus is seen in :
explanation:
Laryngeal Crepitus is the grating sensation experienced while moving the Thyroid cartilage over the underlying cervical vertebra. It is present in normal people.

It is absent in

  1. Post-cricoid carcinoma
  2. Prevertebral abscess
  3. Fracture of thyroid cartilage
  4. Retropharyngeal abscess

Absence of laryngeal crepitus is called Moure’s sign.

REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no - 454

question_text: A 50-year-old male patient was diagnosed to have carcinoma of the larynx. His CT scan was suggestive of involvement of the anterior commissure and the right vocal cord. He has also developed perichondritis of the thyroid cartilage. Which of the following statements is true for management in this case?
option_a: He should be given radical radiotherapy as this can cure early tumor
option_b: He should be treated with a combination of radiotherapy and chemotherapy
option_c: He should first receive radiotherapy, and if residual tumor is present, then undergo laryngectomy.
option_d: He should first undergo laryngectomy and then postoperative radiotherapy.
explanation:
Explanation for the Answer:

  • Thyroid cartilage perichondritis indicates invasion of the thyroid cartilage.
  • Invasion of thyroid cartilage means a T4a tumour.
  • Total laryngectomy followed by radiotherapy is used as a modality for stage 4a tumour with thyroid cartilage invasion.

question_text: A 52 year old female patient suffering from thyroid carcinoma underwent total thyroidectomy. While surgery, both side recurrent laryngeal nerves got damaged. What are the expected post-operative symptoms of patient?
option_c: Respiratory distress with poor quality of voice
option_d: Respiratory distress with stridor and normal voice
explanation:
This clinical situation will lead to Bilateral abductor palsy of vocal cord as the only muscle left working in this nerve injury is cricothyroid which is an adductor of vocal cord (supplied by SLN). Both vocal cords come to lie in the median or paramedian position and are paralyzed. Hence patient will have respiratory distress and stridor with normal voice (Wagner and Grossman hypothesis).

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no – 348, 349

question_text: While surgical removal of an impacted fish bone, the surgeon has accidentally injured internal laryngeal nerve.  What is the possible site of impaction of fish bone?
explanation:
Pyriform sinus

  • Is a common site of impaction of foreign body.
  • Internal laryngeal nerve runs submucosally in the lateral wall of the sinus and thus is easily accessible for local anaesthesia/ injury during surgery.
  • It is also through this nerve that pain is referred to the ear in carcinoma of the pyriform sinus.

Pyrifrom sinus is a part of hypopharynx

Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no – 284, 285

question_text: A surgeon has planned for a biopsy procedure for a supraglottic lesion. Before the procedure, he placed a cotton soaked in Xylocaine in the Pyriform Sinus region. Which nerve is being anesthetized?
explanation: The superior laryngeal nerve, a branch of a vagus nerve produces two branches: the internal laryngeal nerve (its sensory branch) which supplies sensory fibers to the laryngeal mucosa, and the external laryngeal nerve (its motor branch) which innervates the cricothyroid muscle. Local anesthetic injections to block the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN) can anesthetize the supraglottic region, down to the bottom of the epiglottis, and block the cricothyroid muscle, which relaxes the vocal cords.

question_text: If the pyriform fossa is injured due to a fish bone, which nerve is likely to be damaged?
option_b: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
explanation:
Explanation:

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is responsible for irritation.

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve courses beneath the mucosa along the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus. When a foreign body becomes lodged in this area, it can irritate the nerve. Because the nerve is superficial here, it can be readily targeted for local anesthesia. Pain from carcinoma of the pyriform sinus is often referred to the ear through this nerve.

The pyriform fossa lies on each side of the larynx, forming a lateral food channel that extends from the pharyngoepiglottic fold down to the upper end of the esophagus. Its boundaries are:

  • Medial: Aryepiglottic fold and the posterolateral surfaces of the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages
  • Lateral: Thyrohyoid membrane and thyroid cartilage

Explanations for other Options:

Vagus nerve (Option A):The vagus gives off the internal superior laryngeal nerve but its main trunk lies much deeper in the neck, well protected by surrounding structures.
A superficial injury inside the pyriform fossa is unlikely to reach the main vagus.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C): This nerve ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and enters the larynx below the thyroid cartilage, far away from the mucosal surface of the pyriform sinus.Damage here would cause vocal-cord paralysis, but its location is too inferior and medial to be injured by a fish bone in the fossa.

Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D): The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the oropharynx and posterior third of the tongue and passes high in the parapharyngeal space.It does not course through the pyriform sinus, so a local mucosal injury there would not affect it.

question_text: Which structures pass between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
option_b: Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery
explanation:
Explanation:

The stylopharyngeus muscle (derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch) and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) (the nerve of the 3rd arch) pass through the gap between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors.

Explanation of other options:

Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery (Option B): Pass through the thyrohyoid membrane in the gap between the middle and inferior constrictor muscles.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C): Enters the larynx deep to the inferior constrictor muscle.

Ascending palatine artery (Option D): A branch of the facial artery that passes through the sinus of Morgagni, the gap between the base of the skull and the superior border of the superior constrictor muscle.

Key Takeaways:

  • Between Superior & Middle Constrictor: Stylopharyngeus & CN IX.
  • Between Middle & Inferior Constrictor: Internal Laryngeal Nerve & Vessel.

question_text:
A patient of T3N0M0 carcinoma larynx has undergone total laryngectomy. He has permanent tracheostomy following this surgery. He is using the device given in picture for vocal rehabilitation

What is the name of this device?
explanation:
Electrolarynx or artificial larynx

  • Battery operated, hand held portable device.
  • Its vibrating disc is held against the soft tissues of the neck and a low-pitched sound is produced in the hypopharynx which is further modulated into speech by the tongue, lips, teeth and palate.
  • Used in those who fail to learn oesophageal speech

Blom singer prosthesis and panje’s prosthesis are tracheo- oesophageal speech devices.

Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no 365

question_text: A anaesthetic was performing the procedure of superior laryngeal nerve block. Picture given below. What will be the landmark he will use for superior laryngeal nerve block?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The larynx is supplied by the vagus nerve. It gives 2 branches to the larynx The superior laryngeal nerve and the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • The superior laryngeal nerve arises from the Inferior ganglion of vagus just below the base of the skull and descends down
  • In the neck, at the level of the greater cornu of hyoid bone, it gives off two branches
  • The external laryngeal nerve,as the name suggests, lies externally deep to the superior thyroid artery and supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only intrinsic muscle of the larynx lying externally.
  • The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and, along with the superior laryngeal artery, passes between the middle and inferior constrictor, and gives sensory supply to the larynx and hypopharynx above the vocal cords.

Key takeaway:

The superior laryngeal nerve divide at the level of Greater cornu of hyoid bone. So it can be used as a landmark for blocks

question_text: Which of the following is true about laryngeal cancer stage T1bNOMO?
option_a: Both vocal cords involved and fixed
option_b: Both vocal cords involved, and no metastasis
option_c: One vocal cord involved and metastasis
option_d: One vocal cord involved, and mobile
explanation:
Explanation:

The T1bN0M0 stageof laryngeal cancer indicates that the tumor is confined to both vocal cords, and is not metastatized

question_text: A 50-year-old male patient has been diagnosed with carcinoma larynx. His endoscopy and CT scan reveal that the tumour involves both sides vocal cords, but the mobility of the vocal cords is normal. The tumour is not extending into any other regions of the larynx. What will be the T staging in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tumour is limited to the vocal cords only with normal mobility, suggestive of T1 stage. Moreover, it involves both vocal cords; thus stage is T1b.

  • T1: Tumour limited to vocal cord (s) (may involve anterior or posterior commissure) with normal mobility.
    • T1a - tumour limited to one vocal cord
    • T1b - tumour involved both vocal cords
  • T2: Tumour extends to supraglottis and/or subglottis, and/or with impaired vocal cord mobility
  • T3: Tumour limited to larynx with vocal cord fixation and/or invades paraglottic space, and/or with minor thyroid cartilage erosion (inner cortex)
  • T4a Tumour invades through thyroid cartilage or invades tissues beyond the larynx, e.g. trachea, soft tissues of neck including deep/extrinsic muscle of tongue (genioglossus, hyoglossus, palatoglossus and styloglossus), strap muscles, thyroid and oesophagus
  • T4b: Tumour invades prevertebral space, mediastinal structures, or encases carotid artery- table

question_text: Delphian nodes are
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The Delphian node is a Level VI nodewhich lies in the central/anterior compartment of the neck.
  • These are prelaryngeal lymph nodes located just above the thyroid isthmus, on the cricothyroid membrane.
  • Mainly drains the subglottic region of larynx and pyriform sinuses.

question_text: Laryngeal crepitus is absent in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Normally, the larynx moves during deglutition and can also be shifted laterally, producing a characteristic grating sound called laryngeal crepitus.
  • Fixity of the larynx indicates inflammation or infiltration by a growth into surrounding structures, leading to loss of laryngeal crepitus.
  • Loss of laryngeal crepitus most reliably indicates a prevertebral abscess or advanced post-cricoid carcinoma.
  • In prevertebral abscess, laryngeal crepitus is absent because the infection fixes the larynx to the spine.

Explanation of other options:

Post-cricoid malignancy (Option A): In post-cricoid malignancy, early-stage tumours do not fix the larynx. Laryngeal crepitus is preserved in initial stages and is lost only when the malignancy advances and invades surrounding tissues.

Hypopharyngeal abscess (Option B): Hypopharyngeal abscess, although it may partially restrict laryngeal movement, laryngeal crepitus is usually preserved and is absent only in cases of a very large abscess.

Parapharyngeal abscess (Option C): A parapharyngeal abscess is located lateral to the larynx and rarely causes fixation. While extensive abscesses may slightly restrict movement, laryngeal crepitus is usually preserved.

question_text: A 55-year-old individual presents with hoarseness and dysphagia and is subsequently diagnosed with laryngeal carcinoma. Surgical treatment is performed, and a post-operative image is provided. Based on the clinical background and image findings, which surgical procedure was most likely carried out?
explanation:
Explanation:

A total laryngectomy is a surgical procedure in which the entire larynx is removed.

  • This procedure is typically performed in advanced laryngeal cancer cases that have not responded to other treatments, such as radiation therapy or chemotherapy.
  • During a total laryngectomy, the trachea is rerouted to the front of the neck to create an opening called a stoma, which serves as the new airway.
  • This procedure has significant implications for speech and swallowing, and patients typically require extensive rehabilitation to learn new communication and eating methods.

Indications for total laryngectomy:

  1. T4a with thyroid cartilage invasion.
  2. Stage 3 and 4 patients who cannot tolerate chemotherapy.
  3. Stage 3 and 4 recurrent tumours
  4. Bilateral arytenoid involvement.

Explanation for other options:

Partial laryngectomy (Option A): A partial laryngectomy is a surgical procedure in which only a part of the larynx is removed, leaving the rest of the organ intact.

Percutaneous tracheostomy (Option B): Percutaneous tracheostomy is a minimally invasive procedure where a tube is inserted into the trachea via a small neck incision. It's commonly used for temporary or permanent airway support in conditions like obstructive sleep apnea or chronic respiratory failure, but it's not suitable for treating laryngeal cancer.

Standard tracheostomy (Option C): A standard tracheostomy involves creating a neck incision to access the trachea, commonly used for temporary or permanent airway support in breathing difficulties. However, it's typically avoided in laryngeal cancer cases as it doesn't address the cancerous tissue in the larynx.

question_text: A patient presents with hoarseness of voice. On examination, there is an ulceroproliferative mass on the right vocal cord, but the cord remains mobile. There is no regional lymph node involvement or distant metastasis. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In this patient, the ulceroproliferative mass is confined to the right vocal cord and the vocal cord remains mobile. There is no regional lymph node involvement and no distant metastasis.
  • These findings indicate an early-stage laryngeal carcinoma (T1–T2).
  • For such localized tumors, radiotherapy is the treatment of choice.
  • It effectively eradicates the tumor while preserving voice function and avoiding more invasive surgery.

Laryngeal Carcinoma

  • A major risk factor is smoking due to carcinogenic chemicals like benzopyrene.
  • Laryngeal carcinoma is classified based on the site of origin within the larynx into three main types: Supraglottic, glottic and subglottic.

Simplified tumor staging of laryngeal cancer

  • T1: Involves only one named structure of the larynx
  • T2: Involves more than one named structure
  • T3: Fixed or immobile vocal cord. Also includes invasion of the pre-epiglottic space or paraglottic space.
  • T4: Indicates the tumor has expanded beyond the larynx.
    • T4a: Involves invasion of the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, or extra-laryngeal extension into neck structures like the thyroid gland or neck muscles (strap muscles).
    • T4b: Involves carotid artery involvement or invasion of the prevertebral space. These are considered very advanced and often inoperable.

Management based on tumour staging

Explanation of other options:

Conservative laryngectomy (Option C): Conservation laryngeal surgery aims to preserve voice and avoid a permanent tracheal opening. However, only carefully selected cases are suitable for this approach. In the present case, conservative laryngectomy is not done as radiotherapy is the preferred first-line treatment for early-stage vocal cord cancer (T1 N0 M0) with no lymphatic spread.

Chemotherapy (Option D): For stage III and IV laryngeal cancers, induction chemotherapy with radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiation offers effective organ preservation with better locoregional control compared to surgery. However, since concurrent chemoradiation has higher toxicity, proper case selection is crucial.

question_text: What is the stage of laryngeal carcinoma show:

T4aN1M0: This indicates a locally advanced tumor with the following Characteristics:

  • T4a: The tumor has invaded through the thyroid cartilage, which is a major structure in the larynx.
  • N1: Regional lymph nodes are involved, indicating spread to nearby lymph nodes.
  • M0: There is no evidence of distant metastasis.

Walsham forceps are specifically designed for closed reduction of nasal bone fractures.

question_text: The image below depicts a surgical procedure performed on the patient. Identify the procedure.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a tracheostomy procedure, in which a surgical opening is created in the trachea to establish an airway.

Tracheostomy

A tracheostomy is a surgical procedure in which an opening is created in the neck directly into the trachea to provide an airway when the upper airway is blocked or compromised.

The procedure involves making an incision below the vocal cords and inserting a tracheostomy tube.


Complications of Tracheostomy

Immediate complications:

  • Hemorrhage: Most common; bleeding from vessels like the anterior jugular or thyroid vessels.
  • Surgical emphysema: Air collects under the skin if tracheal air leaks or skin sutures are too tight.
  • Apnea: Temporary cessation of breathing due to rapid CO2 washout.
  • Pneumothorax: Rare; more common in children due to injury to the apical pleura.
  • Loss of voice: Air bypasses the vocal cords, preventing normal phonation.

Late complications:

  • Infection: At the tracheostomy site due to poor hygiene or dressing care.
  • Subglottic stenosis: Narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords from trauma or infection.

Explanation of other options:

Endotracheal intubation (Option A): Endotracheal intubation involves placing a tube into the trachea via the mouth or nose, without any surgical neck incision.

Needle cricothyroidotomy (Option B): An emergency procedure in which a needle is inserted through the cricothyroid membrane to provide temporary airway access, not a permanent opening like a tracheostomy.

Oropharyngeal airway (Option D): It is a mouth-inserted device that maintains airway patency in unconscious patients, without any surgical incision or permanent airway creation.

question_text: What is the probable cause of surgical emphysema in a patient following an emergency tracheostomy?
explanation:
Explanation:
Surgical emphysema (subcutaneous air) post-tracheostomy occurs when air leaks from the airway into the subcutaneous tissues of the neck. The most common cause is a tear in the posterior tracheal wall created during the procedure. This allows air from the trachea to escape into the paratracheal fascia and then dissect through the subcutaneous planes of the neck and chest.

Explanation of other options:
High tracheostomy (Option A): A high incision (above the 2nd tracheal ring) risks injury to the cricoid cartilage and subglottic stenosis, but it is not a direct cause of surgical emphysema.
Block in tracheostomy (Option C): A blocked tube would cause respiratory distress and failure to ventilate, not subcutaneous air.
Tight suture around tracheostomy site (Option D): Over-tight skin sutures can cause skin necrosis or impair healing but do not typically allow air to track into subcutaneous tissues.

Key Takeaways:

  • Surgical emphysema after tracheostomy suggests an air leak, most commonly from an iatrogenic injury to the posterior tracheal wall.
  • The posterior tracheal wall is vulnerable as it is thin and lies immediately anterior to the esophagus.

question_text: A child is brought to the ER with sudden onset of respiratory distress, cough, inability to speak after consumption of apple. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

A child with sudden onset of respiratory distress and cough after consumption of apple likely has Foreign Body Aspiration. The most appropriate first step in management of this patient would be Heimlich Maneuver. Management of Foreign Body Aspiration is as follows:

  • Conscious Patient (Partial Obstruction): Encourage coughing to clear the airway.
  • Conscious Patient (Complete Obstruction):
    • Infants (<1 year): Alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts. (No abdominal thrusts).
    • Children (>1 year) & Adults: Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver).
    • Pregnant/Obese: Sternal thrusts.
  • Unresponsive Patient: Immediately start CPR (chest compressions); check airway after 30 compressions.
  • Medical Intervention (if basic measures fail):
    • Direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps or suction for visible objects.
    • Cricothyrotomy for supraglottic obstruction.
    • Endotracheal intubation to push object into mainstem bronchus for temporary ventilation (if subglottic).
    • Bronchoscopy (rigid) is the definitive procedure for diagnosis and removal, especially for suspected partial obstructions or if basic measures fail.

Explanation of Other Options:

CPR (Option A)

CPR is reserved for unconscious patients who are not breathing or have no pulse. In this case, the child is still conscious.

Endoscopy (Option B)

Endoscopic removal of foreign bodies is definitive management, but not the first step. It should be done after initial resuscitation or if Heimlich fails.

Blind finger sweep (Option D)

Dangerous and outdated. Blind sweeps can push the object further into the airway and should never be performed, especially in children.

Key Takeaway:

In a conscious child with complete airway obstruction after food ingestion (inability to speak/cough), the Heimlich maneuver is the immediate life-saving intervention.

question_text: Following a building collapse, a male patient was brought to the emergency department with a copious amount of debris in the mouth, making endotracheal intubation impossible. The emergency procedure shown in the image was performed. Which of the following statements regarding this procedure is true?
option_a: It is used for effective ventilation for up to 6 hours
option_b: It is used to measure central venous pressure
option_c: It should be followed by a tracheostomy
option_d: The work of breathing is more than with bag-and-mask ventilation
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a needle cricothyroidotomy, a rescue procedure for a "Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate" (CICO) airway emergency.

  • This is a temporary, life-saving measure that is not a definitive airway; therefore, it must be converted to a formal surgical airway, such as a tracheostomy, as soon as the patient is stabilized.
  • This procedure allows for emergency oxygenation but is inadequate for effective ventilation (CO2removal) and can only be used for a very short duration (30-45 minutes), not hours (Option A ruled out).
  • It accesses the airway through the cricothyroid membrane and has no connection to the central venous system, so it cannot be used to measure central venous pressure (Option B ruled out).
  • As it is performed to bypass a complete upper airway obstruction where bag-and-mask ventilation has failed, it dramatically decreases the work of breathing (Option D ruled out).
